lessons.title: What an Operating System Is
lessons.content:
Imagine a busy school with a thousand students, forty classrooms, one playground, one library and one small canteen. If nobody was in charge, every class would rush into the same room, two teachers would fight over one blackboard, and the canteen line would never end. So the school has a headmaster and an office. They decide which class sits in which room, who uses the playground when, and who gets the library at what time. A computer has the same problem. Many programs want the same CPU, the same memory, the same disk and the same screen. The part of the computer that acts like the headmaster and the office is called the operating system, or OS for short.

What it is: An operating system is a program that sits between the hardware and all the other programs. It manages the hardware, shares it fairly and safely among programs, and gives programs and people a simpler, friendlier way to use the machine. Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS are all operating systems. When you switch on your phone and see the home screen, the OS has already been working for several seconds.

Two ways to look at an OS: Textbooks describe the OS from two views. The first view is the OS as a resource manager. The computer has resources: CPU time, memory space, storage space and input/output devices like the keyboard, network card and printer. The OS decides who gets what, for how long, and makes sure nobody grabs more than their share or touches what belongs to someone else. The second view is the OS as an extended machine. Raw hardware is ugly. To read a file from a disk directly, you would have to talk to the disk controller, give block numbers, wait for interrupts and handle errors. The OS hides all of this and gives you a neat idea called a file, so a program just says "open notes.txt and read it". The OS turns the ugly real machine into a nicer, imaginary one.

The kernel: The OS is not one single blob. Its heart is called the kernel. The kernel is the part that is always running in memory, has full control of the hardware, and does the most important jobs: running programs, sharing memory, talking to devices. Around the kernel there are system programs like the file manager, the command shell and settings apps. When people say "Linux", they often mean only the kernel; a full system like Ubuntu adds many programs around it.

What happens without an OS: In the very first computers of the 1940s and early 1950s, there was no OS at all. A programmer booked the whole machine for, say, one hour, walked in with a stack of punched cards, loaded the program by hand, and watched lights blink. If the program finished in ten minutes, the expensive machine sat idle for fifty minutes. If it had a bug, the hour was wasted. The history of operating systems is mostly the story of people trying to stop this waste.

Batch systems: The first fix was batch processing. An operator collected many jobs, put similar ones together into a batch, and a small program called a resident monitor loaded and ran them one after another automatically. No more waiting for each programmer to walk in. But there was still a big waste: when a job waited for a slow card reader or tape, the CPU did nothing.

Multiprogramming: The next big idea was multiprogramming. Keep several jobs in memory at the same time. When job A has to wait for input or output, the OS switches the CPU to job B. When B waits, switch to C. The CPU stays busy almost all the time. Think of a cook in a Dhaka restaurant: while the rice is boiling, she does not stand and stare at the pot; she cuts onions for the next dish. Multiprogramming needs the OS to manage memory for several jobs and to decide which job runs next, which is called CPU scheduling. Both are big topics in this course.

Time-sharing: Batch and multiprogramming kept the CPU busy, but a programmer still had to wait hours for results. Time-sharing, also called multitasking, solved that. The OS switches between users or programs so fast, many times a second, that every user feels they have the whole computer. You type a command and get an answer within a second. Your laptop does this today: music plays, a browser loads a page and a download runs, all seemingly at once, even on a single CPU core, because the OS switches between them every few milliseconds.

Personal computers and phones: In the late 1970s and 1980s computers became small and cheap enough for one person. Operating systems like MS-DOS, and later Windows and Mac OS, were built for a single user who cares most about ease of use. Then came smartphones. Android, which is built on the Linux kernel, and Apple's iOS are operating systems designed for touch screens, batteries, cameras and mobile networks. Saving battery became as important as speed.

Types of operating systems: A batch OS runs jobs without user interaction, still used today for big payroll or bank jobs that run at night. A time-sharing or multitasking OS lets many programs or users share the machine interactively; Windows, Linux and macOS are examples. A real-time OS must finish tasks within strict deadlines. In a hard real-time system, like an airbag controller or a pacemaker, missing a deadline is a failure. In a soft real-time system, like video streaming, missing a deadline just lowers quality. A distributed OS manages a group of networked computers so they look like one system to the user. An embedded OS runs inside devices like washing machines, routers and smart TVs, usually small and focused on one job. A mobile OS runs phones and tablets.

The two big worries: Once many programs share one machine, two worries appear again and again in this course. The first is sharing: how do we split time and space fairly and efficiently, so the machine does lots of useful work and nobody waits too long? The second is protection: how do we stop one program, by mistake or on purpose, from crashing another program, reading its secrets or hogging the whole machine? A good OS answers both. It is like a good hostel superintendent who makes sure everyone gets their turn in the dining hall and also that nobody walks into someone else's room.

Main jobs of an OS: Let us list the jobs this course will study one by one. Process management: creating and stopping running programs, and deciding which one gets the CPU. Memory management: giving each program its own memory and keeping programs from stepping on each other. Storage and file management: organising data into files and folders on disks and SSDs. Device or I/O management: talking to keyboards, screens, network cards and printers through drivers. Protection and security: making sure programs and users only touch what they are allowed to. And the user interface: a command line or a graphical screen through which people talk to the computer.

Real-life example 1, your Android phone: Say you are on a Pathao ride, listening to music on your phone while checking bKash and replying on Messenger. The music app, bKash, Messenger and the Maps app are all running. The Android OS gives each app a slice of CPU time in turn, so they all appear to run together. It gives each app its own private memory, so a bug in a game cannot read your bKash PIN. When memory gets full, it quietly closes apps you have not used for a while. When a message arrives, the network hardware raises a signal, and the OS wakes up Messenger. When the battery is low, it slows background apps. You never see any of this, which is exactly the point.

Real-life example 2, a bank server at night: A bank in Motijheel runs an end-of-day job that calculates interest for millions of accounts. Nobody sits and clicks; the job is queued and runs on a Linux server, much like old batch processing. At the same time, the same server answers ATM requests from all over the country. The OS must give the interactive ATM requests quick responses while the big batch job uses the leftover CPU time. It must also make sure the two jobs never write to the same account record at the same moment, which is a synchronisation problem we will study later.

Why study operating systems: Every program you will ever write runs on top of an OS. If you understand how the OS schedules threads, you write faster programs. If you understand memory and paging, you understand why your app crashes with "out of memory" or why a laptop gets slow when too many Chrome tabs are open. If you understand files and disks, you understand why saving can fail or why a sudden power cut can corrupt data. Jobs in backend development, cloud computing, embedded systems, cybersecurity and game development all need this knowledge. Interview questions about deadlock, threads and virtual memory are very common.

How this course is organised: First we look at what the OS offers and how it is built, including how programs safely ask the kernel for help through system calls. Then we spend many lessons on processes and threads: how they are created, how they talk, and how the CPU is shared through scheduling algorithms like FCFS, SJF and Round Robin, with many worked Gantt charts. Next comes synchronisation: what goes wrong when two threads change the same data, and tools like locks, semaphores and monitors to fix it. Then deadlocks, where processes wait for each other forever, including the famous banker's algorithm. After that comes memory: paging, virtual memory and page replacement with worked examples. Finally we cover disks, file systems, input/output, protection and virtual machines.

Common mistakes: Many students think the OS is just the desktop with icons. The desktop is only the user interface; the real OS work happens underneath. Another mistake is thinking multitasking on one core means programs truly run at the same instant. On one core only one runs at any instant; they take turns very fast. A third mistake is mixing up the kernel with the whole OS. In exams you will often be asked to define an OS, list its functions, compare batch, time-sharing and real-time systems, and explain the difference between multiprogramming and multitasking.

Recap: An operating system is the manager of the computer. It shares the CPU, memory, storage and devices among programs, protects them from each other, and gives a simpler view of the machine. Its core is the kernel. OS history went from no OS, to batch systems, to multiprogramming, to time-sharing, to personal and mobile systems, each step reducing waste and improving the user experience. In the next lesson we look at the services an OS provides and the different ways kernels are built.
key_points: An operating system sits between hardware and programs: it manages resources and gives a simpler view of the machine.
The two classic views are the OS as a resource manager and the OS as an extended (easier) machine.
The kernel is the core part of the OS that is always in memory and has full control of the hardware.
Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU switches to another job when one waits for I/O.
Time-sharing switches between programs so quickly that each user feels they have the whole computer.
Hard real-time systems must never miss a deadline; soft real-time systems only lose quality when they do.
Main OS jobs: process, memory, storage/file and I/O management, protection and security, and the user interface.
lessons.tip: For every topic in this course, ask two questions: what resource is being shared, and what could go wrong if the OS did not manage it? Almost every OS idea is an answer to one of those questions.
lessons.task: Open the Task Manager on Windows (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), Activity Monitor on a Mac, or Settings > Developer options > Running services on Android. Count how many processes are running, find the one using the most memory, and write down three things the OS is managing for them right now.

quiz.q: What is the main reason multiprogramming was invented?
options: To let a programmer debug faster
To keep the CPU busy by switching to another job when one waits for I/O
To add a graphical user interface
quiz.explain: In multiprogramming, several jobs sit in memory. When the running job waits for slow I/O, the OS gives the CPU to another job, so the CPU is rarely idle.

quiz.q: Which part of the operating system is always in memory and has full control of the hardware?
quiz.explain: The kernel is the core of the OS. It stays in memory and directly controls the CPU, memory and devices. Other system programs run around it.

quiz.q: An airbag controller must react within a few milliseconds every single time. What kind of OS does it need?
quiz.explain: Missing the deadline for an airbag is a failure, so it needs a hard real-time OS. Soft real-time systems, like video streaming, only lose quality when late.

quiz.q: On a laptop with a single CPU core, music plays while a web page loads. What is really happening?
options: Both programs run at exactly the same instant on the one core
The OS switches the core between the programs many times a second
The music program runs on the disk instead of the CPU
The web page waits until the song ends
quiz.explain: One core can run only one program at an instant. Time-sharing switches between them every few milliseconds, so they look simultaneous.

quiz.q: Viewing the OS as an "extended machine" means what?
options: The OS adds more RAM to the computer
The OS makes the hardware physically bigger
The OS hides ugly hardware details behind simpler ideas like files
The OS connects several computers into one
quiz.explain: As an extended machine, the OS gives programs easy abstractions, like files and processes, instead of making them deal with raw disk controllers and interrupts.

lessons.title: OS Services and Structure
lessons.content:
Think of a big government office like a passport office in Agargaon. You, the citizen, never walk into the back room and print your own passport. You go to a counter, fill in a form, and the staff behind the counter do the real work using machines you are not allowed to touch. The counter is a clear, fixed set of services: submit an application, take your photo, check your status, collect your passport. An operating system works the same way. It offers a fixed set of services through a counter, and programs ask for those services instead of touching the hardware themselves. In this lesson we look at what services an OS offers and at the different ways the inside of an OS, the back room, can be organised.

Services for users and programs: Some OS services exist mainly to help users and programs get work done. Program execution: the OS loads a program into memory, runs it and ends it, normally or with an error. I/O operations: programs cannot drive devices directly, so the OS does reading and writing for them. File-system manipulation: create, delete, read, write, search and list files and folders, and manage permissions. Communication: let processes exchange information, either on the same computer or across a network. Error detection: notice problems such as a memory error, a disk failure, a printer out of paper or a program dividing by zero, and take sensible action.

Services for the system itself: Other services exist to keep the whole system running well when many users and programs share it. Resource allocation: decide who gets CPU time, memory and devices. Logging and accounting: keep track of which user or program used how much, for billing or for spotting problems. Protection and security: make sure processes cannot interfere with each other, users must log in, and outside attackers are kept out. These are like the office's own rules and record keeping, which the public never sees but which keep things fair.

User interfaces: People reach the OS through an interface. A command-line interface, or CLI, lets you type commands. The program that reads your commands is called a shell; bash and zsh on Linux and macOS, and PowerShell on Windows, are shells. If you type ls in a Linux shell, it lists the files in the folder. A graphical user interface, or GUI, gives windows, icons, menus and a mouse pointer. A touch interface on phones uses taps and swipes. Many power users still prefer the CLI because one short command can do what takes twenty clicks, and commands can be saved in scripts and run again.

System programs: Between the kernel and your apps sit system programs, also called utilities. They include file managers, text editors, compilers, program loaders, network tools and status tools like a task manager. Most users judge an OS by these programs and its interface, even though they are not the kernel.

Policy and mechanism: A very useful design idea is to separate mechanism from policy. The mechanism is how something is done; the policy is what will be done or who decides. For example, a timer that can interrupt the CPU every 10 milliseconds is a mechanism. The rule "give each program 10 milliseconds, then switch" is a policy. If the two are kept separate, the policy can be changed later without rewriting the mechanism. Exam questions love this pair, so remember: mechanism equals how, policy equals what.

Why structure matters: A modern OS kernel has millions of lines of code. The Linux kernel source is well over twenty million lines today, much of it device drivers. Such a huge program must be organised, or nobody can understand, test or fix it. There are several classic ways to structure an OS, each with trade-offs between speed, safety and ease of change.

Simple or monolithic structure: In a monolithic kernel, almost all OS services, such as scheduling, memory management, file systems and device drivers, live together in one big program that runs in kernel mode, the powerful mode we will meet in the next lesson. Every part can call every other part directly, like functions in one program. This is fast, because there is no extra message passing. The weakness is that a bug in any part, even one small driver, can crash the whole system, and the code is harder to maintain. The original UNIX and Linux are monolithic kernels. MS-DOS was even simpler, with almost no separation at all, so one bad program could crash the whole machine.

Layered structure: In a layered design, the OS is split into layers like floors of a building. Layer 0 is the hardware. Each higher layer uses only the services of the layers below it. For example, layer 1 might handle CPU scheduling, layer 2 memory, layer 3 device communication, and so on up to the user interface at the top. The big advantage is that each layer can be built and tested on its own, starting from the bottom. The disadvantages are that it is hard to decide the right order of layers, since real parts often need each other, and every request has to pass down through several layers, which slows things down. Pure layered systems are rare today, but the idea of layers is used everywhere.

Microkernel structure: A microkernel moves as much as possible out of the kernel. The kernel keeps only the bare minimum: basic process and thread handling, a little memory management and communication between processes. File systems, device drivers and network stacks run as normal user programs, called servers. When an app wants to read a file, it sends a message to the file server through the microkernel, and the reply comes back the same way. Advantages: the kernel is tiny and easier to verify; if a driver crashes, it can be restarted without bringing down the system; adding new services is easy. Disadvantage: all that message passing costs time, so performance can suffer. Mach, MINIX 3 and QNX are well-known microkernels; QNX is used in car systems.

Modular structure: Most modern kernels use loadable kernel modules. The core kernel is small-ish, and extra parts, such as a driver for a new USB device or a new file system, can be loaded into the kernel while it is running, and unloaded when not needed. Modules run in kernel mode and call each other directly, so they are fast like a monolithic kernel, but the design stays tidy like a layered one. Linux uses modules heavily; you can list loaded modules with the command lsmod.

Hybrid structure: Real operating systems mix these ideas, so they are called hybrid. Windows has a kernel that is mostly monolithic for speed but borrows ideas from microkernels, such as separate subsystems. Apple's macOS and iOS are built on a kernel called XNU, which combines the Mach microkernel with parts of BSD UNIX, all running in kernel mode for speed. Android uses the Linux kernel, on top of which sits a layer of libraries and the Android runtime, and then the app framework and apps. Remember the lesson from this: there is no single perfect structure; designers mix ideas to balance speed, safety and flexibility.

Booting the computer: When you press the power button, memory is empty, so how does the OS get running? Step one: the CPU starts executing a small program stored in firmware on the motherboard. On older PCs this firmware was called BIOS; modern PCs use UEFI. Step two: the firmware runs a quick hardware check, often called POST, and finds a bootable device such as the SSD. Step three: it loads a boot loader from that device. On Linux the common boot loader is GRUB; Windows has its own Windows Boot Manager. Step four: the boot loader loads the kernel into memory and starts it. Step five: the kernel sets up memory management, detects devices, loads drivers and mounts the root file system. Step six: the kernel starts the first user process. On many Linux systems this is systemd, with process ID 1, which then starts all the background services and finally the login screen. A phone follows a similar chain, with its own firmware and boot loader.

A quick worked comparison: Suppose a file read request in a monolithic kernel costs 1 unit of overhead, because it is a direct function call inside the kernel. In a microkernel, the same request might go app to kernel, kernel to file server, file server to kernel, and kernel back to app, which is four crossings. If each crossing also costs about 1 unit, the microkernel spends roughly 4 units of overhead on the same request. The real numbers vary hugely between systems, and modern microkernels have made messages very cheap, but this simple count shows why monolithic designs were long preferred for speed and why microkernels are chosen when reliability matters more.

Real-life example 1, a Dhaka office building: Picture three companies. The first puts every department in one giant open hall where anyone can walk to anyone's desk. Work moves fast, but if one person spills tea on the main power board, the whole hall goes dark. That is a monolithic kernel. The second puts only a tiny reception in the middle, and every department sits in a separate locked room; all requests are passed as notes through reception. It is slower, but a fire in the accounts room does not stop the HR room. That is a microkernel. The third uses the open hall for the core teams, but lets contractors set up a desk for a few days and leave when the job is done. That is a modular kernel.

Real-life example 2, plugging in a new printer: You plug a new USB printer into a Linux laptop in your university lab. The kernel notices the new device, finds a matching driver module and loads it into the running kernel without a reboot. The printing system, which is a system program, then makes the printer appear in your print menu. When you unplug it, the module can be unloaded. On an old MS-DOS machine you might have needed to edit configuration files and restart the computer.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think a microkernel is always slower, full stop. It usually has more overhead per request, but careful designs can be quite fast, and the reliability benefit can be worth it. Another mistake is calling Linux a microkernel; it is a monolithic kernel with loadable modules. Some also confuse the shell with the kernel; the shell is just a user program that reads commands. Typical exam questions: list OS services; compare monolithic, layered, microkernel and modular structures with advantages and disadvantages; explain mechanism versus policy with an example; describe the boot process.

Recap: The OS offers services for users, such as running programs, I/O, files, communication and error handling, and services for the system, such as resource allocation, accounting and protection. People reach these services through a CLI, GUI or touch interface. Inside, an OS can be monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular or a hybrid of these. When the computer starts, firmware loads a boot loader, the boot loader loads the kernel, and the kernel starts the first process. Next lesson: how a program actually crosses the counter and asks the kernel for help, using dual mode and system calls.
key_points: OS services help users (program execution, I/O, files, communication, error detection) and the system (resource allocation, accounting, protection).
A shell is a user program that reads commands; it is not the kernel.
Mechanism is how something is done; policy is what is done. Keeping them separate makes change easy.
A monolithic kernel puts all services in one kernel-mode program: fast, but one bug can crash everything.
A microkernel keeps only the minimum in the kernel and runs services as user-space servers: safer but with more message overhead.
Modern systems are hybrids: Linux is monolithic with loadable modules, macOS uses XNU (Mach plus BSD), Android runs on the Linux kernel.
Booting: firmware (BIOS/UEFI) runs, loads a boot loader, which loads the kernel, which starts the first user process.
lessons.tip: When comparing kernel structures in an exam, draw a small box picture for each one and write one advantage and one disadvantage under it. Pictures plus a trade-off line earn most of the marks.
lessons.task: If you have a Linux or macOS computer, open a terminal and type uname -a to see your kernel version. On Linux, also try lsmod to list loaded kernel modules. On Windows, open System Information and find the OS version and the BIOS mode (Legacy or UEFI). Write down what you found.

quiz.q: A timer that can interrupt the CPU every 10 ms is an example of what?
quiz.explain: The timer is the mechanism, the "how". Deciding to give each program 10 ms before switching is the policy, the "what".

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a microkernel?
options: It has no message passing at all
Every driver runs in kernel mode for speed
A crashed driver or service can be restarted without crashing the whole system
It never needs a boot loader
quiz.explain: In a microkernel, drivers and services run as separate user-space servers, so a failure in one does not bring down the kernel.

quiz.q: Which description best fits the Linux kernel?
options: A monolithic kernel with loadable modules
quiz.explain: Linux is monolithic, with most services in kernel mode, but it supports loadable kernel modules that can be added and removed while running.

quiz.q: In the boot process, what does the boot loader do?
options: It checks the hardware with POST
It loads the kernel into memory and starts it
It is the first user process with ID 1
quiz.explain: Firmware runs first and loads the boot loader; the boot loader, such as GRUB, loads the kernel and passes control to it.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of a layered OS design?
options: Each layer cannot be tested separately
It is hard to order the layers and requests must pass through many layers, adding overhead
It has no kernel at all
It cannot run on modern hardware
quiz.explain: Layers make testing easy, but deciding which layer goes below which is tricky, and passing through several layers slows each request.

lessons.title: Dual Mode, Interrupts and System Calls
lessons.content:
Imagine a bank branch in Gulshan. Customers can walk freely in the main hall, fill in forms and sit on the chairs. But the vault, the cash drawers and the computer that changes account balances are behind a locked door. Only staff can go there. If a customer wants money, they cannot walk into the vault; they hand a slip to the cashier at the counter, the cashier goes in, does the job safely, and comes back with the money. Computers use the same trick to stay safe. Normal programs live in the main hall, called user mode. The kernel lives behind the locked door, in kernel mode. And the counter slip is called a system call.

Why we need two modes: If every program could do anything, one buggy or evil program could wipe the disk, read another program's passwords, switch off the timer and keep the CPU forever, or talk to the network card directly and send anything. The OS cannot protect anybody unless the hardware itself helps. So modern CPUs support at least two modes of operation: user mode, where programs have limited power, and kernel mode, also called supervisor mode, system mode or privileged mode, where the OS has full power.

The mode bit: The CPU keeps a small piece of hardware state, often described as a mode bit, that says which mode it is in right now. In textbooks, kernel mode is often shown as 0 and user mode as 1. When the computer boots, it starts in kernel mode. The OS loads and then starts user programs in user mode. Whenever an interrupt, trap or system call happens, the hardware switches to kernel mode automatically and jumps to OS code. Before giving the CPU back to a user program, the OS switches back to user mode. The important thing: a user program cannot simply set the bit to kernel mode itself. The only way into kernel mode is through these controlled doors that lead straight into OS code.

Privileged instructions: Some machine instructions are marked privileged. They can only run in kernel mode. Examples are instructions that do I/O directly, change the memory management settings, turn interrupts on or off, set the timer, or halt the CPU. If a user program tries to run a privileged instruction, the CPU does not run it. Instead it raises a trap, the OS takes control, and usually it ends the misbehaving program with an error. Real CPUs often have more than two levels; x86 processors have four rings, numbered 0 to 3, but common operating systems mainly use ring 0 for the kernel and ring 3 for user programs. ARM processors have exception levels such as EL0 for apps and EL1 for the kernel.

The timer: There is one more danger. A user program could enter an endless loop like while(1){} and never give the CPU back. To prevent this, the OS sets a hardware timer before handing the CPU to a program. The timer counts down and, when it reaches zero, raises an interrupt. The interrupt forces the CPU into kernel mode and into the OS, which can then decide to let the program continue or switch to another one. Setting the timer is a privileged instruction, so the program cannot turn it off. This timer is the heartbeat that makes time-sharing possible.

Interrupts and traps, a quick recap: You met interrupts in Microprocessors. An interrupt is a signal from hardware, such as a key press, a disk finishing a read, or the timer, telling the CPU to stop what it is doing and run a handler. A trap, also called an exception, is caused by the running program itself: either by an error, such as dividing by zero or touching an illegal address, or on purpose, by a special instruction that asks the OS for a service. That purposeful trap is how system calls work. A modern OS is said to be interrupt-driven: most of the time the kernel is not running at all; it wakes up only when an interrupt, trap or system call needs it.

What a system call is: A system call is the programming interface through which a user program asks the kernel to do something it cannot do itself. Opening a file, reading from the keyboard, creating a new process, sending data on the network, asking for more memory and getting the current time are all system calls. Every OS has a fixed list of them. Linux has a few hundred; each has a number. For example, on 64-bit x86 Linux, read is system call number 0 and write is number 1.

Step by step, a system call: Suppose your C program calls read(fd, buf, 100) to read 100 bytes from a file. Step one: your code calls the read function in the C library, which is ordinary user code. Step two: the library puts the system call number for read in a particular CPU register and the three arguments in other registers. Step three: it runs a special trap instruction; on modern x86-64 Linux that is the syscall instruction. Step four: the hardware switches to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed entry point inside the kernel, which the kernel set up at boot. Step five: the kernel looks up the number in its system call table, a table of function pointers, and calls the matching kernel function. Step six: that function checks the arguments, for example that the buffer address really belongs to your program, then does the work, possibly asking the disk for data and putting your process to sleep until it arrives. Step seven: the result, such as the number of bytes read, or an error code, is placed in a register. Step eight: the CPU switches back to user mode and returns to the library, which returns to your code.

Passing parameters: There are three common ways to pass arguments to a system call. Registers are fastest, used when there are only a few arguments. If there are many, the program can store them in a block in memory and pass the address of the block in one register. Or the arguments can be pushed onto the stack and popped by the OS. Linux on x86-64 uses registers for up to six arguments.

API versus system call: Programmers rarely make system calls directly. They use an API, an application programming interface, such as the POSIX API on Linux and macOS or the Windows API. The API functions are in libraries like the C library, glibc. Some API functions are thin wrappers around one system call, like read. Others do more: printf formats your text in user space and then, usually when its buffer is full or a newline is printed to a terminal, calls write. Some API functions, like strlen or sqrt, never call the kernel at all. Using an API makes programs portable, because the same API can sit on top of different systems, and it hides messy details.

Types of system calls: Textbooks usually group them into six types. Process control: create and end processes, load and run programs, wait for a process, allocate memory; on Linux fork, exec, exit, wait. File management: create, delete, open, close, read, write files; open, read, write, close, unlink. Device management: request and release devices, read and write them; ioctl is a Linux example. Information maintenance: get or set time, date and system data; getpid, time, uname. Communication: create connections, send and receive messages, share memory; pipe, socket, shmget. Protection: get and set permissions; chmod, chown, umask. Windows has its own names for similar calls, such as CreateProcess, ReadFile and WriteFile.

The cost of crossing: Switching into the kernel and back is not free. The CPU must save some registers, switch mode, possibly switch to a kernel stack and do safety checks. A system call takes much longer than a normal function call, often hundreds of nanoseconds or more depending on the hardware and the call. That is why libraries buffer data: instead of calling write once for each character, printf collects many characters and writes them with one system call. If you write a program that reads a 1 MB file one byte at a time with read, you make about a million system calls; reading in 4 KB chunks needs only 256. That simple change can make the program many times faster.

Real-life example 1, sending a bKash payment: You tap Send Money in the bKash app. The app cannot touch the phone's modem or Wi-Fi chip directly, because it runs in user mode. It calls Android's networking library, which in the end makes system calls on the Linux kernel, such as calls on a socket to send data. The kernel checks that the app has permission to use the internet, hands the data to the network driver, and the driver talks to the hardware. When the server replies, the network chip raises an interrupt, the kernel collects the data, and the app's waiting read returns. Every step of crossing between app and kernel goes through the controlled door.

Real-life example 2, a student's infinite loop: In a C lab at your university, a classmate writes a loop that never ends and runs it on a shared Linux server. Without the timer, the whole server would freeze for everyone. Instead, the timer interrupt fires every few milliseconds, the kernel takes control and gives the CPU to other users' programs too. The server only gets a bit slower. When the teacher presses Ctrl+C, the terminal sends a signal and the kernel ends that program. If the program had tried to run a privileged instruction like halting the CPU, the CPU would have trapped and the kernel would have killed it at once.

Common mistakes and exam questions: A common mistake is to think a system call is just a normal function call. It is a trap into the kernel with a mode switch, which is why it is slower and safer. Another is thinking the OS runs all the time like a normal program; it is interrupt-driven and runs only when needed. Students also confuse interrupts, which come from hardware, with traps, which come from the running program. Typical exam questions: why is dual mode needed; list privileged instructions; explain the steps of a system call with a diagram; compare API and system call; name the six types of system calls with examples; explain why a timer is needed.

Recap: Hardware gives two modes, user mode for programs and kernel mode for the OS, tracked by a mode bit. Privileged instructions only run in kernel mode, and the only way in is through interrupts, traps and system calls. A timer interrupt stops any program from keeping the CPU forever. A system call puts a number and arguments in registers, traps into the kernel, which looks up the system call table, does the work and returns. Programmers usually use an API, like POSIX through the C library, which wraps system calls. Next lesson: the most important idea of the OS, the process.
key_points: CPUs have user mode for programs and kernel mode for the OS; a mode bit records the current mode.
Privileged instructions (I/O, timer, interrupt control, memory settings, halt) run only in kernel mode; trying them in user mode causes a trap.
The only ways into kernel mode are interrupts, traps (exceptions) and system calls, which jump to fixed OS code.
A hardware timer interrupt stops any program from keeping the CPU forever and makes time-sharing possible.
A system call places a call number and arguments in registers, executes a trap instruction, and the kernel uses its system call table to run the right function.
APIs such as POSIX or the Windows API wrap system calls in library functions and make programs portable.
Six types of system calls: process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, communication and protection.
lessons.tip: Draw the system call journey once as a picture with two halves, user mode above and kernel mode below, and number the arrows. If you can redraw it from memory, you can answer almost any system call question.
lessons.task: On Linux, run strace -c ls in a terminal to count every system call the ls command makes, then look at which calls appear most. On macOS or Windows without strace, write a list of six things your phone did in the last minute, like playing a song, and guess which type of system call each one needed.

quiz.q: What happens when a user-mode program tries to execute a privileged instruction?
options: The CPU switches to kernel mode and runs the instruction for it
The CPU traps to the OS, which usually ends the program
quiz.explain: Privileged instructions are only allowed in kernel mode. In user mode the CPU raises a trap, and the OS normally terminates the program.

quiz.q: Why does the OS set a hardware timer before giving the CPU to a program?
options: To measure how long the computer has been on
To make sure the OS gets control back even if the program never gives up the CPU
quiz.explain: The timer raises an interrupt when it reaches zero, forcing the CPU into the kernel. This stops infinite loops from freezing the system.

quiz.q: Which of these is a system call in Linux, rather than a library-only function?
quiz.explain: write is a system call that asks the kernel to send bytes to a file or device. strlen and sqrt never enter the kernel, and printf only uses write when it flushes its buffer.

quiz.q: A program reads a 1 MB file one byte per read call. Roughly how many system calls does it make, compared with reading 4 KB chunks?
quiz.explain: 1 MB is 1,048,576 bytes, so one byte at a time needs about a million calls. 1,048,576 / 4096 = 256 calls with 4 KB chunks.

quiz.q: In the system call steps, what is the system call table used for?
options: Finding the kernel function that matches the system call number
Recording how long each process has run
Keeping the list of open windows
quiz.explain: The table is an array of function pointers. The kernel uses the system call number as an index to find and run the right kernel function.

lessons.title: Processes
lessons.content:
Think of a recipe for biryani written in your mother's cookbook. The recipe itself is just words on paper. It does nothing. But when your mother actually starts cooking, there is a pot on the stove, rice half soaked, meat marinating, a timer running, and she remembers which step she is on. That live cooking, with all its ingredients and its current step, is very different from the recipe on the page. In computers, the recipe is a program, and the live cooking is a process. The process is the single most important idea in an operating system.

Program versus process: A program is a passive thing: a file on disk full of instructions, like chrome.exe or a.out. A process is a program in execution: an active thing with its own memory, its own current position in the code, open files and other resources. One program can have many processes. If you open Notepad three times, you have one program and three processes, each with its own text. If three students on a shared server run the same compiler, that is one program and three separate processes. A program becomes a process when it is loaded into memory and started.

What a process contains: A process is more than its code. It has the program counter, which tells the CPU the address of the next instruction to run. It has the contents of the CPU registers. It has its memory, divided into sections. It has a list of open files and network connections. It has an identity, a number called the process ID or PID, and it knows which user owns it. And it has bookkeeping like how much CPU time it has used.

Memory layout of a process: The memory of a process is usually drawn as a tall box, with low addresses at the bottom and high addresses at the top. At the bottom is the text section, which holds the machine code. Above it is the data section, which holds global and static variables. In C, int count = 5; written outside any function lives here. Above that is the heap, the area for memory allocated while the program runs, for example with malloc in C or new in C++ and Java. The heap grows upward as you allocate more. At the top is the stack, which holds function call information: parameters, local variables and return addresses. Each time a function is called, a new stack frame is pushed; when it returns, the frame is popped. The stack grows downward. The empty space between the heap and the stack lets both grow. If a recursive function calls itself forever, the stack keeps growing until it hits its limit, and you get the famous stack overflow error.

Tiny example: Look at this small C program: int g = 10; int main() { int x = 5; int *p = malloc(4); }. The variable g is in the data section. The code of main is in the text section. The local variable x and the pointer p themselves are on the stack, in the frame of main. The 4 bytes that p points to are on the heap. Exams love this kind of question: given code, say which section each variable lives in.

Process states: A process is not always running. As it executes, it changes state. The classic five-state model has these states. New: the process is being created. Ready: it is waiting in memory, fully able to run, but the CPU is busy with someone else. Running: its instructions are being executed on a CPU right now. Waiting, also called blocked: it cannot continue until some event happens, such as a disk read finishing, a key being pressed or a network packet arriving. Terminated: it has finished, and the OS is cleaning up. On one CPU core, only one process can be running at any instant, but many can be ready or waiting.

State transitions: Let us walk through the arrows between states. New to ready: the OS admits the process once it is set up. Ready to running: the scheduler picks this process, which is called being dispatched. Running to ready: the process is interrupted, for example its time slice runs out, and it goes back to the ready queue. Running to waiting: the process asks for I/O or waits for an event. Waiting to ready: the event happens, for example the disk read finishes, so the process is ready again. Notice that it goes to ready, not straight to running; it has to wait for its turn. Running to terminated: the process finishes or is killed. A very common exam trap: there is no arrow from waiting straight to running, and no arrow from ready to waiting, because a process must be running to ask for I/O.

The process control block: How does the OS remember everything about every process? For each process it keeps a data structure called the process control block, or PCB, sometimes called a task control block. In Linux it is a C structure called task_struct. The PCB holds the process state; the PID and parent's PID; the saved program counter and CPU registers; CPU scheduling information such as priority and pointers into scheduling queues; memory management information such as page tables or base and limit registers; accounting information such as CPU time used; and I/O status information such as the list of open files. The PCB is like the patient file a hospital keeps at the nurses' desk: anyone picking up the file knows the patient's state, history and what to do next.

Scheduling queues: The OS keeps PCBs in queues. The ready queue holds all processes that are ready to run. Each I/O device may have a wait queue of processes waiting for it. A process moves between these queues during its life: it sits in the ready queue, gets the CPU, asks for disk I/O and moves to the disk's wait queue, then comes back to the ready queue when the I/O finishes. Picture a queue diagram with circles and arrows, which you will often draw in exams.

The context switch: When the CPU moves from one process to another, the OS performs a context switch. The context of a process is everything needed to resume it later: mainly the registers, the program counter and memory management information. Step one: an interrupt or system call enters the kernel while process A is running. Step two: the kernel saves A's context into A's PCB. Step three: the scheduler picks process B. Step four: the kernel loads B's context from B's PCB. Step five: the CPU returns to user mode and continues B exactly where it left off. Later, A's context is reloaded and A continues as if nothing happened, just like a bookmark lets you continue a story book.

Context switch cost: A context switch is pure overhead: while switching, no user process does useful work. The direct cost is saving and loading registers, typically a few microseconds on modern hardware, depending on the system. There is also an indirect cost: the new process finds the CPU caches and the TLB full of the old process's data, so it runs slowly for a while until they warm up. That is why the OS should not switch too often. A worked example: if each time slice is 10 ms and each context switch costs 0.1 ms, then out of every 10.1 ms, 0.1 ms is wasted, which is about 1 percent. If the time slice were only 0.1 ms, half of all CPU time would be wasted on switching. We will use this idea again when we choose the time quantum for Round Robin.

CPU-bound and I/O-bound processes: Processes behave differently. An I/O-bound process spends most of its time waiting for I/O and only uses the CPU in short bursts; a text editor, a chat app or a web server waiting for requests are examples. A CPU-bound process spends most of its time computing and rarely does I/O, like a video encoder, a scientific simulation or a program calculating prime numbers. A good OS keeps a mix of both, so the CPU and the devices are all kept busy. If all processes were I/O-bound, the CPU would sit idle; if all were CPU-bound, the devices would sit idle.

Seeing processes yourself: You can watch all of this on a real machine. On Linux or macOS, the command ps aux lists every process with its PID, owner, CPU and memory use, and a letter for its state; for example R means running or runnable and S means sleeping, which is the waiting state. The command top shows the same list updating every few seconds. On Windows, Task Manager shows processes and their PIDs in the Details tab. Try it once and you will see dozens or even hundreds of processes, most of them sleeping quietly while they wait for something to happen.

Real-life example 1, a Daraz order: When you open the Daraz app, Android creates a process for it. You browse; the process is running. You tap to load product pictures; it asks the network for data and goes to waiting. Meanwhile Messenger, which was ready, gets the CPU. The pictures arrive, an interrupt fires, and the Daraz process goes back to ready, then running when its turn comes. If you switch to YouTube for long and memory gets tight, Android may kill the Daraz process; when you come back, the app may restart and restore your screen from saved state. That is why sometimes your cart page reloads.

Real-life example 2, a hospital doctor: A doctor in a busy Dhaka hospital sees many patients. While patient A goes for a blood test, the doctor does not wait; she writes notes in A's file and sees patient B. When A's report comes back, A joins the waiting line again. The doctor is the CPU, patients are processes, the blood test is I/O, and the patient file is the PCB. Picking up and reading a new file before seeing a patient is the context switch, and it costs a little time each time.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often say program and process are the same thing. They are not: one is a file, the other is a running activity. Another mistake is drawing an arrow from waiting directly to running. And many forget that local variables are on the stack, not the heap, even when they are pointers to heap memory. Typical questions: define process and distinguish from program; draw and explain the five-state diagram; list the contents of a PCB; explain a context switch with a diagram and why it is overhead; given code, show which memory section each variable is in.

Recap: A process is a program in execution, with its own program counter, registers and memory made of text, data, heap and stack sections. It moves through the states new, ready, running, waiting and terminated, following fixed transitions. The OS keeps everything about a process in its PCB and keeps PCBs in queues. Switching the CPU from one process to another is a context switch: save one PCB, load another. It is necessary but wasteful, so it should not happen too often. Next lesson: how processes are born and how they die, with fork, exec and wait.
key_points: A program is a passive file of instructions; a process is a program in execution with its own state and resources.
Process memory has four sections: text (code), data (globals), heap (dynamic memory, grows up) and stack (function frames, grows down).
The five states are new, ready, running, waiting (blocked) and terminated.
A waiting process goes to ready when its event happens, never straight to running.
The PCB stores the state, PID, saved program counter and registers, scheduling, memory, accounting and I/O information.
A context switch saves the old process's context into its PCB and loads the new one's; it is pure overhead.
I/O-bound processes use short CPU bursts; CPU-bound processes compute for long periods. A good mix keeps everything busy.
lessons.tip: Learn the five-state diagram by drawing it with your eyes closed: five boxes, six arrows. Then for each arrow, say one real event that causes it, like "time slice ran out" or "disk read finished".
lessons.task: Write a tiny C program with one global variable, one local variable, one malloc and a recursive function. Next to each line, write which memory section is used: text, data, heap or stack. If you have a computer, print the addresses with printf("%p") and check that heap and stack addresses are far apart.

quiz.q: A process is waiting for a disk read. The read finishes. Which state does it move to next?
quiz.explain: When the event a waiting process needs happens, it moves to the ready queue. It must wait for the scheduler before it runs again.

quiz.q: In C, where does a local variable declared inside main live?
quiz.explain: Local variables live in the stack frame of their function. Globals live in the data section, and memory from malloc lives on the heap.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT normally stored in a process control block?
options: The source code comments of the program
quiz.explain: The PCB holds state, PID, saved registers and program counter, scheduling, memory, accounting and I/O information. Source comments are not part of a running process at all.

quiz.q: Each time slice is 10 ms and a context switch costs 0.1 ms. About what fraction of CPU time is wasted on switching?
quiz.explain: For every 10 ms of work there is 0.1 ms of switching: 0.1 / 10.1 is about 0.0099, roughly 1 percent.

quiz.q: A video encoding program runs for minutes doing calculations and rarely reads files. What kind of process is it?
quiz.explain: A process that spends most of its time computing with long CPU bursts and little I/O is CPU-bound.

lessons.title: Process Creation and Termination
lessons.content:
Imagine a big joint family in Comilla. The grandfather is at the top. He has children, they have children, and soon you have a family tree with cousins, uncles and grandchildren. Everyone has a parent, except the grandfather at the very top. Processes in an operating system live in exactly this kind of family tree. Every process, except the very first one, is created by another process, its parent. In this lesson we see how a process is born, how it can turn into a completely different program, how a parent waits for its child, and what happens when things go wrong, like zombie and orphan processes.

The process tree: When a process creates another, the creator is the parent and the new one is the child. The child can create its own children, so processes form a tree. Each process has a unique number, the process ID or PID. It also knows its parent's ID, the PPID. On many Linux systems, the first user process started by the kernel is systemd with PID 1, and every other user process is its descendant. If you run the command pstree on Linux, it draws this tree for you. When you open a terminal and run a program, the terminal's shell is the parent and your program is its child.

Choices a parent has: When a parent creates a child, the OS designers must decide a few things. Resource sharing: the child may share all, some or none of the parent's resources such as open files. Execution: the parent may keep running at the same time as the child, or it may wait until the child finishes. Address space: the child may be a duplicate of the parent, running the same program, or it may load a brand new program. UNIX answers these questions with a few simple system calls: fork, exec, wait and exit.

fork: The fork system call creates a new process that is an almost exact copy of the caller. The child gets a copy of the parent's memory: same code, same variables with the same values, same open files. Both processes then continue running from the very next instruction after fork. So how can the code tell who is who? By the return value. In the child, fork returns 0. In the parent, fork returns the PID of the new child, which is a positive number. If fork fails, for example because the system has too many processes, it returns -1 in the parent and no child is made. That is a call that is entered once but returns twice, once in each process, which is the strangest and most important thing about fork.

A first fork example: Look at this C code: int x = 5; pid_t pid = fork(); if (pid == 0) { x = x + 1; printf("child %d", x); } else { wait(NULL); printf("parent %d", x); }. The child prints child 6. The parent waits for the child to finish and then prints parent 5. Why is the parent's x still 5? Because after fork the two processes have separate copies of memory. Changing x in the child does not touch x in the parent. They are like twins who each got their own copy of the same school book; scribbling in one book does not change the other.

Copy-on-write: Copying all the memory of a big process on every fork would be slow and wasteful, especially because the child often throws it away immediately to run a new program. Modern systems use copy-on-write. After fork, parent and child share the same physical memory pages, marked read-only. Only when one of them tries to write to a page does the OS make a private copy of that one page. Pages that are never written are never copied. We will see more about this in the virtual memory lessons.

Counting forks, worked: Exams love counting processes. Rule: each fork doubles the number of processes running that line, because every existing process runs it. Example one: fork(); fork(); printf("hi"); Start with 1 process. After the first fork, 2 processes. Both run the second fork, so 4 processes. All 4 print, so hi appears 4 times. Example two: for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) fork(); After the loop there are 2 times 2 times 2 = 8 processes in total, the original plus 7 new children. In general, n forks in a row give 2 to the power n processes and 2^n minus 1 newly created ones. Example three: if (fork() == 0) fork(); Only the child of the first fork runs the second fork, so we get 1 parent, 1 child and 1 grandchild, a total of 3 processes. Always ask which processes actually reach each fork line.

exec: Usually a child wants to run a different program, not a copy of the parent. The exec family of system calls, such as execl, execvp and execve, does this. Exec replaces the memory of the calling process with a new program loaded from disk: new code, new data, new heap and stack. The PID stays the same, and open files normally stay open. If exec succeeds, it never returns, because the old code that called it is gone. If it returns at all, something went wrong, such as a wrong file name. Think of it as a person who keeps their national ID number but completely changes their job and everything on their desk.

wait and exit: A process ends by calling exit with a status number, by convention 0 for success and non-zero for failure, or by returning from main, which calls exit for it. The OS then frees its memory, closes its files and releases its resources. But a little piece remains: the exit status and the PCB entry, kept so the parent can find out how the child ended. The parent collects this with the wait or waitpid system call. Wait blocks the parent until a child finishes, then returns the child's PID and status. Only after wait is the child's last trace removed.

How a shell runs your command: Now put it together. When you type ls in a terminal, the shell does three steps. Step one: it calls fork, making a copy of itself. Step two: the child calls exec to replace itself with the ls program. Step three: the parent shell calls wait, sleeps until ls finishes, and then shows the prompt again. If you type ls followed by an ampersand, the shell skips the wait and shows the prompt immediately, so ls runs in the background. This fork, exec, wait pattern is the backbone of UNIX.

Zombie processes: Suppose a child has exited, but its parent has not called wait yet. The child is dead; its memory is freed. But its PCB entry with the exit status is still kept, waiting to be collected. Such a process is called a zombie. A few zombies for a short time are normal. But if a buggy parent creates many children and never calls wait, zombies pile up, each holding a PID, and the system can eventually run out of PIDs. In the ps command, zombies show the state Z, sometimes with the word defunct. You cannot kill a zombie, because it is already dead; you fix it by making the parent call wait, or by ending the parent.

Orphan processes: The opposite case is when the parent ends before the child. The child is still running but has no parent. It is called an orphan. UNIX systems handle this by having the orphan adopted, traditionally by init, the process with PID 1, or on newer Linux systems possibly by a special subreaper process. The adopter regularly calls wait, so when the orphan finally exits, it does not stay a zombie forever. Some systems instead use cascading termination, where all children are killed when the parent dies.

Other ways a process ends: A process can also be ended by another process, usually its parent, using a signal. On Linux, the kill command sends a signal; kill -9 PID sends SIGKILL, which cannot be ignored. A parent might kill a child because the child used too many resources, its task is no longer needed, or the parent itself is exiting. The kernel can also kill a process that does something illegal, such as touching memory it does not own, which gives the famous segmentation fault.

Windows is different: Windows does not use fork. It uses CreateProcess, a single call that creates a new process and loads a given program into it in one step. It takes many parameters, including the program name, the command line, security settings and startup information. A parent can wait for it with WaitForSingleObject. Both approaches reach the same goal; UNIX splits it into two simple pieces, Windows does it in one bigger piece.

Real-life example 1, Chrome tabs: Chrome on your laptop uses many processes: typically a main browser process plus separate processes for renderers, extensions and other jobs. Each tab you open is usually handled by a renderer process, created by the main process. If one website's code crashes its renderer, you see a sad face in that tab, but the other tabs keep working, because they are in different processes with separate memory. When you close the tab, the main process ends that child and collects its exit status. The browser is using the process tree to keep one bad page from taking everything down.

Real-life example 2, a web server in Dhaka: A news website's server receives thousands of visitors during a cricket match. Some classic servers handle this with a parent process that creates a pool of worker children in advance. Each worker serves requests; if a worker crashes or gets too old, the parent notices through wait, collects its status and forks a fresh worker. The parent itself never handles visitors; it is just a careful manager. If the programmers forgot to call wait, the server would slowly fill up with zombies after every crash.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think the child starts running from the beginning of main after fork. It does not; it continues right after the fork call. Another mistake is thinking exec creates a new process; it only replaces the program inside the current process. Many also mix up zombies, which are dead but not collected, and orphans, which are alive without a parent. Typical exam questions: how many times is hello printed after a given set of forks; what does fork return in parent and child; explain fork, exec and wait in a shell; define zombie and orphan; compare fork with Windows CreateProcess.

Recap: Processes form a tree where each has a PID and a parent. fork makes a copy of the caller, returning 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent; copy-on-write makes it cheap. n forks in a row give 2^n processes. exec replaces the program inside a process and does not return on success. exit ends a process and wait lets the parent collect the exit status. A dead child not yet waited for is a zombie; a live child whose parent died is an orphan, adopted by PID 1 or a subreaper. Next lesson: how processes talk to each other.
key_points: Every process except the first has a parent; processes form a tree identified by PIDs.
fork creates a copy of the calling process: it returns 0 in the child, the child's PID in the parent and -1 on failure.
After fork, parent and child have separate memory, so a change in one does not affect the other; copy-on-write avoids copying until a write.
n forks in a row produce 2^n processes in total (2^n minus 1 new ones).
exec replaces the program in the current process; the PID stays the same and exec does not return on success.
A shell runs commands with fork, exec in the child, and wait in the parent.
A zombie is a finished child whose parent has not called wait; an orphan is a running child whose parent has ended.
lessons.tip: For any fork-counting question, draw a small tree on paper: each fork line splits every process that reaches it into two branches. Count the leaves at the end. Never try to do it only in your head.
lessons.task: Without a computer: draw the process tree for the code for (i = 0; i < 2; i++) { fork(); printf("A"); } and count how many times A is printed. Then, if you have Linux, compile and run it and check your answer (add a newline after A and fflush(stdout) to avoid buffering surprises).

quiz.q: What does fork() return in the child process?
quiz.explain: fork returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent. A return of -1 means fork failed and no child was created.

quiz.q: How many processes exist in total after this code runs: fork(); fork(); fork();
quiz.explain: Each fork doubles the number of processes: 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8. That is 2^3 = 8 in total, with 7 newly created.

quiz.q: A process calls exec successfully. What happens?
options: Its program is replaced by a new one, but its PID stays the same
A new child process is created with a new PID
quiz.explain: exec loads a new program into the current process, replacing its code and data. The PID stays the same and exec does not return.

quiz.q: A child process has exited but its parent never calls wait. What is the child called?
quiz.explain: A finished child whose exit status has not been collected by wait is a zombie. It keeps its PCB entry and PID until the parent waits.

quiz.q: Code: int x = 5; if (fork() == 0) x = x + 1; else { wait(NULL); printf("%d", x); } What does the parent print?
quiz.explain: After fork each process has its own copy of x. The child changes only its own copy, so the parent's x is still 5.

lessons.title: Inter-Process Communication
lessons.content:
Picture two shopkeepers at Newmarket who need to work together. One sells cloth, the other runs a tailoring shop next door. How can they share information? They could put up a shared whiteboard on the wall between their shops, where both can write and read. Or they could send each other written notes through a helper boy. Both ways work, but each has its own rules and risks. Processes in a computer face the same problem. Each process lives in its own private memory, protected from the others. So when two processes need to work together, the OS must give them a way to talk. This is called inter-process communication, or IPC.

Independent and cooperating processes: A process is independent if it cannot affect or be affected by other processes and shares no data with them. A process is cooperating if it can affect or be affected by others. Why would we want cooperating processes? Information sharing: several programs may need the same data, like a shared file or clipboard. Computation speed-up: a big job can be split into parts that run in parallel on several cores. Modularity: a system is easier to build as separate pieces, each doing one job. Convenience: a user may edit, compile and print at the same time, and these programs need to pass work along.

Two basic models: There are two fundamental IPC models. In the shared memory model, the processes agree on a region of memory that both can read and write. Once it is set up, they exchange data just by reading and writing memory, with no kernel help, so it is very fast. In the message passing model, processes send and receive messages through the kernel, using operations like send(message) and receive(message). It is simpler and safer, because the processes never touch each other's memory, and it works even across a network, but each message needs system calls, so it is slower for large amounts of data. Most operating systems support both.

Shared memory in detail: Normally the OS forbids one process from touching another's memory. With shared memory, the processes explicitly ask the OS to create a shared segment and attach it to their address spaces. On POSIX systems this is done with calls like shm_open and mmap, or the older System V calls shmget and shmat. After that, the OS steps back. The processes themselves are responsible for not stepping on each other, for example by not writing the same place at the same time. That is a synchronisation problem, which is the subject of several later lessons.

The producer-consumer problem: The classic example of cooperating processes is producer and consumer. The producer makes items, the consumer uses them. A compiler produces assembly code that an assembler consumes; a web server produces web pages that a browser consumes. To let them run at the same time, we put a buffer between them. With an unbounded buffer, the producer never has to wait. With a bounded buffer, which has a fixed size, the producer must wait when the buffer is full and the consumer must wait when it is empty.

Bounded buffer with a circular array: A common way to build a bounded buffer in shared memory is a circular array of size N with two indexes: in, the next free slot, and out, the next full slot. The buffer is empty when in equals out. The buffer is full when (in + 1) mod N equals out. Producer: while ((in + 1) % N == out) wait; buffer[in] = item; in = (in + 1) % N. Consumer: while (in == out) wait; item = buffer[out]; out = (out + 1) % N. Worked example with N = 5: start with in = 0, out = 0, empty. The producer adds items at slots 0, 1, 2, 3, so in becomes 4. Now (4 + 1) mod 5 = 0, which equals out, so the buffer is full, even though slot 4 is unused. This simple version can hold at most N minus 1 items. The consumer takes slot 0, out becomes 1, and now the producer can add again. Later lessons fix the wasted slot and the busy waiting using semaphores.

Message passing in detail: If processes P and Q want to talk by messages, they need a communication link and two operations, send and receive. Designers must make several choices about the link. Naming: in direct communication, each process names the other explicitly, as in send(Q, message) and receive(P, message). In indirect communication, messages go through a mailbox, also called a port: send(A, message) puts a message into mailbox A, and any process allowed to read A can receive it. Mailboxes allow many senders and many receivers.

Blocking or not: Send and receive can each be blocking, also called synchronous, or non-blocking, called asynchronous. A blocking send waits until the message is received. A non-blocking send drops the message and continues at once. A blocking receive waits until a message is available. A non-blocking receive returns either a message or nothing straight away. When both send and receive are blocking, the two processes meet at the moment of transfer; this is called a rendezvous.

Buffering: Messages wait in a queue attached to the link. With zero capacity, no message can wait, so the sender must block until the receiver takes it, which is a rendezvous. With bounded capacity of n messages, the sender only blocks when the queue is full. With unbounded capacity, the sender never blocks, though in real life memory always runs out somewhere.

Pipes: Pipes were one of the first IPC methods in UNIX and are still everywhere. An ordinary pipe is a one-way channel: one end for writing, one for reading. In C, pipe(fd) creates it, giving fd[0] for reading and fd[1] for writing. Usually a parent creates a pipe and then forks, so the child inherits both ends; the parent closes its read end and writes, the child closes its write end and reads. Ordinary pipes exist only between related processes and disappear when they finish. When you type ls | grep txt in a shell, the shell makes a pipe, runs ls with its output going into the pipe and grep with its input coming from it. Named pipes, called FIFOs in UNIX, have a name in the file system, so unrelated processes can use them, and they last until deleted. Windows has anonymous pipes and named pipes too.

Message queues: Besides pipes, POSIX systems offer message queues, created with mq_open and used with mq_send and mq_receive. Unlike a pipe, which is just a stream of bytes, a message queue keeps each message as a separate packet, so the receiver always gets whole messages, never half of one. Each message can also carry a priority number, and mq_receive hands back the oldest message of the highest priority first. This is the mailbox idea from above, built into the OS: several processes can send to the same queue, and the kernel keeps the messages safe until someone reads them.

Signals: A signal is a small notification sent to a process to tell it that some event happened. It carries almost no data, just a signal number. Pressing Ctrl+C in a terminal sends SIGINT; the kill command sends SIGTERM by default; dividing by zero causes SIGFPE; touching bad memory causes SIGSEGV; a child ending sends SIGCHLD to its parent. A process can handle most signals with its own handler function, ignore them, or let the default action happen, which is often to terminate. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored. Signals are like a doorbell: they tell you someone is there, but not much more.

Sockets and remote procedure calls: To talk across a network, processes use sockets. A socket is an endpoint for communication, identified by an IP address and a port number. A web server listens on port 80 for HTTP or 443 for HTTPS; your browser connects from its own socket. Sockets also work between processes on the same machine. Built on top of messages is the remote procedure call, or RPC: a program calls what looks like a normal function, but the arguments are packed into a message, sent to another machine, run there, and the result sent back. Modern systems such as gRPC follow this idea.

Shared memory versus message passing: Shared memory is faster for big data, since after setup there are no system calls, but processes must handle synchronisation themselves and it only works on one machine. Message passing is easier to get right, avoids conflicts because nothing is shared, and works across networks, but each message costs system calls and copying. A rule of thumb: use shared memory for large, frequent data between processes on the same machine; use messages for small data, for safety, or across machines. On multicore chips, message passing can sometimes perform well too, because shared memory causes cache coherence traffic between cores.

Real-life example 1, Android apps sharing: When you tap Share on a photo in your gallery and pick WhatsApp, two separate app processes must cooperate. Android uses a message-passing system called Binder to send an Intent, a message describing what to share, from the gallery process to the WhatsApp process. The photo itself is not copied byte by byte into the message; instead, access to it is shared. Each app stays inside its own protected memory, and the kernel driver for Binder checks permissions on the way.

Real-life example 2, a shell pipeline: A student in a university lab has a log file with a million lines and wants to know how many lines mention error. She types grep error log.txt | wc -l. Two processes run at the same time: grep reads the file and writes matching lines into a pipe; wc reads from the pipe and counts lines. If grep runs faster, the pipe's buffer fills and grep blocks until wc catches up, which is the bounded buffer in action. Neither program knows anything about the other; the pipe and the OS do all the coordination.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think shared memory needs a system call for every read and write; it only needs system calls for setup, after which it is plain memory access. Another mistake is forgetting that ordinary pipes are one-way; for two-way talk you need two pipes. Some think signals carry data; they carry only a number. Typical exam questions: compare shared memory and message passing; explain direct versus indirect communication; define blocking and non-blocking send and receive; write producer and consumer code for a bounded buffer; explain how ls | wc works.

Recap: Processes have private memory, so cooperation needs IPC. The two models are shared memory, which is fast but needs synchronisation, and message passing, which is simpler, safer and network friendly but costs more per message. Message passing can be direct or indirect, blocking or non-blocking, with zero, bounded or unbounded buffering. Pipes, signals and sockets are common real mechanisms. The producer-consumer bounded buffer, built with a circular array, shows why cooperating processes need careful coordination. Next lesson: threads, which share memory inside one process.
key_points: Cooperating processes need IPC because each process has private, protected memory.
Shared memory: the processes share a memory region; it is fast after setup, but they must synchronise themselves.
Message passing: processes send and receive messages through the kernel; simpler and works across networks, but slower per message.
Communication can be direct (naming the process) or indirect (through mailboxes), and blocking (synchronous) or non-blocking (asynchronous).
In a circular bounded buffer of size N, it is empty when in == out and full when (in + 1) % N == out, so it holds at most N minus 1 items.
An ordinary pipe is one-way between related processes; a named pipe (FIFO) has a file name and works between unrelated processes.
Signals are short notifications like SIGINT and SIGKILL; sockets are network endpoints made of an IP address and a port.
lessons.tip: Make a two-column table, shared memory versus message passing, with rows for speed, safety, synchronisation, network use and setup. Almost every IPC comparison question is answered by that one table.
lessons.task: Simulate a bounded buffer with five cups on a table and two friends. One friend is the producer who fills a cup with water and moves the in marker; the other is the consumer who drinks and moves the out marker. Use the rule full when (in + 1) mod 5 equals out, and count how many cups can be full at once.

quiz.q: Which IPC model needs system calls only to set up, after which processes just read and write memory?
quiz.explain: With shared memory, the OS sets up the shared region once. After that the processes read and write it directly, which is fast but needs their own synchronisation.

quiz.q: In a circular buffer of size N = 8 using in and out indexes, when is it full?
