quiz.explain: in == out means empty. Full is when moving in forward by one would make it equal out, that is (in + 1) % N == out, so at most N minus 1 slots are used.

quiz.q: What happens in the shell command ls | wc -l?
options: ls writes into a pipe and wc reads from it, both running at the same time
wc runs first and then ls
ls and wc share all their memory
The output is saved to a file named wc
quiz.explain: The shell creates a pipe, connects ls's output to the write end and wc's input to the read end, and runs both processes at the same time.

quiz.q: A send operation waits until the receiver has taken the message. What is this called?
quiz.explain: A blocking or synchronous send makes the sender wait until the message is received. A non-blocking send continues immediately.

quiz.q: Which signal can NOT be caught or ignored by a process?
quiz.explain: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) cannot be caught, blocked or ignored. SIGINT and SIGTERM can be handled, and SIGCHLD is often ignored or handled.

lessons.title: Threads and Concurrency
lessons.content:
Think about a restaurant kitchen in Old Dhaka during iftar time. There is one kitchen, one store room of ingredients, one set of recipes on the wall. But there are several cooks working at the same time: one fries piyaju, one makes jilapi, one stirs haleem. They share the kitchen, the ingredients and the recipes, yet each cook has their own hands, their own current step and their own little workspace. If the owner opened a whole new kitchen for every cook, it would cost a fortune. Threads are the cooks, and the process is the kitchen. A thread is a separate flow of work inside a process that shares the process's memory and resources.

What a thread is: A thread is the basic unit of CPU use. Each thread has its own thread ID, its own program counter, its own set of registers and its own stack. But all threads of the same process share the code section, the data section with global variables, the heap, open files and other resources. A traditional process has a single thread of control. A multithreaded process has several threads, so it can do several things at once. Your web browser, your word processor and almost every modern app are multithreaded.

Why each thread needs its own stack: Each thread may be in the middle of different function calls. One thread may be inside a function that downloads a file, another inside a function that draws the screen. Their local variables and return addresses must not mix, so each thread gets its own stack. Their registers and program counter must also be separate, because they are at different points in the code. Everything else is shared, which is both the strength and the danger of threads.

Benefits of threads: Textbooks list four benefits. Responsiveness: if one thread is blocked, for example waiting for a download, other threads keep the program responsive, so the window does not freeze. Resource sharing: threads share memory automatically, without setting up shared memory or message passing. Economy: creating a thread is much cheaper than creating a process, because there is no new address space to set up, and switching between threads of the same process is cheaper than a full process context switch. Scalability: on a multicore machine, threads of one process can truly run in parallel on different cores.

Concurrency versus parallelism: These two words are often mixed up. Concurrency means several tasks are making progress over the same period of time. On a single core, the OS switches between them quickly, so they take turns. Parallelism means several tasks run at exactly the same instant, which needs multiple cores. So you can have concurrency without parallelism, as on a one-core phone, but not parallelism without concurrency. A juggler with two balls is concurrency: one hand, many balls in the air. Two jugglers, each with one ball, is parallelism.

Multicore programming challenges: Using many cores well is not automatic. The programmer must divide the work into tasks that can run separately, balance the work so no core sits idle, split the data, handle data dependencies where one task needs another's result, and test and debug programs whose behaviour may change from run to run. Two common styles help. Data parallelism splits the data: four threads each sum one quarter of a big array. Task parallelism splits the jobs: one thread computes the average, another the maximum, of the same data.

Amdahl's law, worked: How much faster can more cores make a program? Amdahl's law answers this. If S is the fraction of the program that must run serially, one step after another, and N is the number of cores, then speedup is at most 1 divided by (S + (1 minus S) divided by N). Example one: a program is 75 percent parallel, so S = 0.25. With N = 4 cores, speedup is 1 / (0.25 + 0.75 / 4) = 1 / (0.25 + 0.1875) = 1 / 0.4375, about 2.29 times. Not 4 times! Example two: even with infinite cores, the parallel part shrinks to zero time, and the speedup is 1 / S = 1 / 0.25 = 4 times at most. Example three: if a program is 90 percent parallel and you use 8 cores, speedup is 1 / (0.1 + 0.9 / 8) = 1 / 0.2125, about 4.7. The lesson: the serial part limits everything, so shrinking it matters more than adding cores.

User threads and kernel threads: Threads can be supported at two levels. User threads are managed by a thread library in user space, without the kernel knowing about each one. Kernel threads are created and scheduled by the OS kernel itself. Today, Windows, Linux and macOS all support kernel threads. There must be some relationship between user threads and kernel threads, and there are three classic models.

Many-to-one model: Many user threads map to a single kernel thread. Thread management is done by the library in user space, so it is fast. But if one thread makes a blocking system call, the whole process blocks, because the kernel sees only one thread. And because only one kernel thread exists, the user threads cannot run in parallel on multiple cores. Old Solaris green threads used this model; it is rare now.

One-to-one model: Each user thread maps to its own kernel thread. This gives more concurrency: when one thread blocks, others keep running, and threads can run in parallel on multiple cores. The cost is that creating a user thread means creating a kernel thread, which is heavier, so systems may limit the number of threads. Linux and Windows both use the one-to-one model. On Linux, threads and processes are both created with the clone system call; a thread is just a task that shares memory with others.

Many-to-many model: Many user threads are multiplexed onto a smaller or equal number of kernel threads. The programmer can create as many user threads as needed, and they can still run in parallel and not block each other. It is the most flexible but hard to implement, so it is uncommon in general-purpose kernels. A variation, the two-level model, allows many-to-many mapping and also lets a user thread be bound to its own kernel thread. Some language runtimes do something similar: Go, for example, runs many lightweight goroutines on a smaller number of OS threads.

Pthreads, a tiny example: POSIX threads, or Pthreads, is the standard thread API on Linux and macOS. To create a thread in C you call pthread_create(&tid, NULL, runner, arg), where runner is the function the new thread will execute. The main thread can wait for it with pthread_join(tid, NULL), which is like wait for processes. Imagine summing the numbers 1 to 1000 using two threads: thread A adds 1 to 500, thread B adds 501 to 1000, each into its own variable, then main joins both and adds the two results: 125250 plus 375250 gives 500500, the same as the formula 1000 times 1001 divided by 2. Java has its own Thread class, and Windows has CreateThread.

Thread pools: Creating a fresh thread for every request, say every visitor to a website, wastes time and could create thousands of threads that overload the system. A thread pool solves this. When the program starts, it creates a fixed number of threads that wait for work. When a task arrives, an idle thread from the pool takes it; when finished, the thread goes back to the pool instead of dying. If all threads are busy, tasks wait in a queue. This is faster, because threads already exist, and it puts a limit on how many run at once.

Implicit threading: Writing and managing threads by hand is error-prone, so many tools let the compiler or a library create threads for you. This is called implicit threading. With OpenMP in C, you write #pragma omp parallel for above a loop, and the loop iterations are shared among threads automatically. Java offers the fork-join framework, which splits a big task into smaller tasks and joins their results. Apple systems provide Grand Central Dispatch, where you hand blocks of work to queues and the system decides how many threads to use. The programmer says what can run in parallel; the runtime decides how.

Threading issues: Threads bring some tricky questions. If one thread of a multithreaded program calls fork, does the child copy all threads or only the calling one? Some UNIX systems offer both behaviours. Which thread should receive a signal? It depends on the signal: a signal caused by a thread's own error goes to that thread; others may go to any thread that has not blocked it. How do you cancel a thread safely? Asynchronous cancellation kills it immediately, which can leave shared data half-updated; deferred cancellation lets the thread check for cancellation at safe points, which is safer. Finally, because threads share data, two threads changing the same variable can corrupt it, which is the race condition we study in the synchronisation lessons.

Real-life example 1, a messaging app: When you use Messenger on your phone, one thread runs the user interface, reacting to your taps. Another thread waits on the network for new messages. Another may upload a photo you sent. Another decodes a video. If everything ran in one thread, the screen would freeze each time the network was slow. Android in fact requires that slow network work does not run on the main UI thread, precisely to keep apps responsive.

Real-life example 2, a game on a laptop: A cricket video game on a four-core laptop might use one thread for game logic, one for physics like the ball's movement, one for sound and one for loading the next stadium from disk. On four cores, these can truly run in parallel. But if the game logic is the serial part that the others depend on, Amdahl's law says doubling the cores to eight will not double the frame rate.

Common mistakes and exam questions: A big mistake is to think threads have their own heap or global variables; they share them, and only the stack, registers and program counter are private. Another is to think concurrency and parallelism are the same. Many students also apply Amdahl's law wrongly by forgetting the serial part. Typical exam questions: compare process and thread; list the benefits of multithreading; explain the three multithreading models with diagrams; distinguish concurrency and parallelism; compute speedup with Amdahl's law; explain thread pools.

Recap: A thread is a flow of execution inside a process with its own ID, program counter, registers and stack, sharing code, data, heap and files with the other threads. Threads give responsiveness, resource sharing, economy and scalability. Concurrency is making progress together, parallelism is running at the same instant. Amdahl's law shows the serial part limits speedup to 1 / S. User threads map to kernel threads by many-to-one, one-to-one or many-to-many models; Linux and Windows use one-to-one. Thread pools reuse threads to save time. Next lesson: how the OS decides which thread or process gets the CPU next, the basics of CPU scheduling.
key_points: A thread has its own thread ID, program counter, registers and stack, but shares code, data, heap and open files with other threads of its process.
Benefits of threads: responsiveness, resource sharing, economy (cheaper than processes) and scalability on multicore.
Concurrency means tasks make progress over the same period; parallelism means they run at the same instant on different cores.
Amdahl's law: speedup is at most 1 / (S + (1 minus S) / N), and never more than 1 / S, where S is the serial fraction.
Many-to-one is fast but one blocking call blocks all and there is no parallelism; one-to-one (Linux, Windows) allows parallelism.
Many-to-many maps many user threads onto fewer or equal kernel threads; it is flexible but complex.
Thread pools create threads in advance and reuse them, saving creation time and limiting the number of threads.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a thread question, first say out loud what is private (stack, registers, program counter) and what is shared (code, data, heap, files). Most thread answers follow from that one list.
lessons.task: Use Amdahl's law to fill a small table for a program that is 80 percent parallel: compute the speedup for 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 cores, and the limit for infinite cores. Plot the numbers on graph paper and see how the curve flattens.

quiz.q: Which of these is private to each thread rather than shared by all threads in a process?
quiz.explain: Each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter. The heap, global data, code and open files are shared by all threads of the process.

quiz.q: A program is 75 percent parallel. What is the maximum speedup on 4 cores according to Amdahl's law?
In the many-to-one model, what happens if one user thread makes a blocking system call?
options: The kernel creates a new kernel thread
The thread moves to another core
quiz.explain: All user threads share one kernel thread, so when it blocks, the kernel cannot run any other thread of that process.

quiz.q: Which threading model do Linux and Windows use?
quiz.explain: Linux and Windows map each user thread to its own kernel thread, the one-to-one model, allowing parallelism on multiple cores.

quiz.q: On a single-core phone, music plays while you scroll a feed. What does this show?
quiz.explain: With one core, tasks take turns very quickly. They make progress over the same period (concurrency) but never run at the same instant (parallelism).

lessons.title: CPU Scheduling Basics
lessons.content:
Think of a single barber in a small salon in Mirpur on Eid morning. Ten customers are waiting. One wants a quick trim, another wants a full haircut, shave and head massage, and a little boy is crying because he has been waiting for an hour. The barber can serve only one person at a time. Whom should he serve next? First come, first served? The shortest job first? The crying child first? Each choice makes some people happier and others angrier. A CPU core faces exactly this problem many times every second. The part of the OS that decides which ready process or thread gets the CPU next is the CPU scheduler, and the rules it follows are called a scheduling algorithm.

Why scheduling exists: In a system with multiprogramming, many processes sit in memory. The goal is to keep the CPU busy doing useful work. Whenever the running process has to wait, for example for I/O, the OS takes the CPU away and gives it to another process. On a time-sharing system, the OS also switches regularly so every user gets a quick response. Scheduling decides the order, and a good order can make the same machine feel much faster.

The CPU-I/O burst cycle: Almost every process alternates between two kinds of activity: a CPU burst, where it computes, and an I/O burst, where it waits for input or output. A process starts with a CPU burst, then does some I/O, then another CPU burst, and so on, until a final CPU burst ends with a request to terminate. When people measured real programs, they found that most CPU bursts are short and only a few are long. I/O-bound programs have many short CPU bursts; CPU-bound programs have a few long ones. This pattern is important when choosing an algorithm.

Three kinds of scheduler: Textbooks describe three schedulers. The long-term scheduler, or job scheduler, decides which jobs are admitted into memory from a pool on disk. It controls the degree of multiprogramming, meaning how many processes are in memory. It runs rarely and is mostly found in batch systems; ordinary desktops and phones barely have one. The short-term scheduler, or CPU scheduler, picks one process from the ready queue to run next. It runs very often, perhaps every few milliseconds, so it must be fast. The medium-term scheduler can swap a process out of memory to disk to reduce load, and later swap it back in. Whenever this course says scheduler without a word in front, it means the short-term scheduler.

The dispatcher: Choosing a process is one job; actually handing it the CPU is another. The dispatcher is the module that gives control of the CPU to the process chosen by the scheduler. It switches context, switches to user mode and jumps to the right place in the user program to restart it. The time the dispatcher takes to stop one process and start another is called dispatch latency. Because the dispatcher runs on every switch, it must be as fast as possible.

When scheduling decisions happen: There are four moments when the scheduler may need to choose. One: a process switches from running to waiting, for example it asks for I/O. Two: a process switches from running to ready, for example a timer interrupt arrives. Three: a process switches from waiting to ready, for example its I/O completes. Four: a process terminates. In cases one and four, there is no choice; the CPU is free, so a new process must be picked. In cases two and three, the OS may decide to keep running the current process or switch.

Preemptive and non-preemptive: If scheduling happens only in cases one and four, it is non-preemptive, also called cooperative: once a process gets the CPU, it keeps it until it waits or finishes. If the OS may also take the CPU away in cases two and three, it is preemptive. All modern general-purpose operating systems, such as Windows, Linux and macOS, use preemptive scheduling. Preemption gives better response times, but it brings a danger: a process may be stopped halfway through updating shared data, and another process may then read the half-updated data. That is the race condition problem we will solve in the synchronisation lessons.

Scheduling criteria: How do we decide if an algorithm is good? We use five common criteria. CPU utilisation: keep the CPU as busy as possible; real systems range from about 40 percent when lightly loaded to 90 percent when heavily used. Throughput: the number of processes completed per unit time. Turnaround time: from the moment a process arrives to the moment it finishes, including waiting, running and I/O. Waiting time: the total time a process spends waiting in the ready queue; the scheduler only affects this part directly. Response time: from arrival until the first response is produced, which for interactive systems is often the first time it gets the CPU. We want high utilisation and throughput, and low turnaround, waiting and response times.

The formulas: For each process, we use three numbers: arrival time, burst time and completion time. Then turnaround time = completion time minus arrival time. Waiting time = turnaround time minus burst time, when the process has only one CPU burst and no I/O, which is the usual exam setting. Response time = time of first run minus arrival time. For a non-preemptive algorithm, response time equals waiting time, because once a process starts, it runs to the end. Usually we report the average over all processes.

Gantt charts: A Gantt chart is a horizontal bar showing which process ran during which time. You write the process names in boxes from left to right and the times underneath. For example, P1 runs from 0 to 5, P2 from 5 to 8, P3 from 8 to 9: draw three boxes labelled P1, P2 and P3 with times 0, 5, 8 and 9 under the borders. Every scheduling exam question asks you to draw one, so get used to drawing them neatly. If the CPU is idle for a while because no process has arrived, draw an idle box.

A full worked example: Three processes arrive: P1 at time 0 with burst 5, P2 at time 1 with burst 3, P3 at time 2 with burst 1. Use first-come, first-served order, which we study in detail next lesson. Gantt chart: P1 from 0 to 5, P2 from 5 to 8, P3 from 8 to 9. Completion times: P1 = 5, P2 = 8, P3 = 9. Turnaround: P1 = 5 minus 0 = 5, P2 = 8 minus 1 = 7, P3 = 9 minus 2 = 7. Average turnaround = 19 / 3, about 6.33. Waiting: P1 = 5 minus 5 = 0, P2 = 7 minus 3 = 4, P3 = 7 minus 1 = 6. Average waiting = 10 / 3, about 3.33. Throughput: 3 processes finished in 9 time units, so one third of a process per unit. Notice how poor P3 waited 6 units for a 1-unit job; the next lessons show smarter orders.

Order matters, a second example: Now suppose the same three jobs, with bursts 5, 3 and 1, all arrive together at time 0. In the order P1, P2, P3, the Gantt chart is P1 0 to 5, P2 5 to 8, P3 8 to 9, so the waiting times are 0, 5 and 8, an average of 13 / 3, about 4.33. In the order P3, P2, P1, the chart is P3 0 to 1, P2 1 to 4, P1 4 to 9, so the waiting times are 0, 1 and 4, an average of 5 / 3, about 1.67. Same jobs, same CPU, same total work of 9 units, yet the average wait drops by more than half. And if the first job had arrived at time 2 instead of 0, the CPU would sit idle from 0 to 2; in 11 units of time it would be busy for 9, a utilisation of about 82 percent.

Different systems, different goals: There is no single best algorithm, because different systems care about different criteria. A batch system, like a bank's overnight payroll, cares most about throughput and turnaround. An interactive desktop or phone cares most about response time; a user notices a delay of a few hundred milliseconds. A real-time system cares about meeting deadlines. Even fairness matters: no process should wait forever. Often we try to make response time predictable, because users prefer a steady 1 second over a response that is sometimes 0.1 and sometimes 5 seconds.

Scheduling threads, not processes: On modern systems the kernel actually schedules kernel threads, not whole processes. The ideas are the same, and textbooks use the words process scheduling and thread scheduling almost interchangeably. When a process has several threads, each thread is a separate entry the scheduler can pick, and on a multicore machine several of them can run at once.

Real-life example 1, a ticket counter at Kamalapur: At the railway station before Eid, one counter clerk sells tickets. Customers arrive at different times. Each customer's service time is like a CPU burst. If the clerk serves in arrival order, a man buying tickets for a family of fifteen can make everyone behind him wait a long time, even those who need just one ticket. The average waiting time depends heavily on the order. That is why some stations open a separate counter for single tickets: it is a scheduling decision to reduce average waiting.

Real-life example 2, your phone during a game: While you play a game, your phone is also syncing photos, checking emails and receiving messages. The game needs smooth frames, so its rendering thread must get the CPU quickly and often, which means short response time. Photo syncing can wait, because nobody is watching it, so it can be given less priority. The phone's OS is preemptive: when the game's thread becomes ready, the scheduler can interrupt the background sync to let the game run. That is why you can play smoothly even while big uploads run in the background.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Many students confuse turnaround time and waiting time. Turnaround includes the running time; waiting does not. Another mistake is starting the Gantt chart at the wrong time or forgetting idle periods when no process has arrived yet. Some also forget that the dispatcher and scheduler are different: one chooses, the other hands over. Typical questions: explain the CPU-I/O burst cycle; compare long-term, short-term and medium-term schedulers; define preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling; define the five criteria; compute average waiting and turnaround times from a Gantt chart.

Recap: Scheduling decides which ready process or thread gets the CPU. Processes alternate between CPU bursts and I/O bursts, and most CPU bursts are short. The short-term scheduler chooses often and the dispatcher performs the switch, costing dispatch latency. Non-preemptive scheduling only switches when a process waits or ends; preemptive scheduling can also interrupt it. We judge algorithms by CPU utilisation, throughput, turnaround, waiting and response time, calculated with simple formulas and Gantt charts. Next lesson: our first algorithms, first-come first-served and shortest job first.
key_points: The CPU scheduler picks a process or thread from the ready queue; the dispatcher actually switches to it, taking dispatch latency.
Processes alternate CPU bursts and I/O bursts; most CPU bursts are short.
The long-term scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming, the short-term scheduler picks the next process often, and the medium-term scheduler swaps processes out and in.
Non-preemptive scheduling switches only when the running process waits or ends; preemptive scheduling can also take the CPU away.
Criteria: maximise CPU utilisation and throughput; minimise turnaround, waiting and response time.
Turnaround = completion minus arrival; waiting = turnaround minus burst; response = first run minus arrival.
A Gantt chart shows which process ran when and is the basis of every scheduling calculation.
lessons.tip: For every scheduling problem, make a table with columns arrival, burst, completion, turnaround and waiting before you draw anything. Fill completion from the Gantt chart, then the other two columns are just subtraction.
lessons.task: Time five friends making tea, toast, noodles, an egg and a glass of juice in one small kitchen with one stove. Write the time each one arrives and how long each takes. Try two orders, first come first served and shortest job first, and compute the average waiting time for each on paper.

quiz.q: Which scheduler runs most often and must therefore be very fast?
quiz.explain: The short-term scheduler picks the next process every time the CPU becomes free or a switch is needed, which can be every few milliseconds.

quiz.q: A process arrives at time 2, has a burst of 4, and completes at time 10. What is its waiting time?
quiz.explain: Turnaround = 10 minus 2 = 8. Waiting = turnaround minus burst = 8 minus 4 = 4.

quiz.q: In which situation does a non-preemptive scheduler pick a new process?
options: When a higher priority process arrives
Only when the running process waits or terminates
quiz.explain: Non-preemptive scheduling never takes the CPU away. A new choice is made only when the running process blocks for I/O or finishes.

quiz.q: What is dispatch latency?
options: The time a process waits in the ready queue
The time the dispatcher takes to stop one process and start another
The time a process spends doing I/O
The total running time of a process
quiz.explain: Dispatch latency is the cost of the switch itself: saving and loading context and changing mode. It is pure overhead.

quiz.q: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 5, P2 at 1 with burst 3, P3 at 2 with burst 1, run in FCFS order. What is the average waiting time?
quiz.explain: Gantt: P1 0-5, P2 5-8, P3 8-9. Waiting: P1 0, P2 4, P3 6. Average = 10 / 3, about 3.33.

lessons.title: FCFS, SJF and SRTF Scheduling
lessons.content:
Imagine the queue at a bKash agent shop on the first day of the month. Everyone is in line to cash out money. The first man in line has forty transactions for his whole village. Behind him stand five people who each need one quick cash out of 500 taka. If the agent serves strictly in arrival order, the five quick customers wait a long time behind the big job. If the agent serves the quick ones first, the average waiting time drops a lot, but the big customer might get upset. This lesson studies exactly these two ideas as CPU scheduling algorithms: first-come, first-served, and shortest job first, plus its preemptive cousin, shortest remaining time first.

First-come, first-served (FCFS): The simplest algorithm. The process that asks for the CPU first gets it first. The ready queue is a plain FIFO queue: new processes join the tail, and the scheduler always takes the head. FCFS is non-preemptive: once a process has the CPU, it keeps it until it finishes its burst or waits for I/O. It is easy to understand and easy to code, and it is fair in the sense that nobody jumps the line.

FCFS worked example 1: Three processes arrive at time 0 in the order P1, P2, P3, with burst times 24, 3 and 3. Gantt chart: P1 from 0 to 24, P2 from 24 to 27, P3 from 27 to 30. Waiting times: P1 = 0, P2 = 24, P3 = 27. Average waiting time = (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 51 / 3 = 17. Now suppose the same processes arrive in the order P2, P3, P1. Gantt chart: P2 from 0 to 3, P3 from 3 to 6, P1 from 6 to 30. Waiting times: P2 = 0, P3 = 3, P1 = 6. Average = 9 / 3 = 3. The same three jobs give an average of 17 or 3 depending only on the order. FCFS performance depends heavily on luck.

The convoy effect: The bad case above has a name: the convoy effect. When one long CPU-bound process holds the CPU, many short I/O-bound processes pile up behind it, like small cars stuck behind a slow truck on the Dhaka-Chittagong highway. While they wait, the I/O devices sit idle. When the big process finally does I/O, the short ones rush through the CPU quickly and then all wait on I/O, and now the CPU sits idle. Both the CPU and the devices end up badly used. FCFS is also a poor choice for interactive systems, because one long job can make everyone wait.

FCFS worked example 2, with arrival times: Four processes: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8, P2 at 1 with burst 4, P3 at 2 with burst 9, P4 at 3 with burst 5. FCFS runs them in arrival order. Gantt: P1 0 to 8, P2 8 to 12, P3 12 to 21, P4 21 to 26. Waiting time = start time minus arrival time for non-preemptive algorithms: P1 = 0, P2 = 8 minus 1 = 7, P3 = 12 minus 2 = 10, P4 = 21 minus 3 = 18. Average waiting = 35 / 4 = 8.75. We will reuse these four processes to compare all algorithms in this lesson.

Shortest job first (SJF): The idea is simple: when the CPU is free, give it to the process with the smallest next CPU burst. If two have the same burst, break the tie with FCFS. A more accurate name is shortest next CPU burst, because it looks at the next burst, not the whole job. SJF in its basic form is non-preemptive: once a process starts, it runs its burst to the end.

SJF worked example: Same four processes. At time 0 only P1 has arrived, so P1 runs from 0 to 8, and nobody can interrupt it. At time 8, P2 (burst 4), P3 (burst 9) and P4 (burst 5) are waiting. The shortest is P2, so P2 runs from 8 to 12. Then P4 (5) beats P3 (9): P4 runs from 12 to 17. Finally P3 runs from 17 to 26. Waiting: P1 = 0, P2 = 8 minus 1 = 7, P4 = 12 minus 3 = 9, P3 = 17 minus 2 = 15. Average waiting = (0 + 7 + 9 + 15) / 4 = 31 / 4 = 7.75. Turnaround: P1 = 8, P2 = 11, P4 = 14, P3 = 24, average 57 / 4 = 14.25. Better than FCFS's 8.75 average wait.

Why SJF is optimal: SJF is provably optimal: for a given set of processes that are all available, it gives the minimum possible average waiting time. The reason is simple. Moving a short job in front of a long job reduces the short job's wait by more than it increases the long job's wait, because the short job only delays the long one by a little. Think of it this way: each job's burst is added to the waiting time of every job behind it. Putting the smallest bursts first means the smallest numbers get added most often.

The big problem with SJF: The CPU does not know how long the next burst will be. A process does not come with a label saying "I will compute for 6 milliseconds". In batch systems, users could give an estimate of their job's time limit. For short-term CPU scheduling, the OS must predict the next burst from the past.

Exponential averaging: The usual prediction formula is tau(n+1) = alpha times t(n) + (1 minus alpha) times tau(n). Here t(n) is the actual length of the most recent burst, tau(n) is the old prediction, tau(n+1) is the new prediction, and alpha is a number between 0 and 1 that sets how much we trust recent history. With alpha = 0, recent bursts are ignored; with alpha = 1, only the last burst counts. A common choice is alpha = 0.5. Worked: start with tau(0) = 10 and alpha = 0.5. The process's actual bursts are 6, 4, 6, 4. After the first burst: 0.5 times 6 plus 0.5 times 10 = 8. After the second: 0.5 times 4 plus 0.5 times 8 = 6. After the third: 0.5 times 6 plus 0.5 times 6 = 6. After the fourth: 0.5 times 4 plus 0.5 times 6 = 5. The predictions 10, 8, 6, 6, 5 follow the real behaviour while smoothing out noise. Older bursts count less and less, each time multiplied by another (1 minus alpha), which is why it is called exponential averaging.

Shortest remaining time first (SRTF): SJF can also be made preemptive. Then it is called shortest remaining time first, or preemptive SJF. Whenever a new process arrives, the scheduler compares the new process's burst with the remaining time of the running process. If the new one is shorter, the running process is preempted and goes back to the ready queue.

SRTF worked example: Same four processes. Time 0: only P1, so P1 starts. Time 1: P2 arrives with burst 4. P1 has 7 left. 4 is less than 7, so P2 preempts P1. Time 2: P3 arrives with 9; P2 has 3 left, keep P2. Time 3: P4 arrives with 5; P2 has 2 left, keep P2. Time 5: P2 finishes. Remaining: P1 7, P3 9, P4 5. P4 is shortest, runs 5 to 10. Then P1 with 7 runs 10 to 17. Then P3 runs 17 to 26. Gantt: P1 0-1, P2 1-5, P4 5-10, P1 10-17, P3 17-26. Waiting time with preemption = turnaround minus burst. P1: finishes at 17, arrived at 0, burst 8, so waiting = 17 minus 0 minus 8 = 9. P2: 5 minus 1 minus 4 = 0. P3: 26 minus 2 minus 9 = 15. P4: 10 minus 3 minus 5 = 2. Average = (9 + 0 + 15 + 2) / 4 = 26 / 4 = 6.5. So for this set: FCFS 8.75, SJF 7.75, SRTF 6.5.

Comparing the three: Put the results side by side for our four processes. Average waiting time: FCFS 8.75, SJF 7.75, SRTF 6.5. Number of preemptions: FCFS none, SJF none, SRTF one, when P2 interrupted P1. So SRTF wins on average waiting, but it pays with extra context switches and needs to know burst lengths. FCFS needs no knowledge at all and never preempts, but it is the slowest on average. SJF sits in the middle. When an exam asks you to "compare", give exactly this kind of small table with numbers, plus one line on the trade-off.

Starvation: SJF and SRTF have a dark side. If short processes keep arriving, a long process may wait forever, never being the shortest. This is called starvation or indefinite blocking. Imagine the bKash agent always serving whoever has the smallest transaction: the man with forty transactions might never be served on a busy day. SRTF also causes more context switches than SJF, and both depend on guesses of burst length that may be wrong. Aging, which we see in the next lesson, is a common cure for starvation.

Real-life example 1, a print queue in a computer lab: Twenty students send print jobs to one printer before a deadline. One student sends a 200-page thesis, others send 2-page assignments. With FCFS, if the thesis arrives first, everyone waits for 200 pages. Some print systems let an admin move short jobs ahead, which acts like SJF and cuts the average wait dramatically. But if short jobs keep coming all afternoon, the thesis might never print: starvation in real life.

Real-life example 2, a doctor's chamber: In a crowded chamber in Dhanmondi, the assistant sees a patient who only needs a report checked, which takes 2 minutes, and another who needs a full check-up taking 20 minutes. Many assistants quietly send the 2-minute patient in first. That is SJF thinking: it reduces the average waiting time for the room. If a new 1-minute patient arrives while a 20-minute check-up is still in progress, the doctor usually does not stop the check-up; that is non-preemptive. A doctor who did stop would be using SRTF.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In SJF, students often forget that a process can only be chosen after it has arrived. At time 0, only processes that have arrived count. In SRTF, many compare the new process's full burst with the running process's full burst, instead of its remaining time. Another common slip is computing waiting time as start minus arrival in a preemptive algorithm; that only works for non-preemptive ones. Typical questions: draw Gantt charts for FCFS, SJF and SRTF and compare average waiting and turnaround times; explain the convoy effect; prove or explain why SJF is optimal; compute predictions with exponential averaging; explain starvation.

Recap: FCFS serves in arrival order; it is simple but suffers from the convoy effect and its average wait depends on order. SJF runs the shortest next burst first and gives the minimum average waiting time, but needs burst predictions, made with exponential averaging tau(n+1) = alpha t(n) + (1 minus alpha) tau(n). SRTF is preemptive SJF: a newly arrived shorter job interrupts the running one. In our example, average waits were FCFS 8.75, SJF 7.75 and SRTF 6.5. Both SJF and SRTF can starve long jobs. Next lesson: priority scheduling and Round Robin.
key_points: FCFS runs processes in arrival order using a FIFO queue; it is non-preemptive and simple.
The convoy effect: short processes wait behind one long process, leaving devices or CPU idle.
SJF picks the process with the shortest next CPU burst and gives the minimum average waiting time.
SJF needs burst prediction: tau(n+1) = alpha times t(n) + (1 minus alpha) times tau(n).
SRTF is preemptive SJF: a new arrival with a shorter burst than the running process's remaining time preempts it.
For non-preemptive algorithms, waiting = start minus arrival; for preemptive ones, waiting = completion minus arrival minus burst.
SJF and SRTF can starve long processes if short ones keep arriving.
lessons.tip: In SRTF problems, write the remaining time of every arrived process above the Gantt chart at each arrival time. Make the decision only at arrival and completion times; between them nothing changes.
lessons.task: Take the processes P1 (arrival 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4). Draw Gantt charts for FCFS, SJF and SRTF and compute the average waiting time for each. Check that SRTF gives the smallest and FCFS the largest.

quiz.q: Three processes arrive at time 0 with bursts 24, 3 and 3 in that order. What is the average waiting time under FCFS?
quiz.explain: Gantt: 0-24, 24-27, 27-30. Waits are 0, 24 and 27, so the average is 51 / 3 = 17.

quiz.q: Which algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time for a set of available processes?
quiz.explain: SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time, because short jobs placed first delay fewer and smaller amounts of other jobs.

quiz.q: Using exponential averaging with alpha = 0.5, the previous prediction is 10 and the actual burst was 6. What is the next prediction?
quiz.explain: tau = 0.5 times 6 + 0.5 times 10 = 3 + 5 = 8.

quiz.q: In SRTF, P1 (burst 8) started at time 0. At time 1, P2 arrives with burst 4. What happens?
options: P1 keeps running because it started first
Both run at the same time
P2 preempts P1, because 4 is less than P1's remaining 7
quiz.explain: SRTF compares the newcomer's burst (4) with the running process's remaining time (8 minus 1 = 7). The shorter one runs, so P2 preempts P1.

quiz.q: What is the convoy effect?
options: Many short processes wait behind one long process, wasting CPU and device time
Processes run in a circle with a time quantum
A process waits forever because of low priority
Two processes wait for each other forever
quiz.explain: In FCFS, a long CPU-bound job holds the CPU while short I/O-bound jobs pile up behind it, like cars behind a slow truck.

lessons.title: Priority and Round Robin Scheduling
lessons.content:
Think of a hospital emergency room in Dhaka. A patient with a small cut and a patient having a heart attack arrive at the same time. Nobody serves them in arrival order; the heart attack patient goes first because the case is more important. That is priority scheduling. Now think of a mother sharing one phone among three children who all want to play a game. She says: each of you gets five minutes, then pass the phone to the next one, and keep going round until everyone is done. That is Round Robin. These two ideas, importance and taking turns, are the heart of how real operating systems share the CPU, and this lesson works through both with full examples.

Priority scheduling: Each process gets a priority number, and the CPU goes to the process with the highest priority. Ties are broken by FCFS. In this course, as in most textbooks, a smaller number means a higher priority, so priority 0 beats priority 5. Be careful: some systems use the opposite convention, so always read the question. SJF is actually a special case of priority scheduling, where the priority is the predicted next burst: the shorter the burst, the higher the priority.

Where priorities come from: Priorities can be internal or external. Internal priorities are computed by the OS from measurable things, such as memory needs, number of open files, time limits or the ratio of I/O bursts to CPU bursts. External priorities are set from outside the OS, for example by the importance of the process, the department paying for the computer time, or a user's choice. On Linux, the nice command lets a user lower the priority of a program; nice values run from -20, the highest priority, to 19, the lowest, and only an administrator may raise priority above normal.

Non-preemptive priority, worked: Five processes all arrive at time 0. P1 has burst 10 and priority 3; P2 burst 1, priority 1; P3 burst 2, priority 4; P4 burst 1, priority 5; P5 burst 5, priority 2. Sorted by priority: P2 (1), P5 (2), P1 (3), P3 (4), P4 (5). Gantt chart: P2 0 to 1, P5 1 to 6, P1 6 to 16, P3 16 to 18, P4 18 to 19. Waiting times: P1 = 6, P2 = 0, P3 = 16, P4 = 18, P5 = 1. Average waiting = (6 + 0 + 16 + 18 + 1) / 5 = 41 / 5 = 8.2.

Preemptive priority, worked: Priority scheduling can also be preemptive: when a new process arrives with a higher priority than the running one, it takes the CPU at once. Example: P1 arrives at 0 with burst 5 and priority 3; P2 at 1 with burst 2 and priority 1; P3 at 2 with burst 3 and priority 2. Time 0: only P1, it runs. Time 1: P2 arrives with priority 1, better than 3, so P2 preempts P1 and runs 1 to 3. At time 2, P3 arrived with priority 2, worse than P2's 1, so it waits. Time 3: P2 finishes; P3 (priority 2) beats P1 (priority 3), so P3 runs 3 to 6. Then P1 runs its remaining 4 units from 6 to 10. Waiting: P1 = 10 minus 0 minus 5 = 5, P2 = 0, P3 = 6 minus 2 minus 3 = 1. Average = 6 / 3 = 2.

Starvation and aging: The big danger in priority scheduling is starvation. A low-priority process may wait forever if higher-priority processes keep arriving. There is a famous story, often told in OS textbooks, that when the IBM 7094 at MIT was shut down in 1973, a low-priority job submitted in 1967 had still not been run. The cure is aging: gradually increase the priority of processes that have waited a long time. For example, if priorities range from 127, lowest, to 0, highest, and we raise a waiting process's priority by 1 every 15 minutes, then even the lowest-priority process reaches the top in 127 times 15 = 1905 minutes, about 32 hours. Waiting long enough always wins in the end.

Round Robin (RR): Round Robin is designed for time-sharing. It is like FCFS but with preemption added. The OS defines a small unit of time called the time quantum or time slice, typically 10 to 100 milliseconds. The ready queue is a circular FIFO queue. The scheduler takes the first process and sets a timer for one quantum. If the process's burst is shorter than the quantum, it finishes or blocks on its own and gives up the CPU. If it is longer, the timer interrupts it after one quantum, a context switch happens, and the process goes to the tail of the ready queue. Then the next process gets its quantum.

RR worked example 1: P1, P2 and P3 arrive at time 0 with bursts 24, 3 and 3, and the quantum is 4. P1 runs 0 to 4 and is preempted with 20 left. P2 runs 4 to 7 and finishes, since 3 is less than 4. P3 runs 7 to 10 and finishes. Now only P1 is left, so it gets quantum after quantum from 10 to 30. Waiting: P1 = 30 minus 24 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7. Average = 17 / 3, about 5.67. Compare FCFS with the same order: average 17. The short jobs no longer wait behind the long one.

RR worked example 2: Four processes arrive at time 0 in order: P1 burst 5, P2 burst 3, P3 burst 1, P4 burst 4, quantum 2. Round 1: P1 runs 0 to 2 (3 left), P2 2 to 4 (1 left), P3 4 to 5 (done), P4 5 to 7 (2 left). Round 2: P1 7 to 9 (1 left), P2 9 to 10 (done), P4 10 to 12 (done). Round 3: P1 12 to 13 (done). Completion times: P1 13, P2 10, P3 5, P4 12. Turnaround = completion, since all arrived at 0, so average turnaround = 40 / 4 = 10. Waiting = turnaround minus burst: P1 8, P2 7, P3 4, P4 8, average 27 / 4 = 6.75. Response times: P1 0, P2 2, P3 4, P4 5, average 2.75. Notice how quickly everybody gets a first turn; that is the whole point of RR.

A useful guarantee: With n processes in the ready queue and quantum q, each process gets 1 / n of the CPU time in chunks of at most q, and no process waits more than (n minus 1) times q time units before its next quantum. With 5 processes and q = 20 ms, nobody waits more than 4 times 20 = 80 ms. That predictability is why RR suits interactive systems.

Choosing the quantum: The quantum size matters a lot. If it is very large, larger than all bursts, RR becomes plain FCFS. If it is very small, the system spends most of its time context switching. Example: if a context switch takes 1 ms and the quantum is also 1 ms, half of all CPU time is wasted on switching. If the quantum is 99 ms, the waste is only 1 percent. A common rule of thumb is that about 80 percent of CPU bursts should be shorter than the quantum, so most bursts finish in one go. Real systems use quanta of roughly 10 to 100 ms, while a context switch typically costs only microseconds. Turnaround time does not always improve with a bigger quantum; it is best when most processes finish their burst within one quantum.

Priority plus Round Robin: The two ideas mix naturally: run the highest-priority processes first, and use Round Robin among processes that share the same priority. Example with quantum 2, all arriving at 0: P1 (burst 4, priority 3), P2 (5, 2), P3 (8, 2), P4 (7, 1), P5 (3, 3). P4 has the best priority and runs alone from 0 to 7. Then P2 and P3 share priority 2 and alternate: P2 7 to 9, P3 9 to 11, P2 11 to 13, P3 13 to 15, P2 15 to 16 and done, then P3 alone 16 to 20. Finally P1 and P5 alternate: P1 20 to 22, P5 22 to 24, P1 24 to 26, P5 26 to 27. Total time 27, which equals the sum of all bursts, as it must.

Comparing the algorithms: FCFS is simple and non-preemptive, but suffers the convoy effect. SJF gives the best average waiting time but needs burst prediction and can starve long jobs. SRTF does even better on average waiting but has more context switches. Priority scheduling lets important work run first, but needs aging to avoid starvation. RR gives the best response time and is fair, but its average turnaround is often higher than SJF's, and performance depends on the quantum. Real systems combine these ideas, as we see in the next lesson.

Real-life example 1, a cricket net session: At a cricket academy in Mirpur, one bowling machine is shared by six batsmen. The coach says each batsman faces 6 balls, then steps out and joins the end of the line. This is Round Robin with a quantum of one over. Everyone gets a turn quickly, nobody hogs the machine, and a batsman who only needs one more over finishes and leaves. If the coach made the quantum 60 balls, it would be basically FCFS, and the last batsman would wait ages. If he made it 1 ball, too much time would go into changing batsmen.

Real-life example 2, a phone's priorities: On your phone, an incoming call has very high priority: even if a game is running, the call screen must appear at once. That is preemptive priority. Background photo backup has low priority. If the phone never let low-priority work run, backup would starve forever; real systems make sure low-priority work eventually gets some time, which is the spirit of aging. Meanwhile, apps of the same priority take turns in time slices, which is Round Robin.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In priority problems, students forget to check whether lower numbers mean higher or lower priority. In RR, a common mistake is putting a newly arrived process and a just-preempted process in the queue in the wrong order. Most textbooks put the new arrival in the queue first if it arrives at the same time as the preemption, so state your rule clearly. Many also forget that a process with a burst shorter than the quantum gives up the CPU early, and the next process starts immediately. Typical questions: draw Gantt charts for priority and RR; compute average waiting, turnaround and response; explain starvation and aging; explain the effect of quantum size.

Recap: Priority scheduling runs the highest-priority process, preemptive or not; SJF is a special case. Low-priority processes may starve, and aging fixes this by slowly raising their priority. Round Robin gives each process a time quantum in turn using a circular queue; it is preemptive and gives good response time. A very large quantum turns RR into FCFS; a very small one wastes time on context switches. In our examples, priority gave an average wait of 8.2, and RR with quantum 2 gave 6.75 with an average response of only 2.75. Next lesson: combining queues, multiprocessor and real-time scheduling.
key_points: Priority scheduling gives the CPU to the highest-priority process; in most textbooks a smaller number means higher priority.
Priority scheduling can be preemptive or non-preemptive; SJF is a special case where priority is the predicted burst.
Starvation means a low-priority process may wait forever; aging gradually raises the priority of waiting processes.
Round Robin gives each process one time quantum in turn from a circular queue, then preempts it to the tail.
With n processes and quantum q, no process waits more than (n minus 1) times q for its next turn.
A very large quantum makes RR behave like FCFS; a very small one wastes CPU time on context switches.
RR usually gives the best response time but often a higher average turnaround than SJF.
lessons.tip: In Round Robin problems, write the ready queue contents under the Gantt chart after every time slice. Most RR mistakes come from forgetting who is in the queue and in which order.
lessons.task: Use the processes P1 (burst 6), P2 (burst 3), P3 (burst 4), all arriving at 0. Draw Round Robin Gantt charts with quantum 1, 2, 3 and 10. For each, count the context switches and compute the average waiting time. See which quantum gives the best balance.

quiz.q: In non-preemptive priority scheduling (smaller number = higher priority), processes at time 0 have (burst, priority): P1 (10, 3), P2 (1, 1), P3 (2, 4), P4 (1, 5), P5 (5, 2). What is the average waiting time?
What is aging in CPU scheduling?
options: Removing processes that have run too long
Gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait a long time
Lowering the priority of new processes
Making the time quantum longer over time
quiz.explain: Aging fights starvation: the longer a process waits, the higher its priority becomes, until it eventually runs.

quiz.q: Under Round Robin with quantum 4, P1 (24), P2 (3) and P3 (3) arrive at time 0. When does P3 finish?
quiz.explain: P1 runs 0-4, P2 runs 4-7 and finishes, P3 runs 7-10 and finishes. P1 then runs 10-30.

quiz.q: What happens if the Round Robin time quantum is made extremely large?
quiz.explain: If the quantum is bigger than every burst, no process is ever preempted, so processes simply run in arrival order, which is FCFS.

quiz.q: There are 6 processes in the ready queue and the quantum is 10 ms. At most how long does a process wait before its next quantum?
quiz.explain: The longest wait is (n minus 1) times q = 5 times 10 ms = 50 ms, while the other five processes each use one quantum.

lessons.title: Multilevel, Multiprocessor and Real-Time Scheduling
lessons.content:
Think of Shahjalal airport. There is not just one queue. There is a fast lane for diplomats and crew, a queue for business class, a long queue for economy, and a special desk for families with babies. Each queue has its own rules, and staff decide how to divide their time between queues. And there are many counters working in parallel, not just one. Real operating systems schedule the CPU in the same way: several queues with different rules, many CPU cores working at once, and some tasks with hard deadlines that must never be missed. This lesson covers multilevel queues, multilevel feedback queues, multiprocessor scheduling and real-time scheduling, and ends with how Linux does it.

Multilevel queue scheduling: Processes often fall into clear groups. Foreground interactive processes, such as a text editor, need quick response. Background batch processes, such as a nightly backup, just need to finish eventually. A multilevel queue scheduler splits the ready queue into several separate queues, and each process is permanently assigned to one queue based on its type, memory size or priority. Each queue has its own algorithm: for example, Round Robin for the foreground queue and FCFS for the background queue.

Scheduling between queues: There must also be a rule for choosing between queues. One option is fixed priority: the foreground queue always beats the background queue, so a background process runs only when the foreground queue is empty. That risks starvation for the background. Another option is time slicing between queues: for example, the foreground queue gets 80 percent of CPU time, divided among its processes by Round Robin, and the background queue gets 20 percent, used in FCFS order. A textbook example uses five queues in order of priority: real-time processes, system processes, interactive processes, interactive editing processes and batch processes.

Multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ): The weakness of a multilevel queue is that a process is stuck in one queue forever. A multilevel feedback queue lets processes move between queues based on their behaviour. The idea: a process that uses a lot of CPU time is probably CPU-bound, so move it to a lower-priority queue. A process that gives up the CPU quickly, for I/O, is probably interactive, so keep it high. A process that has waited too long in a low queue can be moved up, which is aging, preventing starvation.

MLFQ worked example: Take three queues. Queue 0 uses Round Robin with a quantum of 8 ms and has the highest priority. Queue 1 uses Round Robin with a quantum of 16 ms. Queue 2 uses FCFS and has the lowest priority. A process in a lower queue runs only when all higher queues are empty, and a newly arriving process in a higher queue preempts a lower one. Every new process enters queue 0. Now consider a process with a CPU burst of 30 ms. In queue 0 it uses its full 8 ms and does not finish, so it drops to queue 1 with 22 ms left. In queue 1 it uses its full 16 ms, still not done, so it drops to queue 2 with 6 ms left. There it finishes the last 6 ms in FCFS order whenever queues 0 and 1 are empty. Meanwhile, an interactive process with bursts of 3 ms always finishes within its first quantum in queue 0, so it stays at the top and gets fast response. The scheduler learns what each process is like simply by watching it.

What defines an MLFQ: An MLFQ is described by several parameters: the number of queues, the scheduling algorithm for each queue, the rule for moving a process up, the rule for moving it down, and which queue a new process enters. It is the most general CPU scheduling scheme, and many real systems use some form of it, but it is also the most complex to tune.

Multiprocessor scheduling: With several CPU cores, scheduling gets new questions. In asymmetric multiprocessing, one core, the master, makes all scheduling decisions and handles system work, and the others just run user code. It is simple but the master can become a bottleneck. In symmetric multiprocessing, SMP, each core schedules itself. Almost all modern systems, including Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS, use SMP. With SMP there are two ways to keep ready threads: one common ready queue shared by all cores, which needs locking and can become a bottleneck, or a separate private ready queue for each core, which is the common approach today.

Processor affinity: When a thread runs on a core, that core's cache fills with the thread's data. If the thread then moves to another core, the new cache is cold, and the old one is wasted. So the OS tries to keep a thread on the same core. This is called processor affinity. Soft affinity means the OS tries to keep the thread on the same core but does not promise. Hard affinity means a program can ask to run only on certain cores; Linux supports this with the sched_setaffinity system call. On NUMA machines, where each processor has its own nearby memory, affinity also helps a thread stay close to its memory.

Load balancing: With per-core queues, one core may be overloaded while another sits idle. Load balancing spreads work evenly. In push migration, a periodic task checks the load on each core and pushes threads from busy cores to idle ones. In pull migration, an idle core pulls a waiting thread from a busy core. Linux uses both. Note the tension: load balancing moves threads, but affinity wants to keep them in place. Schedulers must balance these two goals.

Multithreaded cores: Many modern cores can run two hardware threads at once, a technique Intel calls hyper-threading and others call simultaneous multithreading. When one hardware thread stalls waiting for memory, which can take a long time, the core switches to the other one. To the OS, a 4-core chip with 2 hardware threads per core looks like 8 logical CPUs. The OS should know this: two busy threads on the same physical core share its resources and run slower than on two separate cores.

Real-time scheduling basics: In a real-time system, being correct means being on time. Soft real-time systems give real-time tasks preference but do not guarantee deadlines. Hard real-time systems must meet every deadline. Two delays matter: interrupt latency, from the moment an interrupt arrives until its handler starts, and dispatch latency, the time to stop one task and start another. Real-time operating systems keep both very small. The basic rule is preemptive, priority-based scheduling: the highest-priority real-time task always runs.

Periodic tasks: Many real-time tasks repeat at fixed intervals. A periodic task has a period p, a processing time t and a deadline d, with 0 less than or equal to t less than or equal to d less than or equal to p. Often the deadline is the end of the period. The CPU utilisation of one task is t divided by p. For example, a sensor task that needs 20 ms of CPU every 50 ms has utilisation 0.4, or 40 percent. The total utilisation of all tasks can never exceed 1, or 100 percent, on one core.

Rate-monotonic scheduling: Rate-monotonic scheduling assigns static priorities: the shorter the period, the higher the priority, and it preempts. It is optimal among static-priority methods. A sufficient test: n tasks are guaranteed schedulable if total utilisation is at most n times (2 to the power 1/n minus 1). For one task the bound is 100 percent, for two tasks about 82.8 percent, for three about 78 percent, and it approaches about 69 percent as n grows. Worked example 1: P1 has period 50 and time 20; P2 has period 100 and time 35. Utilisation = 20/50 + 35/100 = 0.4 + 0.35 = 0.75, below 0.828, so it is guaranteed. Indeed: P1 runs 0 to 20, P2 20 to 50, P1 50 to 70, P2 finishes 70 to 75, before its deadline of 100. Worked example 2: P1 period 50, time 25; P2 period 80, time 35. Utilisation = 0.5 + 0.4375 = 0.9375, above the bound. P1 runs 0 to 25, P2 25 to 50, P1 preempts at 50 and runs to 75, P2 needs 10 more and finishes at 85, missing its deadline of 80.

Earliest-deadline-first: EDF assigns priorities dynamically: whichever task has the nearest deadline runs first. On one core, EDF can in theory schedule any set of tasks with total utilisation up to 100 percent, ignoring the cost of switching. In example 2 above, EDF works: P1 runs 0 to 25; P2 runs 25 to 50; at time 50, P1's new deadline is 100 but P2's deadline is 80, which is earlier, so P2 continues to 60 and finishes on time. Then P1 runs 60 to 85, well before its deadline of 100. Both meet their deadlines where rate-monotonic failed.

How Linux and Windows do it: Linux has scheduling classes. Real-time tasks use the SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR policies with fixed priorities, and they always beat normal tasks. For normal tasks, Linux used the Completely Fair Scheduler, CFS, from version 2.6.23. CFS keeps, for each task, a virtual runtime that grows as the task runs, faster for low-priority tasks and slower for high-priority ones, and it always picks the task with the smallest virtual runtime, stored in a red-black tree. So tasks that have had less CPU get it next, which is fair. Since version 6.6, Linux uses a newer scheduler called EEVDF that builds on the same fairness ideas. Windows uses a preemptive priority scheduler with 32 priority levels, where levels 16 to 31 are a real-time class, and it gives a temporary priority boost to threads that wake up from waiting on I/O, such as keyboard input, to keep them responsive.

Real-life example 1, a laptop running a video call: During a Zoom class, your laptop runs the call, a browser with many tabs and an antivirus scan. An MLFQ-like scheduler notices that the video call threads use short CPU bursts and often wait for network and camera data, so they stay in high-priority queues and respond quickly. The antivirus scan uses long CPU bursts, so it slides down to lower priority and runs in the gaps. On four cores, the OS spreads the work, trying to keep each thread on the same core for cache warmth.

Real-life example 2, a garment factory machine: An automatic cutting machine in a Gazipur garment factory reads a position sensor every 10 ms and controls a motor every 20 ms. Both are periodic hard real-time tasks. Engineers compute the utilisation of each task, check it against the rate-monotonic bound or use EDF, and test that every deadline is met even in the worst case. Missing a deadline could mean a wrongly cut piece of cloth or an unsafe machine.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often confuse multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue: in the first, processes never move between queues; in the second, they do. In MLFQ problems, many forget that a process drops only when it uses its whole quantum. In rate-monotonic problems, people sometimes assign priority by processing time instead of by period. Also, being above the rate-monotonic bound does not prove failure; you must simulate. Typical questions: explain MLFQ with a diagram and a worked burst; compare SMP and asymmetric multiprocessing; define processor affinity and load balancing; test a task set with the rate-monotonic bound and with EDF.

Recap: Multilevel queues give each class of process its own queue and algorithm; MLFQ lets processes move down when they use full quanta and up through aging, so interactive work stays fast. Multiprocessor systems use SMP with per-core queues, processor affinity and load balancing. Real-time systems use preemptive priority scheduling; rate-monotonic gives fixed priorities by period with the bound n(2^(1/n) minus 1), and EDF gives dynamic priorities by deadline and can reach 100 percent utilisation. Linux uses fairness-based scheduling for normal tasks and fixed priorities for real-time ones. Next lesson: what goes wrong when concurrent processes share data.
key_points: A multilevel queue gives each class of process its own permanent queue with its own algorithm, with fixed priority or time slicing between queues.
A multilevel feedback queue moves CPU-hungry processes down and long-waiting ones up, so interactive processes stay at high priority.
In the 8 ms, 16 ms, FCFS MLFQ example, a 30 ms burst uses 8 ms in queue 0, 16 ms in queue 1 and the last 6 ms in queue 2.
Modern systems use symmetric multiprocessing (SMP), usually with a ready queue per core.
Processor affinity keeps a thread on the same core to reuse its warm cache; load balancing (push or pull migration) spreads the work.
Rate-monotonic scheduling gives higher priority to shorter periods; n tasks are guaranteed if utilisation is at most n(2^(1/n) minus 1), about 82.8 percent for two tasks.
EDF runs the task with the nearest deadline and can schedule up to 100 percent utilisation on one core in theory.
lessons.tip: For real-time questions, always compute total utilisation first. If it is above 1, nothing works; if it is below the rate-monotonic bound, RM works; in between, draw the timeline to find out.
lessons.task: Two periodic tasks: A with period 40 and time 10, B with period 60 and time 30. Compute the total utilisation and compare it with the two-task rate-monotonic bound of 0.828. Then draw the rate-monotonic timeline from 0 to 120 and check whether every deadline is met.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a multilevel queue and a multilevel feedback queue?
options: A feedback queue lets processes move between queues based on their behaviour
A multilevel queue has only one queue
A feedback queue never uses Round Robin
A multilevel queue lets processes move between queues
quiz.explain: In a plain multilevel queue, each process stays in its assigned queue forever. A feedback queue moves processes down or up depending on how they use the CPU.

quiz.q: In an MLFQ with queue 0 (RR, 8 ms), queue 1 (RR, 16 ms) and queue 2 (FCFS), a new process needs 30 ms of CPU. How much does it run in queue 2?
quiz.explain: It uses 8 ms in queue 0 and 16 ms in queue 1, a total of 24 ms. The remaining 30 minus 24 = 6 ms runs in queue 2.

quiz.q: What does processor affinity mean?
options: Running all threads on one core only
Trying to keep a thread on the same core so its cached data can be reused
Moving threads to the least busy core every millisecond
Giving real-time threads the highest priority
quiz.explain: A thread's data fills the cache of the core it runs on. Keeping it on that core avoids losing the warm cache.

quiz.q: Two tasks: P1 period 50, time 20; P2 period 100, time 35. What is the total CPU utilisation?
quiz.explain: Utilisation = 20 / 50 + 35 / 100 = 0.4 + 0.35 = 0.75, which is below the two-task bound of about 0.828.

quiz.q: In rate-monotonic scheduling, which task gets the highest priority?
options: The task with the longest processing time
The task with the nearest deadline at this moment
The task with the shortest period
quiz.explain: Rate-monotonic assigns fixed priorities by rate: the shorter the period, the higher the priority. Nearest deadline first is EDF.

lessons.title: Synchronisation and the Critical Section Problem
lessons.content:
Imagine a joint bank account shared by two brothers, one in Dhaka and one in Sylhet. The balance is 10,000 taka. At the very same moment, the Dhaka brother deposits 5,000 and the Sylhet brother withdraws 2,000. Each bank branch's computer reads the balance, 10,000, does its calculation and writes back the result. The Dhaka computer writes 15,000. A split second later, the Sylhet computer writes 8,000. The final balance shows 8,000, but it should be 13,000. Five thousand taka has simply vanished. Nobody made a calculation mistake; the problem is only in the timing. This kind of bug is called a race condition, and preventing it is the job of process synchronisation.

Why this happens in an OS: Since the earlier lessons, we know that processes and threads run concurrently, and that a preemptive scheduler can stop a thread at any instruction and run another. On a multicore machine, two threads can even run at exactly the same time. When they share data, such as a global variable, a file or a shared memory region, the result can depend on the exact order in which their instructions happen to run. Whenever the outcome depends on that order, we have a race condition.

counter++ is not one step: Look at the simplest example. Two threads share an integer counter with value 5. Thread A runs counter++ and thread B runs counter--. You expect the final value to be 5 again. But in machine language, counter++ is three steps: register1 = counter; register1 = register1 + 1; counter = register1. And counter-- is: register2 = counter; register2 = register2 minus 1; counter = register2. Each thread has its own registers, saved and restored on context switches.

A bad interleaving step by step: Now suppose the steps interleave like this. Step one: A does register1 = counter, so register1 = 5. Step two: A does register1 = register1 + 1, so register1 = 6. Step three: a context switch happens, and B does register2 = counter, so register2 = 5, because A has not written back yet. Step four: B does register2 = register2 minus 1, so register2 = 4. Step five: A does counter = register1, so counter = 6. Step six: B does counter = register2, so counter = 4. The final value is 4, not 5. If steps five and six were swapped, the result would be 6. The correct answer, 5, only appears when one thread finishes all three steps before the other starts.

A real experiment: If two threads each run counter++ one million times on a multicore computer, without any protection, the final value is very often less than two million, and different every time you run it. Some increments are lost exactly as in the example above. That is what makes race conditions so nasty: the program may work perfectly a thousand times in testing and then fail in front of a customer.

Atomic operations: The word you will hear again and again is atomic. An atomic operation happens all at once from the point of view of everyone else: either it has not started, or it is completely finished, and no other thread can ever see it half done. The whole problem with counter++ is that it is not atomic; another thread can sneak in between the load and the store. Going back to the bank story, the fix is to make "read balance, calculate, write balance" behave like one atomic step. The rest of this lesson and the next ones are about different ways to build such atomic steps.

The critical section: The part of a program where a process touches shared data is called its critical section. The rule we want is simple: when one process is executing in its critical section, no other process may be executing in its critical section for the same data. Each process's code is pictured in four parts. The entry section asks permission to enter. Then comes the critical section. Then the exit section announces that it has left. The rest is the remainder section. The critical section problem is to design the entry and exit sections so that processes can cooperate safely.

Three requirements: Any correct solution must satisfy three conditions. One, mutual exclusion: if a process is in its critical section, no other process can be in its critical section. Two, progress: if no process is in its critical section and some processes want to enter, only those that are not in their remainder sections take part in deciding who goes next, and the decision cannot be postponed forever. In simple words, if the room is empty and someone wants to enter, someone must get in. Three, bounded waiting: after a process asks to enter, there is a limit on how many times other processes can enter before it. In simple words, nobody waits forever. We assume each process runs at some non-zero speed, but we make no assumption about how fast.

The kernel has races too: The kernel itself is full of shared data: the list of open files, memory allocation tables, process lists. Imagine two processes calling fork at the same moment on two cores; both read the next free process ID and both get the same number. Kernels must avoid this. A non-preemptive kernel avoids many races on a single core because a process running in kernel mode is not preempted until it leaves the kernel, blocks or gives up the CPU. A preemptive kernel allows preemption even in kernel mode, which is more responsive and needed for real-time work, but must be carefully designed. Linux and Windows have preemptive kernels.

A first naive attempt: Why not just use a shared variable turn? Process 0 enters when turn == 0, and when it leaves it sets turn = 1; process 1 enters when turn == 1 and leaves by setting turn = 0. This gives mutual exclusion, because only one value of turn is true at a time. But it fails progress: the processes are forced to alternate strictly. If process 0 wants to enter twice in a row while process 1 is busy in its remainder section, process 0 must wait for process 1 to take its turn, even though the critical section is empty.

A second naive attempt: Use a flag for each process instead: flag[i] = true means process i wants to enter. Process i sets flag[i] = true, then waits while flag[j] is true. This avoids forced alternation. But if both processes set their flags at the same moment, both wait for each other forever; nobody enters. Progress fails again. We need to combine both ideas.

Peterson's solution: Gary Peterson published a neat solution for two processes in 1981. It uses two shared variables: int turn and boolean flag[2]. The code for process i, where j is the other process, is: entry section: flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j) do nothing. Then the critical section. Exit section: flag[i] = false. In words: I say I want to enter, but I politely give the turn to the other process. Then I wait only if the other process also wants to enter and it is its turn.

Why Peterson's solution works: Mutual exclusion: suppose both processes were in the critical section together. Then each passed its while loop, so for each, either the other's flag was false or turn was its own number. Both flags are true while they are inside, so turn would have to equal both 0 and 1 at the same time, which is impossible. Whoever wrote turn last gave the turn away and must wait. Progress: if only one process wants to enter, the other's flag is false, so it enters immediately. Bounded waiting: when process j leaves, it sets flag[j] = false, which lets i in. If j tries to come back right away, it sets turn = i, giving way to i. So i waits for at most one entry by j.

Walk-through: Process 0 sets flag[0] = true and turn = 1. Before checking, process 1 sets flag[1] = true and turn = 0. Now turn = 0, because process 1 wrote last. Process 0 checks: flag[1] is true but turn is 0, not 1, so it enters. Process 1 checks: flag[0] is true and turn is 0, which is process 0's number, so process 1 waits. When process 0 leaves, it sets flag[0] = false, and process 1's loop ends. Exactly one got in, and the other followed. That is the polite "after you" rule working.

The catch on modern hardware: Peterson's solution is beautiful for teaching, but it is not guaranteed to work on modern computers as written. To run faster, modern processors and compilers may reorder reads and writes that do not depend on each other. If the write to flag[i] and the write to turn are reordered with the read of flag[j], both processes can enter at once. Correct code today needs hardware support, such as memory barriers and atomic instructions, which is the topic of the next lesson. Also, Peterson's solution uses busy waiting: the waiting process spins in a loop, wasting CPU time.

Real-life example 1, train ticket booking: During Eid, thousands of people try to book seats on the same train through the Bangladesh Railway app at the same second. Two buyers see that seat 23 is free; both press Buy. If the server code reads "seat free", then later writes "seat sold to me" without protection, both buyers may get the same seat. The fix is to make check-and-book a critical section, so only one request can do it at a time, often done with database locks. The second buyer then sees "seat already sold".

Real-life example 2, a shared notebook in a group project: Four students in a group project share one Google Doc. If two of them edit the same sentence at the same moment, the editor must decide what happens; without careful synchronisation, one person's change could silently overwrite the other's. Collaborative editors use special algorithms to merge changes. Inside an operating system, the simpler rule is mutual exclusion: only one writer at a time in the critical section.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often think a single line of C like counter++ is automatically safe; it is not. Another mistake is to forget the progress requirement and accept the strict alternation solution. Some also forget that bounded waiting is about a limit on the number of other entries, not about time. Typical questions: define race condition with the counter example and an interleaving; define critical section and its three requirements; write Peterson's solution and prove it meets all three; explain why it may fail on modern hardware; explain why simple turn or flag solutions fail.

Recap: A race condition happens when concurrent processes share data and the result depends on the order of execution; even counter++ is three machine steps that can interleave badly. A critical section is code that touches shared data, guarded by an entry section and exit section. A correct solution must provide mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Strict alternation and simple flags fail progress; Peterson's solution, combining flags and a turn variable, satisfies all three for two processes, but needs hardware help on modern machines. Next lesson: the hardware instructions and locks that real systems use.
key_points: A race condition occurs when concurrent processes access shared data and the outcome depends on the order of execution.
counter++ is three machine steps (load, add, store), so two threads can interleave and lose updates.
A critical section is code that accesses shared data; it is wrapped by an entry section and an exit section.
A correct solution needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
Strict alternation with a turn variable fails progress; two simple flags can let both processes wait forever.
Peterson's solution: flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j); critical section; flag[i] = false.
Peterson's solution is correct in theory for two processes but may fail on modern CPUs that reorder memory operations, and it busy-waits.
lessons.tip: For any interleaving question, make a table with one row per step and columns for each thread's register and the shared variable. Fill it line by line; the lost update becomes obvious.
lessons.task: Start with counter = 10. Thread A runs counter = counter + 3 and thread B runs counter = counter * 2, each as load, compute, store. List every possible final value by trying different interleavings on paper. How many different answers can you find, and which ones are correct?
