quiz.q: counter is 5. Thread A runs counter++ and thread B runs counter-- at the same time without protection. Which final values are possible?
quiz.explain: If one thread finishes before the other starts, the result is 5. If both load 5 before either stores, the last store wins, giving 4 or 6.

quiz.q: Which requirement says that if the critical section is empty and someone wants in, the decision cannot be postponed forever?
quiz.explain: Progress guarantees that when no process is inside and some want to enter, one of them will be chosen without endless delay.

quiz.q: Two processes use only turn: process i enters when turn == i and sets turn to the other on exit. Which requirement fails?
quiz.explain: Processes are forced to alternate strictly. If one wants to enter twice while the other is in its remainder section, it must wait even though the critical section is empty.

quiz.q: In Peterson's solution, what is the entry section for process i?
options: flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j);
quiz.explain: The process announces interest with flag[i] = true, politely gives the turn to j, then waits only while j is interested and it is j's turn.

quiz.q: Why can Peterson's solution fail on a modern multicore computer?
options: It needs more than two processes
The CPU or compiler may reorder independent reads and writes
It does not use a turn variable
quiz.explain: Modern processors and compilers may reorder memory operations for speed. Without memory barriers, both processes might see the other's flag as false and enter together.

lessons.title: Hardware Support and Locks
lessons.content:
Think of a single-toilet bathroom in a busy Dhaka office. There is a simple sign on the door: when you go in, you flip it to Occupied, and when you leave, you flip it back to Vacant. This works only if flipping the sign is instant and only one person can flip it at a time. If two people looked at Vacant at exactly the same moment and both walked in, the system would fail embarrassingly. Computers need the same kind of door sign for critical sections, called a lock. And just like the sign, the lock only works if checking it and flipping it happen as one indivisible action. Software alone, as we saw with Peterson's solution, struggles to promise this on modern hardware. So the hardware itself provides special instructions, and on top of them we build locks.

Disabling interrupts: On a computer with only one core, there is an old simple trick. A context switch can only happen through an interrupt, such as the timer. So a process could disable interrupts before entering its critical section and enable them again after. Nothing can interrupt it in between, so nobody else can run. But this is a poor general solution. On a multicore machine, disabling interrupts on one core does nothing to stop threads on other cores. Disabling interrupts on all cores is slow, because the message must be sent to every core. And letting user programs disable interrupts would be dangerous: a buggy program could stop the timer and freeze the system. So disabling interrupts is used only inside the kernel, for very short pieces of code.

Memory barriers: In the last lesson we saw that modern processors may reorder memory reads and writes for speed. A memory barrier, also called a memory fence, is an instruction that forces all memory operations before it to complete and become visible to other cores before any memory operation after it starts. Placing a barrier between flag[i] = true; turn = j; and the while loop would make Peterson's solution correct again. Barriers are very low-level; ordinary programmers rarely write them directly, but locks and atomic operations use them internally.

Test-and-set: Most processors provide an atomic instruction that reads a memory word and changes it in one indivisible step. The classic one is test_and_set. It works like this, but as a single hardware action: boolean test_and_set(boolean *target) { boolean rv = *target; *target = true; return rv; }. It returns the old value and always leaves the variable set to true. If two cores run test_and_set on the same variable at the same time, the hardware runs them one after another, never interleaved.

A lock with test-and-set: With a shared boolean lock initialised to false, mutual exclusion is easy: while (test_and_set(&lock)) do nothing; critical section; lock = false. Walk through it. If the lock is free, test_and_set returns false and sets it to true, so the loop ends and the thread enters. Any other thread that tries now gets true back and keeps looping. When the first thread leaves, it sets lock = false, and the next test_and_set by a waiting thread returns false and lets it in. Only one test_and_set can ever see false and flip the lock, so only one thread is ever inside.

Compare-and-swap: The other classic instruction is compare_and_swap, or CAS. It takes three arguments: a memory location, an expected value and a new value. Conceptually: int compare_and_swap(int *value, int expected, int new_value) { int temp = *value; if (*value == expected) *value = new_value; return temp; }. In words: if the location still holds what I expect, replace it with the new value; either way, tell me what was there. Again the whole thing is one atomic hardware action. On x86 processors this is the CMPXCHG instruction used with a LOCK prefix. ARM processors offer exclusive load and store instructions that let software build the same effect.

A lock with CAS: With an int lock initialised to 0: while (compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) != 0) do nothing; critical section; lock = 0. The first thread finds lock equal to 0, the expected value, so CAS sets it to 1 and returns 0, and the thread enters. Others find 1, not 0, so CAS changes nothing and returns 1, and they keep looping. These simple versions guarantee mutual exclusion and progress, but not bounded waiting: an unlucky thread could lose the race again and again. A slightly longer algorithm with a waiting array, in which the leaving thread hands the lock to the next waiting thread in a circular order, fixes that, guaranteeing that any waiting thread enters within n minus 1 turns.

Atomic variables: Often we only need to update a single number safely, like a counter. Most systems provide atomic variables with operations such as atomic increment, built on CAS. An atomic increment can be written as: do { old = *v; } while (compare_and_swap(v, old, old + 1) != old). Read the value, try to swap in old + 1, and if somebody else changed it in the meantime, try again. In C11 there is atomic_int with atomic_fetch_add, in Java AtomicInteger, in C++ std::atomic. With an atomic counter, our two threads incrementing a million times each would always reach exactly two million. But atomic variables only protect one variable; they cannot protect a group of updates that must happen together, like moving money between two accounts.

Mutex locks: Hardware instructions are too low-level for everyday use, so operating systems and libraries offer the mutex lock, short for mutual exclusion lock. A mutex has two operations: acquire, which waits until the lock is free and then takes it, and release, which frees it. A program uses it like this: acquire(); critical section; release(). Calls to acquire and release must themselves be atomic, which is done with test-and-set or CAS internally. In Pthreads these are pthread_mutex_lock and pthread_mutex_unlock. A mutex should be held for as short a time as possible, protecting only the code that really touches shared data.

Spinlocks: The simplest way to implement acquire is to loop until the lock is free, as in the test-and-set code. A lock that waits by looping is called a spinlock, because the waiting thread spins. Spinning wastes CPU time, so it sounds bad. But it has one big advantage: no context switch. If the lock will be held only very briefly, spinning for a few hundred nanoseconds is cheaper than putting the thread to sleep and waking it up, which costs two context switches. A common rule: spinning is a good choice on multicore systems when the lock is held for less than the time of two context switches. On a single core, spinning is pointless, because the lock holder cannot run while you spin. Kernels use spinlocks heavily for very short critical sections.

Blocking locks: For locks that may be held longer, a better approach is to block. If the lock is taken, acquire puts the thread to sleep in a waiting queue for that lock, and the CPU runs something else. When the holder releases the lock, one waiting thread is woken up and moved to the ready queue. No CPU time is wasted on spinning, but each wait costs context switches. Many real mutex implementations are hybrids: they spin for a short time first, hoping the lock becomes free quickly, and then block if it does not.

Lock contention: A lock is uncontended if it is free when a thread tries to acquire it, and contended if the thread has to wait. Uncontended locks are cheap. Highly contended locks hurt performance, because threads keep waiting and the work becomes serial, exactly the serial part that Amdahl's law warns about. Good designs keep critical sections short and use several smaller locks for different data instead of one giant lock for everything.

Priority inversion: Locks and priorities can interact badly. Suppose three tasks have priorities low L, medium M and high H. L holds a lock that H needs, so H waits. Now M, which needs no lock, becomes ready. M has higher priority than L, so it preempts L. Now H, the most important task, is waiting for L, which cannot run because of M. In effect, the medium task is delaying the high one. This is priority inversion. A famous real case happened on NASA's Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997: a priority inversion caused repeated system resets until engineers enabled a fix from Earth. The usual fix is priority inheritance: while L holds a lock that H is waiting for, L temporarily inherits H's priority, so M cannot preempt it. When L releases the lock, its priority goes back to normal.

Real-life example 1, a shared printer in an office: In a Motijheel office, twenty employees print to one printer through a print server. The server's queue of jobs is shared data. Each new job must be added to the queue while holding a lock, so two jobs arriving at the same instant do not overwrite the same slot. Adding a job takes microseconds, so a spinlock or short mutex works well. But actually printing a 50-page document takes minutes, so the server does not hold the queue lock while printing; it removes the job under the lock, releases the lock, and then prints. Keeping the critical section short keeps everybody moving.

Real-life example 2, a mobile wallet's balance: A mobile wallet server updates a customer's balance when payments arrive. If a merchant payment and a cash-in arrive at the same moment, both must update the same balance. Using an atomic add for a single balance could work, but a transfer between two customers changes two balances and must look like one step. So the server takes locks on both accounts, always in the same order, for example lower account number first, does both updates, and releases the locks. Locking in a fixed order also helps avoid deadlock, which we study soon.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Many students think disabling interrupts is a good solution on multicore machines; it is not. Some write test_and_set as if it were two separate steps, missing the point that it is atomic. Others assume spinlocks are always bad; on multicore with short critical sections, they are often the best choice. Typical questions: define test_and_set and compare_and_swap and write a lock using each; explain why disabling interrupts fails on multiprocessors; compare spinlocks and blocking mutexes; explain priority inversion and priority inheritance; show how CAS builds an atomic increment.

Recap: Disabling interrupts only works on one core and only in the kernel. Memory barriers stop harmful reordering. Atomic hardware instructions, test_and_set and compare_and_swap, read and change a word in one indivisible step, and simple loops around them give mutual exclusion. Atomic variables protect single values. Mutex locks wrap this into acquire and release; a spinlock waits by looping and suits very short sections on multicore, while blocking locks sleep and suit longer waits. Priority inversion lets a medium task delay a high one, and priority inheritance fixes it. Next lesson: semaphores and monitors, more powerful tools built on locks.
key_points: Disabling interrupts can protect a critical section only on a single core and only in kernel code.
A memory barrier forces earlier memory operations to complete and become visible before later ones.
test_and_set atomically returns the old value and sets the variable to true; while (test_and_set(&lock)); gives a simple lock.
compare_and_swap atomically replaces a value only if it equals the expected value, and returns the old value.
Atomic variables, built on CAS, protect single values like counters but not groups of related updates.
A spinlock waits by looping: good on multicore when the lock is held shorter than two context switches; blocking locks sleep instead.
Priority inversion: a medium task delays a high-priority task waiting for a lock held by a low task; priority inheritance fixes it.
lessons.tip: When you write lock code with test_and_set or CAS, trace it with two threads arriving at the same instant. Remember that the hardware serialises the two atomic instructions, so ask yourself: which one sees the old free value?
lessons.task: On paper, trace two threads, T1 and T2, using the CAS lock while (compare_and_swap(&lock, 0, 1) != 0); with lock starting at 0. Assume T1's CAS runs first. Write the value of lock and the return value of each CAS for the first three attempts of each thread, then show what happens when T1 sets lock back to 0.

quiz.q: Why is disabling interrupts not a good way to protect critical sections on a multicore machine?
options: Threads on other cores can still run and enter the critical section
It only works for user programs
quiz.explain: Disabling interrupts on one core stops context switches there, but threads on other cores keep running and can still touch the shared data.

quiz.q: What does test_and_set(&lock) return when lock was false before the call?
options: false, and it leaves lock set to true
true, and it leaves lock false
false, and it leaves lock false
It does not return a value
quiz.explain: test_and_set returns the old value (false) and always sets the variable to true, all in one atomic step. Getting false back means the caller has acquired the lock.

quiz.q: When is a spinlock usually a good choice?
options: On a single-core system with long critical sections
When the lock will be held for many seconds
When threads should sleep while waiting
On a multicore system when the lock is held for a very short time
quiz.explain: Spinning avoids two context switches. That is worthwhile only if the wait is shorter than those switches and the holder can run on another core.

quiz.q: compare_and_swap(&x, 5, 9) is called when x is 7. What happens?
options: x becomes 9 and the call returns 5
x becomes 5 and the call returns 9
x stays 7 and the call returns 7
x becomes 9 and the call returns 7
quiz.explain: CAS only writes the new value if the current value equals the expected value. 7 is not 5, so nothing changes and the old value 7 is returned.

quiz.q: What is the standard fix for priority inversion?
quiz.explain: With priority inheritance, the low-priority lock holder temporarily gets the high priority of the waiting task, so a medium-priority task cannot preempt it.

lessons.title: Semaphores and Monitors
lessons.content:
Imagine the parking lot of a shopping mall in Bashundhara with exactly 3 empty spaces. At the gate there is a digital board showing the number of free spaces: 3. When a car enters, the board goes down by one. When a car leaves, it goes up by one. When the board shows 0, the guard stops new cars at the gate, and they wait in a line. As soon as one car leaves, the guard lets the first waiting car in. This little board is a perfect picture of a semaphore, one of the most famous tools in operating systems. It was invented by the Dutch computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra in the 1960s, and it lets processes coordinate in more ways than a simple lock.

What a semaphore is: A semaphore S is an integer variable that, apart from being initialised, can only be accessed through two atomic operations: wait and signal. Dijkstra originally called them P and V, from Dutch words; you will also see them called down and up, or sem_wait and sem_post in POSIX. The simple definitions are: wait(S) { while (S <= 0) do nothing; S--; } and signal(S) { S++; }. The test and the decrement in wait, and the increment in signal, must happen atomically, so no two processes can change S at the same time.

Counting and binary semaphores: A counting semaphore can have any non-negative value and is used to control access to a resource with several identical instances, like the 3 parking spaces or 5 printers. It is initialised to the number of instances. A binary semaphore can only be 0 or 1 and behaves much like a mutex lock. Initialised to 1, it gives mutual exclusion: wait(mutex); critical section; signal(mutex). The first process to call wait brings it from 1 to 0 and enters; the next one finds 0 and must wait until signal brings it back to 1.

Using semaphores for ordering: Semaphores can also force an order between processes, which a plain lock cannot do as neatly. Suppose statement S1 in process P1 must happen before statement S2 in process P2, for example P1 writes a file and P2 must read it only afterwards. Use a semaphore synch initialised to 0. P1 runs: S1; signal(synch);. P2 runs: wait(synch); S2;. If P2 gets there first, it finds synch = 0 and waits. Only after P1 finishes S1 and signals does synch become 1, letting P2 continue. The order is guaranteed no matter how the scheduler interleaves them.

Removing busy waiting: The simple definition of wait spins in a loop, wasting CPU just like a spinlock. A better implementation lets a waiting process sleep. Each semaphore has an integer value and a list of waiting processes. wait(S): S.value--; if (S.value < 0) { add this process to S.list; sleep(); }. signal(S): S.value++; if (S.value <= 0) { remove a process P from S.list; wakeup(P); }. Sleep moves the process to the waiting state; wakeup moves it back to ready. Notice that in this version the value can become negative, and when it is negative, its size tells how many processes are waiting.

Worked example: A lab has 3 printers, so a counting semaphore printers starts at 3. Five processes, A to E, each call wait(printers) in that order. A: value becomes 2, A prints. B: value 1, B prints. C: value 0, C prints. D: value becomes -1, which is negative, so D sleeps in the list. E: value becomes -2, so E sleeps too. The value -2 says two processes are waiting. Now A finishes and calls signal: value becomes -1, which is less than or equal to 0, so one waiting process, D, is woken and gets A's printer. Then B signals: value 0, E wakes up. Then C, D and E finish one by one, and the value climbs back to 3. Count the printers in use at every step and you will see it never goes above 3.

Making wait and signal atomic: The semaphore operations themselves are critical sections, because two processes must not change S.value at the same moment. On a single core, the kernel can disable interrupts during wait and signal. On multicore systems it uses spinlocks or compare-and-swap. So busy waiting is not removed completely; it is moved to the very short critical sections inside wait and signal, which take only a few instructions, instead of the application's critical section, which may be long.

Semaphores in real code: On Linux and other POSIX systems, you create an unnamed semaphore with sem_init(&s, 0, 3), where the last number is the starting value, then call sem_wait(&s) and sem_post(&s), which are wait and signal. The middle argument says whether the semaphore is shared only between threads of one process (0) or between processes (non-zero, in shared memory). Named semaphores, opened with sem_open and a name such as /printers, let completely unrelated processes share one semaphore. There is also sem_trywait, which never sleeps: if the value is 0 it returns an error at once, so a program can do something else instead of waiting.

Semaphore mistakes: Semaphores are powerful but easy to misuse, and the errors are hard to find because they only show up with unlucky timing. If a programmer swaps the order and writes signal(mutex); critical section; wait(mutex);, several processes can be in the critical section at once, so mutual exclusion is broken. If they write wait(mutex); critical section; wait(mutex);, the process blocks itself forever on the second wait, which is a deadlock. If they forget wait, mutual exclusion is lost; if they forget signal, others wait forever.

Semaphores and deadlock: Even correct-looking code can deadlock. Take two semaphores S and Q, both initialised to 1. Process P0 runs wait(S); wait(Q); and process P1 runs wait(Q); wait(S);. If P0 does wait(S) and then P1 does wait(Q), each holds one semaphore and waits for the other. P0 waits on Q, which only P1 can signal; P1 waits on S, which only P0 can signal. Neither can ever continue. This is a deadlock, the subject of two later lessons. A related problem is starvation: if processes are removed from a semaphore's list in LIFO order, some might wait forever.

Monitors: Because semaphores are so error-prone, language designers created a higher-level tool: the monitor. A monitor is like a class or module that contains shared data and the procedures that operate on it, with one key rule enforced by the language: only one process or thread can be active inside the monitor at a time. The programmer does not write wait and signal for mutual exclusion; the compiler adds it automatically around every monitor procedure. So the classic semaphore mistakes cannot happen for mutual exclusion.

Condition variables: Mutual exclusion alone is not enough; sometimes a thread inside the monitor must wait for some condition, such as the buffer not being empty. For this, monitors offer condition variables. A condition variable x supports two operations. x.wait() suspends the calling thread and releases the monitor, so others can enter. x.signal() resumes exactly one thread waiting on x; if no thread is waiting, it does nothing at all. This is different from a semaphore's signal, which always increases the value and is remembered even if nobody is waiting.

Who runs after signal: When thread P calls x.signal() and wakes thread Q, both could be inside the monitor, which breaks the one-at-a-time rule. There are two choices. In signal and wait, P waits until Q leaves the monitor or waits again. In signal and continue, Q waits until P leaves the monitor or waits. Many real systems, including Java and Pthreads, use signal and continue. Because the condition may change before Q actually runs, Q should re-check its condition in a loop: while (!condition) x.wait();. Using if instead of while is a classic bug.

Monitors in real languages: Java gives every object a built-in monitor. A method marked synchronized holds the object's lock while it runs, and wait(), notify() and notifyAll() act as a single condition variable. C# has the lock statement and Monitor class. In C with Pthreads, you build the same thing yourself from a mutex and condition variables: pthread_mutex_lock, pthread_cond_wait, pthread_cond_signal and pthread_mutex_unlock. pthread_cond_wait releases the mutex while sleeping and takes it back before returning, exactly like a monitor's x.wait().

Implementing a monitor with semaphores: Monitors can be built from semaphores, which shows that both tools are equally powerful. A binary semaphore mutex, initialised to 1, guards entry to the monitor: each procedure begins with wait(mutex) and ends with signal(mutex). Each condition variable gets its own semaphore, initialised to 0, plus a counter of waiting threads. The details are fiddly, which is exactly why we prefer the compiler to do it for us.

Real-life example 1, ride-sharing drivers: Imagine an app like Pathao in a small town with 4 available bikes. A counting semaphore bikes starts at 4. Each ride request calls wait(bikes); when a ride ends, signal(bikes). When all 4 bikes are busy, the fifth customer's request sleeps in the waiting list instead of spinning, and is woken as soon as any ride ends. A separate binary semaphore protects the shared list of which bike is where, so two requests never assign the same bike.

Real-life example 2, a kitchen order board: In a busy restaurant, waiters pin orders on a board and the cook takes them. The board is a monitor: only one person may change it at a time. If the cook finds the board empty, he waits on a condition variable orderAvailable instead of staring at it. When a waiter pins a new order, she calls orderAvailable.signal(), and the cook wakes up, checks the board again in a loop, and starts cooking. If no cook was waiting, her signal is simply lost, which is fine, because the next cook who comes will see the order on the board.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often forget that a condition variable's signal does nothing when nobody is waiting, while a semaphore's signal is always remembered in its count. Another mistake is thinking a negative semaphore value is an error; in the blocking version it simply counts waiting processes. Many also write if instead of while around x.wait(). Typical questions: define wait and signal; distinguish counting and binary semaphores; use a semaphore to enforce order; trace a counting semaphore's value with several processes; show how swapping wait and signal breaks things; explain monitors and condition variables; compare signal and wait with signal and continue.

Recap: A semaphore is an integer with atomic wait and signal. Counting semaphores manage several identical resources; binary semaphores give mutual exclusion; a semaphore initialised to 0 enforces order. The blocking implementation keeps a list of sleeping processes, and a negative value counts them. Semaphores are easy to misuse and can deadlock. Monitors package shared data and procedures so that only one thread is inside at a time, with condition variables for waiting; signal on a condition does nothing if nobody waits, and waiters should re-check in a while loop. Next lesson: classic synchronisation problems solved with these tools.
key_points: A semaphore is an integer accessed only through atomic wait (P) and signal (V) operations.
A counting semaphore, initialised to N, controls N identical resources; a binary semaphore initialised to 1 gives mutual exclusion.
A semaphore initialised to 0 enforces order: P1 does S1; signal(synch); and P2 does wait(synch); S2.
In the blocking implementation, a negative value tells how many processes are sleeping on the semaphore.
Swapping wait and signal breaks mutual exclusion; two waits on the same mutex deadlocks; acquiring two semaphores in opposite orders can deadlock.
A monitor allows only one thread inside at a time; condition variables let threads wait inside it.
x.signal() wakes one waiting thread or does nothing if none waits; waiters should re-check their condition with a while loop.
lessons.tip: When tracing semaphore problems, keep three columns: the semaphore value, the list of sleeping processes and who is in the critical section. Update all three after every wait and signal.
lessons.task: A semaphore S starts at 2. Processes call, in order: wait (P1), wait (P2), wait (P3), wait (P4), signal (P1), signal (P2), wait (P5). Using the blocking version, write the value of S and the waiting list after each call. Which processes are waiting at the end?

quiz.q: A counting semaphore for 3 printers starts at 3. Five processes call wait one after another. Using the blocking implementation, what is the value afterwards?
quiz.explain: Each wait subtracts 1: 3 becomes 2, 1, 0, -1, -2. The value -2 means two processes are sleeping in the waiting list.

quiz.q: P2's statement S2 must run only after P1's statement S1. With synch initialised to 0, what should P2 do?
quiz.explain: P2 waits on synch, which is 0 until P1 runs S1 and then signal(synch). This forces S1 to happen before S2.

quiz.q: A programmer writes signal(mutex); critical section; wait(mutex); by mistake. What goes wrong?
options: Several processes may be in the critical section at the same time
The semaphore value becomes negative forever
quiz.explain: signal first raises the value, letting other processes in, so mutual exclusion is violated.

quiz.q: What happens when x.signal() is called on a monitor condition variable and no thread is waiting on x?
options: The signal is saved for the next thread that calls x.wait()
The monitor is unlocked for everyone
quiz.explain: Unlike a semaphore's signal, a condition variable's signal has no memory. If nobody is waiting, it has no effect.

quiz.q: Why should a thread re-check its condition in a while loop after x.wait() returns, in a signal-and-continue monitor?
options: Because the condition may have changed again before the woken thread actually runs
Because monitors allow many threads inside at once
quiz.explain: With signal and continue, the signaller keeps running and other threads may enter first, so the condition may no longer hold when the waiter resumes.

lessons.title: Classic Synchronisation Problems
lessons.content:
Every sport has standard drills. Cricketers practise the same cover drive a thousand times in the nets, because once they master it, they can use it in any match. Operating systems have their own standard drills too: a handful of classic synchronisation problems that capture the patterns found in real systems. If you can solve these, you can recognise and solve most real concurrency problems, and exam papers ask about them almost every year. In this lesson we solve three classics with semaphores and monitors: the bounded buffer, the readers-writers problem and the dining philosophers, and then glance at the sleeping barber.

The bounded buffer problem: We met this producer-consumer problem in the IPC lesson. A producer puts items into a buffer with n slots, and a consumer takes them out. The producer must wait when the buffer is full, the consumer must wait when it is empty, and the two must never modify the buffer at the same instant. Earlier we used a busy-waiting loop and could only fill n minus 1 slots. Semaphores solve all of this cleanly.

Bounded buffer with three semaphores: We use three semaphores. mutex, initialised to 1, guards the buffer itself. empty, initialised to n, counts the empty slots. full, initialised to 0, counts the filled slots. Producer: wait(empty); wait(mutex); add the item to the buffer; signal(mutex); signal(full). Consumer: wait(full); wait(mutex); remove an item from the buffer; signal(mutex); signal(empty). Read it like a story: the producer first waits for an empty slot, then locks the buffer, adds the item, unlocks, and announces one more full slot. The consumer mirrors this. Notice the symmetry: the producer produces full slots for the consumer, and the consumer produces empty slots for the producer.

Tracing the bounded buffer: Let n = 2. Start: empty = 2, full = 0, mutex = 1. The producer adds item A: empty 1, full 1. It adds item B: empty 0, full 2. It tries to add C: wait(empty) makes empty -1 in the blocking version, so the producer sleeps. The consumer now removes A: full becomes 1, and its signal(empty) brings empty to 0 and wakes the producer, which adds C, and full goes back to 2. Every slot is used, and nobody busy-waits.

Why the order of waits matters: What if the producer did wait(mutex) before wait(empty)? Imagine the buffer is full. The producer locks mutex, then blocks on empty while still holding the mutex. The consumer wants to remove an item, but first calls wait(mutex), which is held by the sleeping producer. The consumer blocks too. Now the producer waits for the consumer to free a slot, and the consumer waits for the producer to release mutex. That is a deadlock. Rule: wait on the counting semaphore first, take the mutex last, and hold the mutex for as short a time as possible. The order of the two signals does not matter for correctness.

The bounded buffer as a monitor: The same problem looks even simpler as a monitor. Keep a count of items and two condition variables, notFull and notEmpty. insert(item): while (count == n) notFull.wait(); add the item; count++; notEmpty.signal(). remove(): while (count == 0) notEmpty.wait(); take an item; count--; notFull.signal(). Mutual exclusion comes free from the monitor, so there is no mutex to forget and no wrong order of waits to worry about. The while loops re-check the condition after waking, exactly as the last lesson advised.

The readers-writers problem: Now imagine a shared database, such as a train timetable. Many processes only read it; some processes update it. Reading at the same time is perfectly safe, so we want to allow many readers together. But a writer must have exclusive access: no other writer and no reader may be inside while it writes, or someone could read half-updated data. The challenge is to allow concurrent reading while keeping writing exclusive.

The first readers-writers solution: This version gives readers priority. Shared data: semaphore rw_mutex = 1, semaphore mutex = 1, integer read_count = 0. Writer: wait(rw_mutex); write; signal(rw_mutex). Reader: wait(mutex); read_count++; if (read_count == 1) wait(rw_mutex); signal(mutex); read; wait(mutex); read_count--; if (read_count == 0) signal(rw_mutex); signal(mutex). The first reader to arrive locks writers out, and the last reader to leave lets them in. Readers in the middle just update the counter. The mutex only protects read_count.

Tracing readers-writers: Reader R1 arrives: read_count becomes 1, so R1 does wait(rw_mutex) and takes it. R2 arrives: read_count becomes 2, no need to touch rw_mutex, R2 reads alongside R1. Writer W arrives: wait(rw_mutex) blocks, because the readers hold it. R1 leaves: read_count 1. R2 leaves: read_count 0, so R2 signals rw_mutex, and W wakes up and writes alone. While W writes, a new reader R3 arrives, increments read_count to 1 and blocks on rw_mutex, holding mutex. Any further readers queue up behind it on mutex. When W finishes, R3 gets in, and the queued readers follow.

Starvation in readers-writers: In the first solution, no reader waits just because a writer is waiting. If readers keep arriving so that read_count never drops to zero, a waiting writer may never get in: writer starvation. The second readers-writers problem flips the priority: once a writer is ready, no new readers may start, so writers go as soon as possible. But then readers can starve. Fairer solutions exist, and many systems offer ready-made reader-writer locks, such as pthread_rwlock_t in Pthreads, with a read lock that many can hold and a write lock that only one can hold. They are most useful when reads greatly outnumber writes.

The dining philosophers problem: Dijkstra posed this famous puzzle. Five philosophers sit around a round table, thinking and eating. In the centre is a bowl of rice, and between each pair of neighbours lies a single chopstick, so there are five chopsticks in all. To eat, a philosopher needs both the chopstick on the left and the one on the right, and can pick up only one at a time. After eating, she puts both down and thinks again. The problem represents any situation where several processes need several shared resources at once.

The simple semaphore solution and its deadlock: Represent each chopstick by a semaphore initialised to 1: chopstick[5]. Philosopher i runs: wait(chopstick[i]); wait(chopstick[(i + 1) % 5]); eat; signal(chopstick[i]); signal(chopstick[(i + 1) % 5]); think. This guarantees that no two neighbours eat at once. But suppose all five get hungry at the same moment and each picks up her left chopstick. Now every chopstick is taken, and each philosopher waits forever for her right one. Deadlock. Nobody eats, ever.

Fixing the philosophers: There are several standard remedies. One: allow at most four philosophers at the table at once, using a counting semaphore initialised to 4; then at least one of them can always get both chopsticks. Two: let a philosopher pick up chopsticks only if both are available, doing the check and the pick-up inside a critical section. Three: use an asymmetric rule: odd-numbered philosophers pick up the left chopstick first, even-numbered ones pick up the right first. That breaks the circle of waiting, so a deadlock cannot form.

The monitor solution: A neat monitor solution uses the second idea. Each philosopher has a state: THINKING, HUNGRY or EATING, and a condition variable self[i]. pickup(i) sets state[i] = HUNGRY and calls test(i); if she could not start eating, she does self[i].wait(). test(i) checks: if state[i] is HUNGRY and neither neighbour is EATING, set state[i] = EATING and self[i].signal(). putdown(i) sets state[i] = THINKING and then calls test on the left and right neighbours, in case they were waiting. This solution is deadlock-free, because a philosopher only eats when both chopsticks are free. However, it is still possible for one philosopher to starve if her neighbours keep taking turns eating.

The sleeping barber: One more classic. A barber shop has one barber, one barber chair and n waiting chairs. If there are no customers, the barber sleeps. A customer who arrives and finds all waiting chairs full leaves. If the barber is asleep, the customer wakes him. Otherwise, the customer sits and waits. It is solved with a semaphore customers that counts waiting customers, a semaphore barber that says whether the barber is ready, and a mutex that protects the count of waiting customers. It models a server with a limited queue, like a call centre that plays a busy message when the queue is full.

What these problems teach: Look at the three classics together and two kinds of synchronisation appear. The first is mutual exclusion: only one at a time touches the buffer, only one writer at a time changes the database. The second is condition synchronisation: wait until there is an empty slot, wait until there are no readers, wait until both chopsticks are free. Most real bugs come from mixing these up, from taking locks in different orders, or from rules that let someone wait forever. Whenever you meet a new concurrency problem, ask three questions: what must be exclusive, what must wait for what, and can anyone starve?

Real-life example 1, Facebook News Feed: A huge number of people read posts on Facebook every second, while comparatively few update any one post. Systems like this are designed so that reads proceed in parallel without blocking each other, while updates are coordinated carefully. Inside one server, a reader-writer lock on a data structure is the textbook version of this idea: many readers at once, one writer at a time.

Real-life example 2, a restaurant kitchen: In a busy kitchen, the cook needs a pan and a burner at the same time. If one cook grabs the last pan and waits for a burner, while another grabs the last burner and waits for a pan, both stand still: dining philosophers in real life. Good kitchens have a rule, like always take the burner first, which is exactly the ordering trick that prevents deadlock.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In the bounded buffer, students often swap wait(empty) and wait(mutex), creating deadlock, or forget that empty must start at n, not 0. In readers-writers, many forget that only the first reader locks rw_mutex and only the last reader unlocks it. In dining philosophers, many say that the simple solution is wrong because two neighbours can eat together; it is actually wrong because it can deadlock. Typical questions: write producer and consumer code with three semaphores and explain each semaphore; write the first readers-writers solution and explain who can starve; explain how dining philosophers deadlocks and give three solutions; write the monitor solution.

Recap: The bounded buffer uses mutex = 1, empty = n and full = 0, with the counting wait before the mutex wait. Readers-writers lets many readers share access while a writer gets exclusive access; the first version can starve writers, the second can starve readers. Dining philosophers shows how processes that each grab one resource and wait for another can deadlock; limiting diners to four, picking up both or none, or asymmetric ordering avoids it. The sleeping barber models a server with a limited waiting room. Next lesson: deadlocks in general, their four conditions and how to prevent them.
key_points: Bounded buffer uses three semaphores: mutex = 1, empty = n and full = 0.
Producer: wait(empty); wait(mutex); add; signal(mutex); signal(full). Consumer: wait(full); wait(mutex); remove; signal(mutex); signal(empty).
Doing wait(mutex) before wait(empty) can deadlock when the buffer is full.
In the first readers-writers solution, the first reader locks rw_mutex and the last reader unlocks it; writers may starve.
In the second readers-writers solution, writers get priority and readers may starve; reader-writer locks offer shared read and exclusive write.
Dining philosophers deadlocks if all five pick up their left chopstick at the same time.
Fixes: at most four at the table, pick up both chopsticks or none, or odd and even philosophers pick up in different orders.
lessons.tip: For every classic problem, memorise the starting value of each semaphore and say in one sentence what it counts or protects. If you remember "empty counts empty slots, full counts full slots, mutex protects the buffer", the code writes itself.
lessons.task: Five friends sit around a round table with five pens between them, and each needs two pens to sign a form. Act out the deadlock where everyone grabs the pen on their left. Then try the odd-even rule: friends 1, 3 and 5 grab left first, 2 and 4 grab right first. Check that at least one friend can always sign.

quiz.q: In the bounded buffer solution with n slots, what are the initial values of mutex, empty and full?
quiz.explain: mutex = 1 protects the buffer, empty = n because all slots start empty, and full = 0 because no slots start full.

quiz.q: What happens if the producer calls wait(mutex) before wait(empty) when the buffer is full?
options: The consumer reads an empty slot
Nothing, the order does not matter
Deadlock: the producer sleeps holding mutex, and the consumer cannot get mutex to free a slot
quiz.explain: The producer blocks on empty while holding mutex. The consumer needs mutex to remove an item and signal empty, so both wait forever.

quiz.q: In the first readers-writers solution, which reader calls wait(rw_mutex)?
options: Only the first reader to arrive (when read_count becomes 1)
Only the last reader to leave
quiz.explain: The first reader locks out writers; later readers just increase read_count. The last reader to leave signals rw_mutex.

quiz.q: Who may starve in the first readers-writers solution?
quiz.explain: Readers have priority. If new readers keep arriving, read_count never reaches zero, so a waiting writer may never get rw_mutex.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT prevent deadlock in the dining philosophers problem?
options: Allowing at most four philosophers to sit at once
Every philosopher picking up the left chopstick first
Picking up both chopsticks only if both are free
Odd philosophers picking up left first and even ones right first
quiz.explain: If everyone picks up the left chopstick first, all five can hold one chopstick and wait forever for the right one. The other three rules break the circular wait.

lessons.title: Deadlocks I: Conditions, Graphs and Prevention
lessons.content:
Picture a narrow lane in Old Dhaka, just wide enough for one rickshaw. A rickshaw enters from the north end, and at the same moment another enters from the south end. They meet in the middle. Neither can move forward, because the other is in the way, and neither wants to back out. Behind each of them, more rickshaws pile up. Nobody moves, possibly for a very long time. This is a deadlock: a group of participants, each waiting for something that only another member of the group can give, so none of them can ever proceed. Operating systems face exactly this problem when processes compete for resources, and this lesson explains what causes deadlocks, how to draw them and how to design systems so they cannot happen.

The system model: A system has a fixed number of resource types, such as CPU cycles, memory space, files, printers, mutex locks and semaphores. Each type may have several identical instances; a system with two identical printers has a printer type with two instances. A process uses a resource in three steps. Request: if the resource cannot be granted immediately, the process waits. Use: the process works with the resource. Release: the process gives it back. Requests and releases may be system calls, such as open and close for files, or operations like wait and signal on semaphores, or acquire and release on locks.

What a deadlock is: A set of processes is in a deadlocked state when every process in the set is waiting for an event that can be caused only by another process in the set. The events are usually resource releases. For example, process P1 holds the scanner and waits for the printer; process P2 holds the printer and waits for the scanner. Each waits for the other to release, which will never happen, because each is stuck waiting. A deadlock is different from starvation: in starvation a process could proceed but keeps being passed over; in deadlock nobody in the group can proceed at all. A related situation is livelock, where processes keep actively changing state, like two people in a corridor who both keep stepping aside the same way, yet make no progress.

Deadlock with locks in code: In multithreaded programs, deadlocks often come from locks. Thread 1 does: lock(first); lock(second); work; unlock both. Thread 2 does: lock(second); lock(first); work; unlock both. If Thread 1 gets first and, at the same time, Thread 2 gets second, each then waits forever for the other's lock. What makes this nasty is that it only happens with a particular timing, so the program may run fine for months and then freeze.

Four necessary conditions: In 1971, Coffman and colleagues described four conditions that must all hold at the same time for a deadlock to occur. One, mutual exclusion: at least one resource is non-sharable, so only one process can use it at a time. Two, hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting to get more resources held by others. Three, no preemption: resources cannot be forcibly taken away; a process releases a resource only voluntarily. Four, circular wait: there is a chain of waiting processes P0, P1, ..., Pn, where P0 waits for a resource held by P1, P1 waits for P2, and so on, and Pn waits for P0. All four are necessary. Break any one of them and deadlock becomes impossible. Circular wait actually implies hold and wait, but it is useful to think of them separately.

Resource-allocation graphs: Deadlocks are easiest to see with a picture called a resource-allocation graph. Draw each process as a circle and each resource type as a rectangle, with one dot inside for each instance. A request edge goes from a process to a resource type, Pi to Rj, meaning Pi is waiting for an instance of Rj. An assignment edge goes from an instance dot of a resource to a process, Rj to Pi, meaning that instance is held by Pi. When a request is granted, its request edge turns into an assignment edge; when the resource is released, the assignment edge disappears.

Reading the graph: There are three simple rules. If the graph has no cycle, no process is deadlocked. If there is a cycle and every resource type in the cycle has only one instance, then a deadlock exists, and every process in the cycle is deadlocked. If there is a cycle but some resource types have several instances, a deadlock may or may not exist; you must look more closely. So with single instances, a cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock; with multiple instances, a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

Worked example with a cycle: Three processes, P1, P2, P3, and four resource types: R1 with one instance, R2 with two, R3 with one, R4 with three. Edges: R1 is held by P2, one instance of R2 is held by P1 and the other by P2, R3 is held by P3. P1 requests R1, and P2 requests R3. Follow the arrows: P1 to R1 to P2 to R3 to P3, and P3 is not waiting for anything, so there is no cycle. P3 will finish, release R3, P2 gets it, finishes, releases R1, and P1 can proceed. Now add one more request: P3 requests R2. Both instances of R2 are held, by P1 and P2. Now there are two cycles: P1 to R1 to P2 to R3 to P3 to R2 to P1, and P2 to R3 to P3 to R2 to P2. P3 waits for R2, held by P1 and P2; P2 waits for R3, held by P3; P1 waits for R1, held by P2. Nobody can move. All three are deadlocked.

Worked example of a cycle without deadlock: Four processes. R1 has two instances, one held by P2 and one by P3. R2 has two instances, one held by P1 and one by P4. P1 requests R1, and P3 requests R2. There is a cycle: P1 to R1 to P3 to R2 to P1. But P2 and P4 are not waiting for anything. P4 can finish and release its instance of R2, which P3 then gets. Or P2 can finish and release R1, which P1 gets. The cycle breaks, so there is no deadlock. This is why a cycle alone does not prove deadlock when resources have several instances.

Four ways to handle deadlocks: An OS can deal with deadlocks in four ways. Prevention: design the system so at least one of the four conditions can never hold. Avoidance: use advance information about what processes will need, and grant requests only when it is safe. Detection and recovery: let deadlocks happen, detect them, and recover. Ignore the problem: pretend deadlocks never happen. Surprisingly, the last approach is what most general-purpose operating systems, including Linux and Windows, do for application resources, leaving it to programmers; it is sometimes jokingly called the ostrich algorithm. Databases, by contrast, usually detect deadlocks and recover. This lesson covers prevention; the next covers avoidance, detection and recovery.

Preventing mutual exclusion: Sharable resources, such as read-only files, never need mutual exclusion; many processes can read them together. But some resources, like a mutex lock or a printer in the middle of a page, are by nature non-sharable. So we usually cannot prevent deadlock by denying mutual exclusion. Spooling helps a little for printers: processes write output to a disk queue, and only the printer daemon touches the real printer.

Preventing hold and wait: We must guarantee that whenever a process requests a resource, it holds no others. Option one: a process requests and gets all its resources before it starts running. Option two: a process may request resources only when it holds none, so it must release everything before asking for more. Both work but have costs. Resource utilisation is low, because resources are held long before they are needed. And starvation is possible: a process needing several popular resources may wait forever for all of them to be free at once.

Preventing no preemption: If a process holding some resources requests another that cannot be given immediately, all the resources it holds are taken away, preempted, and added to its list of wanted resources. It restarts only when it can get its old resources plus the new one. Another version: if the requested resource is held by a process that is itself waiting, take it from that waiting process. This works for resources whose state can be saved and restored easily, such as CPU registers and memory. It does not work for things like mutex locks and printers, which cannot be snatched away safely in the middle of use.

Preventing circular wait: This is the most practical approach. Give every resource type a unique number, and require that each process requests resources only in increasing order of number. For example, number the resources tape drive = 1, disk drive = 5 and printer = 12. A process wanting the disk and the printer must request the disk first, then the printer. Why does this prevent circular wait? Suppose a cycle existed: P0 holds Ri and waits for Rj, P1 holds Rj and waits for Rk, and so on back to P0. Increasing order means i is less than j is less than k and so on, around the whole cycle and back to i, which would require i to be less than i, which is impossible. So no cycle can form. For locks, this is the rule "always acquire locks in the same global order". Tools exist to check it; the Linux kernel, for example, has a lock validator called lockdep.

A trap with lock ordering: Ordering only works if programs truly follow it. Consider a bank function transfer(from, to, amount) that does lock(from); lock(to). If one thread calls transfer(A, B) and another calls transfer(B, A) at the same time, the first locks A then wants B, the second locks B then wants A. Deadlock, even though every call locks "from" then "to". The fix is to order by something fixed, such as account number: always lock the lower account number first, whatever the direction of transfer.

Real-life example 1, the Dhaka traffic gridlock: At a four-way junction, cars from all four directions enter the middle and block each other: each lane's front car waits for the space held by the car in front of it, around the square. All four conditions hold: road space is exclusive, each car holds its spot while waiting for the next, cars cannot be lifted away, and the waiting forms a circle. Traffic police break the deadlock by forcing some cars to reverse, which is preemption, and junction rules like "don't enter the box unless your exit is clear" prevent hold and wait.

Real-life example 2, a university lab booking: A lab has one projector and one microphone. Teacher A books the projector and then tries to book the microphone; Teacher B booked the microphone and now wants the projector. Both wait. The lab office makes a rule: always book the projector before the microphone, and the deadlock disappears, because nobody can hold the microphone while waiting for the projector. That is circular-wait prevention by ordering.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often say that a cycle in a resource-allocation graph always means deadlock; it does only when each resource in the cycle has one instance. Many also forget that all four conditions must hold together; breaking any one is enough. Another mistake is confusing deadlock with starvation. Typical questions: state and explain the four necessary conditions; draw a resource-allocation graph and decide whether there is a deadlock; describe how each condition can be prevented and the cost; prove that ordered resource requests prevent circular wait.

Recap: A deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for an event that only another in the set can cause. It needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait all at once. A resource-allocation graph shows request and assignment edges; no cycle means no deadlock, a cycle with single-instance resources means deadlock, and a cycle with multi-instance resources means maybe. Systems can prevent, avoid, detect or ignore deadlocks. Prevention breaks a condition: requesting everything at once, preempting resources, or, most usefully, numbering resources and requesting them in increasing order. Next lesson: deadlock avoidance with the banker's algorithm, and detection and recovery.
key_points: A deadlock is a set of processes, each waiting for an event that only another process in the set can cause.
The four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait; all must hold at once.
In a resource-allocation graph, a request edge goes from process to resource and an assignment edge goes from resource instance to process.
No cycle means no deadlock; a cycle with only single-instance resources means deadlock; with multi-instance resources a cycle means deadlock is possible.
The four strategies are prevention, avoidance, detection and recovery, and ignoring the problem (common in general-purpose OSes).
Preventing hold and wait or no preemption works but lowers resource use and can cause starvation.
Numbering resources and always requesting them in increasing order prevents circular wait.
lessons.tip: When you see a resource-allocation graph, first count the dots in each resource box. With one dot each, just look for a cycle. With more dots, try to find a process that can finish and release its resources, and repeat.
lessons.task: Draw a resource-allocation graph for this situation: P1 holds R1 and requests R2; P2 holds R2 and requests R3; P3 holds R3 and requests R1; each resource has one instance. Is there a deadlock? Now give R3 a second instance held by nobody and redraw. Does the deadlock remain?

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four necessary conditions for deadlock?
quiz.explain: The four conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Starvation is a different problem.

quiz.q: A resource-allocation graph has a cycle, and every resource in the cycle has exactly one instance. What can you conclude?
options: There may or may not be a deadlock
quiz.explain: With single-instance resources, a cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock. Every process in the cycle is deadlocked.

quiz.q: Resources are numbered and every process must request them in increasing order. Which condition does this break?
quiz.explain: If every process requests resources in increasing order, a cycle would need a resource number to be smaller than itself, which is impossible.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of preventing hold and wait by making processes request all resources at the start?
options: Resources are held long before they are needed, lowering utilisation, and starvation is possible
quiz.explain: Grabbing everything early ties up resources that sit unused, and a process needing many popular resources may wait forever for all of them at once.

quiz.q: transfer(from, to) locks from, then to. Two threads run transfer(A, B) and transfer(B, A) together. What can happen, and what fixes it?
options: A race condition; fix by removing locks
Deadlock; fix by always locking the lower account number first
quiz.explain: Each thread may hold one lock and wait for the other. Locking in a fixed global order, such as lower account number first, prevents the circular wait.

lessons.title: Deadlocks II: Avoidance, Banker's Algorithm, Detection and Recovery
lessons.content:
Imagine a small bank in a Bangladeshi town that lends money to local businesses. It has only 12 lakh taka in its vault. Each business tells the bank the maximum it might ever need for its project, and borrows in parts. The banker is careful: before giving out any more money, she asks herself, "If I lend this, is there still some order in which every customer can get the rest of what they need, finish their project and repay me?" If yes, she lends. If no, she makes the customer wait, even though the money is sitting in the vault. This careful banker is exactly the idea behind deadlock avoidance and the famous banker's algorithm, invented by Dijkstra. In this lesson we work through it with full numbers, and then look at how systems detect and recover from deadlocks when they do happen.

The idea of avoidance: Prevention, from the last lesson, makes deadlock impossible by restricting how processes may ask for resources, which can waste resources. Avoidance is smarter: it lets processes ask in any order, but it requires each process to declare in advance the maximum number of each resource type it may need. With that information, the OS decides, for every request, whether granting it could possibly lead to deadlock. If it might, the process waits, even if the resources are free.

Safe state: A state is safe if there exists at least one order of all processes, called a safe sequence, such that each process in turn can get all the resources it might still need, using the currently free resources plus those released by the processes before it in the sequence. If such a sequence exists, the system can always finish everyone, so no deadlock can occur. If no such sequence exists, the state is unsafe. An important point: an unsafe state is not necessarily a deadlock. It just means the OS can no longer guarantee to avoid one; with unlucky requests, a deadlock could follow. Deadlocked states are a subset of unsafe states. Avoidance simply never enters an unsafe state.

Safe state worked example: A system has 12 tape drives. Process P0 may need up to 10 and holds 5; P1 may need up to 4 and holds 2; P2 may need up to 9 and holds 2. So 9 are in use and 3 are free. Is this safe? Try the sequence P1, P0, P2. P1 needs at most 2 more, and 3 are free, so it can finish and release its 4, making 5 free. P0 needs at most 5 more, and 5 are free, so it can finish and release 10. P2 needs at most 7 more, and 10 are free, so it finishes. The sequence works, so the state is safe. Now suppose P2 asks for one more drive and gets it. Free drives drop to 2, and P2 holds 3. P1 can still finish, making 4 free. But now P0 may need 5 and P2 may need 6, and only 4 are free. No safe sequence exists, so the state is unsafe. The avoidance algorithm would make P2 wait instead.

The resource-allocation-graph algorithm: When each resource type has a single instance, avoidance can use a resource-allocation graph with an extra kind of edge, the claim edge, drawn dashed from a process to a resource it may request in the future. When the process actually requests the resource, the claim edge becomes a request edge. The request is granted only if turning the request edge into an assignment edge does not create a cycle in the graph, claim edges included. Checking for a cycle takes about n squared steps for n processes. For multiple instances, we need the banker's algorithm.

Banker's algorithm data structures: Suppose there are n processes and m resource types. Available is a vector of length m: how many instances of each type are free now. Max is an n by m matrix: the maximum demand of each process for each type. Allocation is an n by m matrix: how many of each type each process holds now. Need is an n by m matrix: how many more each process may still request. The key relation is Need = Max minus Allocation, worked out row by row.

The safety algorithm: To test whether a state is safe: Step one: let Work = Available and set Finish[i] = false for every process. Step two: find a process i with Finish[i] = false and Need[i] less than or equal to Work, comparing every resource type. If there is none, go to step four. Step three: pretend process i finishes and returns its resources: Work = Work + Allocation[i], Finish[i] = true, and go back to step two. Step four: if Finish[i] is true for every process, the state is safe, and the order in which they finished is a safe sequence. This takes on the order of m times n squared operations.

The resource-request algorithm: When process i requests a vector Request[i]: Step one: if Request[i] is greater than Need[i] in any type, raise an error, because the process asked for more than it declared. Step two: if Request[i] is greater than Available in any type, the process must wait, because the resources are not free. Step three: pretend to grant it: Available = Available minus Request[i], Allocation[i] = Allocation[i] + Request[i], Need[i] = Need[i] minus Request[i]. Then run the safety algorithm. If the new state is safe, the request is really granted. If it is unsafe, undo the pretend changes and make the process wait.

Banker's worked example, the setup: Five processes, P0 to P4, and three resource types: A with 10 instances, B with 5 and C with 7. Allocation (A B C): P0 0 1 0, P1 2 0 0, P2 3 0 2, P3 2 1 1, P4 0 0 2. Max: P0 7 5 3, P1 3 2 2, P2 9 0 2, P3 2 2 2, P4 4 3 3. Adding the allocations gives A 7, B 2, C 5 in use, so Available = 10 minus 7, 5 minus 2, 7 minus 5 = 3 3 2. Need = Max minus Allocation: P0 7 4 3, P1 1 2 2, P2 6 0 0, P3 0 1 1, P4 4 3 1.

Banker's worked example, the safety check: Work = 3 3 2. P0 needs 7 4 3: no, 7 is more than 3. P1 needs 1 2 2: yes, it fits in 3 3 2. P1 finishes; Work = 3 3 2 + 2 0 0 = 5 3 2. Look again from the top. P0 needs 7 4 3: no. P2 needs 6 0 0: no, 6 is more than 5. P3 needs 0 1 1: yes. Work = 5 3 2 + 2 1 1 = 7 4 3. P0 needs 7 4 3: yes, exactly. Work = 7 4 3 + 0 1 0 = 7 5 3. P2 needs 6 0 0: yes. Work = 7 5 3 + 3 0 2 = 10 5 5. P4 needs 4 3 1: yes. Work = 10 5 5 + 0 0 2 = 10 5 7, which is all the resources, as it should be. Safe sequence: P1, P3, P0, P2, P4. Other safe sequences also exist, such as P1, P3, P4, P2, P0. Any one is enough to prove the state is safe.

Banker's worked example, requests: Now P1 requests 1 0 2. Step one: is 1 0 2 within P1's Need of 1 2 2? Yes. Step two: is it within Available 3 3 2? Yes. Step three: pretend. Available becomes 2 3 0, P1's Allocation becomes 3 0 2, and its Need becomes 0 2 0. Safety check with Work = 2 3 0: P1 needs 0 2 0, fits, Work becomes 5 3 2; P3 needs 0 1 1, fits, Work 7 4 3; P0 needs 7 4 3, fits, Work 7 5 3; P2, Work 10 5 5; P4, Work 10 5 7. Safe, so the request is granted. Next, in this new state, P4 requests 3 3 0. Available is only 2 3 0, so P4 must wait; the resources simply are not there. Then P0 requests 0 2 0. It is within its Need and within Available, so pretend: Available becomes 2 1 0. Now check: P0 needs 7 2 3, P1 needs 0 2 0 but only 1 B is free, P2 needs 6 0 0, P3 needs 0 1 1 but no C is free, P4 needs 4 3 1. Nobody fits. The state would be unsafe, so P0's request is refused and P0 waits, even though the resources are free.

Limits of avoidance: The banker's algorithm is beautiful, but it is rarely used in general-purpose operating systems. Processes must know their maximum needs in advance, which is hard in practice. The number of processes and resources changes all the time. And running the safety check on every request costs time. It is used where needs are well known, and above all it is a favourite exam topic, because it tests careful step-by-step reasoning.

Deadlock detection, single instances: If a system neither prevents nor avoids deadlocks, it can let them happen and then detect them. When each resource has one instance, collapse the resource-allocation graph into a wait-for graph: draw an edge from Pi to Pj if Pi is waiting for a resource that Pj holds. A deadlock exists if and only if the wait-for graph has a cycle. A cycle search takes on the order of n squared steps for n processes. Databases use exactly this to find transactions that block each other.

Deadlock detection, multiple instances: For several instances per type, use an algorithm much like the safety algorithm, but with each process's current Request instead of Need. Example: five processes, resources A 7, B 2, C 6. Allocation: P0 0 1 0, P1 2 0 0, P2 3 0 3, P3 2 1 1, P4 0 0 2. Request: P0 0 0 0, P1 2 0 2, P2 0 0 0, P3 1 0 0, P4 0 0 2. Available 0 0 0. P0 requests nothing, so it can finish: Work 0 1 0. P2 requests nothing: Work 3 1 3. P1 requests 2 0 2, fits: Work 5 1 3. P3 requests 1 0 0: Work 7 2 4. P4 requests 0 0 2: Work 7 2 6. Everyone finishes, so there is no deadlock. Now change P2's request to 0 0 1. After P0 finishes, Work is 0 1 0, and no other process's request fits. P1, P2, P3 and P4 are deadlocked.

Recovery by termination: Once a deadlock is found, the system must break it. One way is to kill processes. Abort all deadlocked processes: simple and certain, but all their work is lost. Or abort one process at a time and re-run detection after each, until the cycle is gone: less waste, but more overhead. The victim is chosen by cost: lower priority, less time already run, fewer resources held, more time still needed, and whether it is interactive or batch.

Recovery by preemption: The other way is to take resources away from some processes and give them to others. Three issues appear. Selecting a victim: pick the one that costs least to interrupt. Rollback: the victim cannot just continue without its resource, so it must be rolled back to a safe earlier state, or simply restarted from the beginning. Starvation: if the same process is always picked as the victim, it may never finish; a common fix is to include the number of times it has been rolled back in the cost.

Real-life example 1, a bank loan officer: The opening story is literal for some loan officers. A bank with 12 crore taka promises credit lines to three garment factories. Before releasing another instalment, the officer checks whether she can still complete every factory's maximum needs in some order. If one big release would leave her unable to fund anyone fully, she delays it, even though the money is in the vault. That is the safety check.

Real-life example 2, a database at an e-commerce company: During a big sale on an online shop, two transactions update stock: one locks shoes then socks, another locks socks then shoes. The database's lock manager builds a wait-for graph, finds the cycle, chooses one transaction as the victim, rolls it back and returns an error to that customer's request, which the app retries a moment later. The customer just sees a short delay. That is detection with recovery by rollback.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The most common banker's mistakes are computing Need wrongly, comparing only one resource type instead of all, and forgetting to add the finished process's Allocation, not its Max, to Work. Another is thinking an unsafe state is already a deadlock. In the request algorithm, students forget to check Request against Need first. Typical questions: compute Need, find a safe sequence, decide whether a request can be granted, run the detection algorithm, draw a wait-for graph, and discuss recovery options.

Recap: Avoidance needs each process's maximum demand and grants a request only if the resulting state is safe, meaning some safe sequence lets every process finish. Unsafe does not mean deadlocked, but it might lead there. The banker's algorithm uses Available, Max, Allocation and Need = Max minus Allocation, a safety algorithm and a request algorithm; in our example, the safe sequence was P1, P3, P0, P2, P4, P1's request 1 0 2 was granted, and P0's later request 0 2 0 was refused. Detection uses a wait-for graph for single instances or a request-based algorithm for multiple instances. Recovery kills processes or preempts resources with rollback. Next lesson: memory management.
key_points: Avoidance requires each process to declare its maximum need and grants requests only if the system stays in a safe state.
A safe state has a safe sequence in which every process can get its remaining needs and finish; unsafe states may lead to deadlock but are not deadlocks yet.
Banker's data: Available, Max, Allocation and Need = Max minus Allocation.
Safety algorithm: Work = Available; repeatedly find a process with Need less than or equal to Work, then Work = Work + its Allocation.
Request algorithm: check Request against Need, then against Available, pretend to grant, and keep the grant only if the new state is safe.
In the classic example (A 10, B 5, C 7) the safe sequence P1, P3, P0, P2, P4 exists, P1's request (1, 0, 2) is granted and P0's later request (0, 2, 0) is refused.
Detection uses a wait-for graph cycle for single instances, or a Request-based safety-like algorithm for multiple instances; recovery kills processes or preempts resources with rollback.
lessons.tip: In banker's problems, write the Need matrix first and circle it. Then keep a running Work line under the table and write the process name each time you add an Allocation row. Your safe sequence is just that list of names.
lessons.task: Redo the classic banker's example yourself without looking: compute Need, find a safe sequence, then test the request (1, 0, 2) from P1 and (0, 2, 0) from P0. Then make up your own request, such as P3 asking for (0, 1, 0), and decide if it can be granted.

quiz.q: In the banker's algorithm, how is the Need matrix computed?
quiz.explain: Need is how much more each process may still request: its declared maximum minus what it already holds.

quiz.q: Available is (3, 3, 2). Which process can finish first if Needs are P0 (7, 4, 3), P1 (1, 2, 2), P2 (6, 0, 0), P3 (0, 1, 1), P4 (4, 3, 1), checking from P0 upward?
quiz.explain: Checking in order, P0 needs 7 A and P2 needs 6 A, both more than 3. P1's (1, 2, 2) fits in (3, 3, 2), so it is the first process found.

quiz.q: What does an unsafe state mean?
options: No process can ever run again
The OS cannot guarantee that deadlock will be avoided, though deadlock has not necessarily happened
quiz.explain: Deadlocked states are a subset of unsafe states. Unsafe only means no safe sequence exists, so unlucky future requests could cause deadlock.

quiz.q: For single-instance resources, which structure is used to detect deadlock?
options: A wait-for graph, where a cycle means deadlock
quiz.explain: Collapsing the resource-allocation graph gives a wait-for graph with an edge Pi to Pj when Pi waits for Pj. A cycle means deadlock.

quiz.q: After granting P1's request in the classic example, Available is (2, 3, 0). P0 requests (0, 2, 0). What happens?
options: It is granted, because the resources are free
It is an error, because P0 asked for more than its Need
P0 must wait, because the resources are not available
P0 must wait, because granting it would leave the system in an unsafe state
quiz.explain: The request fits Need and Available, but after pretending to grant it, Available would be (2, 1, 0) and no process's Need fits, so the state would be unsafe.

lessons.title: Memory Management Basics
lessons.content:
Imagine a big hostel with one long hall of beds, and students arriving and leaving all day. The hostel superintendent must decide where each new student sleeps. A group of five friends wants five beds side by side. There are free beds here and there, but no five free beds in a row, even though there are eight free beds in total. Should the superintendent shuffle everyone around to make space? Should he have put the earlier groups somewhere else? This is the problem of memory management. Main memory, the RAM, is a long row of bytes, and the OS must decide where each process lives, keep processes from stepping on each other, and use the space well. This lesson covers the basic ideas, before paging solves most of the problems in the next lesson.

Why memory management matters: The CPU can only directly access registers and main memory. A program on disk must be brought into memory before it can run, and the data it uses must be in memory too. Registers are accessed within one CPU clock cycle; main memory can take many cycles, which is why caches sit in between, as you learned in Computer Architecture. With many processes in memory at once for multiprogramming, the OS must share memory between them efficiently and safely.

Protection with base and limit registers: Each process must have its own separate memory space, and must not touch anyone else's or the OS's. One simple hardware scheme uses two registers. The base register holds the smallest legal physical address of the process, and the limit register holds the size of its range. Every address the process generates in user mode is checked by hardware: it must be at least base and less than base plus limit. Example: base = 300040 and limit = 120900. Then legal addresses run from 300040 up to 420939, because 300040 + 120900 = 420940 is the first illegal address. If the process tries address 420940 or 299999, the hardware traps to the OS, which treats it as a fatal error. Only the OS, in kernel mode, can load the base and limit registers.

Address binding: In a source program, addresses are symbolic, like a variable named count. A compiler turns them into relocatable addresses, like "14 bytes from the start of this module". Then they must be bound to actual memory addresses. Binding can happen at three times. At compile time, if you know where the process will live in memory, the compiler can produce absolute code; if the location changes, you must recompile. At load time, the compiler produces relocatable code, and the loader fixes the final addresses when the program is loaded. At execution time, binding is delayed until the program runs, so the process can even be moved in memory while running. This needs hardware support, and it is what nearly all modern operating systems use.

Logical and physical addresses: An address generated by the CPU is called a logical address, also called a virtual address. The address actually seen by the memory unit is the physical address. With compile-time or load-time binding, the two are the same. With execution-time binding, they differ. The set of all logical addresses a program can generate is its logical address space; the matching set of physical addresses is its physical address space. The program never sees physical addresses; it lives entirely in its logical world.

The memory management unit: The run-time mapping from logical to physical addresses is done by a hardware device called the memory management unit, or MMU. The simplest MMU uses a relocation register, which is the base register under another name. Every logical address is added to the relocation register to get the physical address. Example: if the relocation register is 14000, a logical address of 346 becomes the physical address 14000 + 346 = 14346. If the OS moves the process to start at 20000, it just changes the relocation register to 20000, and the same logical address 346 now maps to 20346. The program itself never notices. Combined with a limit check, this gives both relocation and protection.

Dynamic loading and linking: To use memory better, a routine does not have to be loaded until it is called. With dynamic loading, unused routines, such as rarely used error handlers, never take up memory. With dynamic linking, common libraries, such as the C library, are linked when the program runs instead of being copied into every program file. These shared libraries, called DLLs on Windows and .so files on Linux, can be loaded into memory once and shared by many processes. Fixing a bug in the library then fixes all programs that use it.

Swapping: Sometimes there is not enough memory for all processes. A process, or part of it, can be swapped temporarily out of memory to a backing store, usually a fast disk or SSD, and brought back later to continue. Swapping whole processes is slow. Example: a 100 MB process and a transfer rate of 50 MB per second takes 2 seconds to swap out and 2 seconds to swap in, 4 seconds in total, an eternity for a CPU. So modern systems rarely swap whole processes. Instead they swap individual pages, which we study in the paging lessons. Mobile systems like Android and iOS generally do not swap to flash storage at all; when memory is low they ask apps to free memory, or end background apps, which is why apps sometimes restart when you switch back to them.

Contiguous memory allocation: In early systems, and as a simple model, each process gets a single contiguous block of memory.
