Memory is often divided into two parts: one for the OS and one for user processes. In the variable-partition scheme, the OS keeps a table of which parts of memory are free and which are in use. At first, all user memory is one big block called a hole. As processes arrive, they are placed in holes; as they leave, their space becomes a hole again, and neighbouring holes merge. After a while, memory looks like a patchwork of processes and holes of many sizes.

Choosing a hole: When a process arrives and needs n bytes, which hole should it get? There are three classic strategies. First fit: give it the first hole that is big enough, searching from the beginning. Best fit: give it the smallest hole that is big enough, which leaves the smallest leftover; this requires searching the whole list unless it is sorted by size. Worst fit: give it the largest hole, hoping the leftover will be big enough to be useful later. Simulations show that first fit and best fit are better than worst fit in both time and storage use, and first fit is usually faster.

Worked example of fits: Free holes in order: 100 KB, 500 KB, 200 KB, 300 KB and 600 KB. Processes arrive in order needing 212 KB, 417 KB, 112 KB and 426 KB. First fit: 212 goes into 500, leaving 288. 417 goes into 600, leaving 183. 112 goes into the 288 leftover, leaving 176. 426: the holes are now 100, 176, 200, 300 and 183, and none is big enough, so it must wait. Best fit: 212 goes into 300, the smallest that fits, leaving 88. 417 goes into 500, leaving 83. 112 goes into 200, leaving 88. 426 goes into 600, leaving 174. All four fit. Worst fit: 212 goes into 600, leaving 388. 417 goes into 500, leaving 83. 112 goes into 388, leaving 276. 426 must wait, since the largest hole is now 300. In this example, best fit is the only one that places every process.

External fragmentation: As processes come and go, free memory gets broken into many small holes. There may be enough total free memory for a new process, but no single hole is large enough. This is external fragmentation. In the first-fit example, the free holes total 100 + 176 + 200 + 300 + 183 = 959 KB, more than double the 426 KB needed, yet the process cannot be placed. Analysis of first fit shows a rule of thumb called the 50-percent rule: with N blocks allocated, about another 0.5 N blocks are lost to fragmentation, so about one-third of memory may be unusable.

Internal fragmentation: Tracking tiny leftover holes costs more than they are worth, so systems often divide memory into fixed-size blocks and give each process a whole number of blocks. Then a process may get slightly more than it asked for. The unused space inside an allocated block is internal fragmentation. Example: with 4 KB blocks, a process needing 10 KB gets 3 blocks, 12 KB, and wastes 2 KB inside its own allocation. External fragmentation is wasted space between allocations; internal fragmentation is wasted space inside them.

Compaction: One fix for external fragmentation is compaction: shuffle the processes in memory so all the free holes come together into one large block. In the hostel story, this is waking everyone and moving their beds so all the empty ones are at one end. Compaction is only possible if relocation is dynamic, done at execution time, because the processes' physical addresses change and only the relocation register needs updating. But it is expensive: copying large amounts of memory takes time, and during compaction the processes cannot run. The other, better fix is to let a process's memory be non-contiguous, so it can use whatever free pieces exist. That is exactly what paging does.

Real-life example 1, parking cars on a street: Cars of different lengths park along a street in Dhanmondi with no marked spaces. Over the day, cars leave and leave behind gaps of odd sizes: one metre here, two metres there. A big microbus arrives and cannot find space, even though the total empty kerb would easily fit three microbuses. That is external fragmentation. Some streets paint fixed-size bays instead: now no odd gaps form, but a small car in a big bay wastes some space inside its bay, which is internal fragmentation.

Real-life example 2, a smartphone running many apps: When you open many apps on a phone with limited RAM, the OS must find memory for each new app. Instead of requiring one long block, modern phones use paging, which avoids external fragmentation. But when total memory runs low, Android ends background apps to free space. That is why, after you play a heavy game, your browser may reload its tabs: its process was ended and its memory given to the game.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up internal and external fragmentation; remember, internal is inside an allocated block, external is between them. Another mistake is forgetting that the limit register holds a size, not an end address, so the last legal address is base plus limit minus one. In fit problems, many forget that a hole shrinks after use and can be used again by later processes. Typical questions: explain address binding times; distinguish logical and physical addresses; compute a physical address with a relocation register; check addresses against base and limit; apply first, best and worst fit to a list of holes; explain fragmentation and compaction.

Recap: Memory management keeps processes in RAM safely and efficiently. Base and limit registers protect each process's range. Addresses can be bound at compile, load or execution time; with execution-time binding, the CPU's logical addresses are translated to physical addresses by the MMU, in the simplest case by adding a relocation register. Dynamic loading and shared libraries save memory, and swapping moves processes to disk when memory is short. Contiguous allocation places each process in one hole using first, best or worst fit, but suffers external fragmentation, which compaction can fix at a high cost. Fixed-size blocks cause internal fragmentation. Next lesson: paging, which lets a process's memory be scattered across many small frames.
key_points: Base and limit registers protect a process: a legal address is at least base and less than base plus limit.
Address binding can happen at compile time, load time or execution time; modern systems bind at execution time.
The CPU generates logical (virtual) addresses; the MMU translates them to physical addresses, simplest by adding a relocation register.
Swapping whole processes is slow (a 100 MB process at 50 MB/s takes 4 s in and out); modern systems swap pages instead.
First fit takes the first big-enough hole, best fit the smallest big-enough hole, worst fit the largest hole.
External fragmentation is enough total free memory split into holes too small to use; internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block.
Compaction moves processes together to merge holes but needs execution-time relocation and is expensive.
lessons.tip: For fit problems, draw the holes as boxes in a row and cross out and rewrite the leftover size each time a process goes in. Never re-sort the list unless the question says so; first fit always scans from the start.
lessons.task: Using holes of 150, 350, 200, 500 and 250 KB (in that order), place processes of 120, 300, 230 and 210 KB with first fit, best fit and worst fit. For each strategy, list the holes left and say whether every process fits.

quiz.q: The base register is 300040 and the limit register is 120900. Which address is illegal?
quiz.explain: Legal addresses are from base up to base plus limit minus one: 300040 to 420939. 420940 equals base plus limit, so it traps.

quiz.q: The relocation register holds 14000. What physical address does logical address 346 map to?
quiz.explain: With a relocation register, physical = relocation + logical = 14000 + 346 = 14346.

quiz.q: Holes are 100, 500, 200, 300 and 600 KB. Using best fit, where does a 212 KB process go?
quiz.explain: Best fit picks the smallest hole that is big enough. 100 and 200 are too small; 300 is the smallest that fits.

quiz.q: A system gives memory in 4 KB blocks. A process needs 10 KB. How much internal fragmentation is there?
quiz.explain: The process gets 3 blocks = 12 KB. 12 minus 10 = 2 KB is wasted inside its own allocation.

quiz.q: What is the main requirement for compaction to be possible?
options: Addresses must be bound at execution time (dynamic relocation)
All processes must be the same size
The system must use first fit
quiz.explain: Compaction moves processes in physical memory. That only works if their addresses are translated at run time, so updating the relocation register is enough.

lessons.title: Paging
lessons.content:
Think of a big book, say a 400-page cricket encyclopaedia, that you need to store in a library whose shelves are full of gaps. There is no single empty shelf long enough for the whole book. But what if you could tear the book into small chapters of equal size and put each chapter in any empty slot, wherever there is space? You would just need an index card that says chapter 1 is in slot 57, chapter 2 is in slot 3, chapter 3 is in slot 120, and so on. Then any free slot can be used, and no gap is too small. That is exactly the idea of paging, the memory management scheme used by almost every modern operating system. It lets a process's memory be scattered across physical memory, which ends external fragmentation.

The basic idea: Physical memory is divided into fixed-size blocks called frames. Logical memory, the process's own view of its addresses, is divided into blocks of the same size called pages. When a process runs, its pages are loaded into any available frames, in any order. A page table for each process records which frame holds each page. The process still sees one neat, continuous logical address space starting from 0, while in reality its pieces may be anywhere in RAM.

Page size: Page and frame sizes are always a power of 2, typically between 512 bytes and 1 GB depending on the architecture. The most common size today is 4 KB, which is 4096 bytes, or 2 to the power 12. Many systems also support larger pages, such as 2 MB, for special uses. Using powers of 2 makes address translation very easy, as we will see.

Splitting an address: Every logical address is split into two parts: a page number p and a page offset d. The page number is used as an index into the page table. The offset is the position within the page. If the logical address space is 2 to the power m and the page size is 2 to the power n, then the high-order m minus n bits of an address are the page number and the low-order n bits are the offset. For a 32-bit address with 4 KB pages, the offset uses 12 bits and the page number uses 20 bits. Mathematically, p = address divided by page size, ignoring the remainder, and d = address mod page size.

Translation step by step: To translate a logical address, the MMU does three steps. Step one: extract the page number p and offset d. Step two: look up p in the page table to find the frame number f. Step three: the physical address is f times page size plus d. In binary, this is simply replacing the page number bits with the frame number bits and keeping the offset bits unchanged. The offset never changes, because a page and a frame are the same size.

Worked example 1, a tiny memory: Page size is 4 bytes, logical memory has 4 pages, which is 16 bytes, and physical memory has 8 frames, which is 32 bytes. The page table says page 0 is in frame 5, page 1 in frame 6, page 2 in frame 1 and page 3 in frame 2. Logical address 0 is page 0, offset 0, so physical address = 5 times 4 + 0 = 20. Logical address 3 is page 0, offset 3, so physical = 20 + 3 = 23. Logical address 4 is page 1, offset 0, so physical = 6 times 4 + 0 = 24. Logical address 13 is page 3, offset 1, because 13 divided by 4 is 3 with remainder 1, so physical = 2 times 4 + 1 = 9. Notice how logical addresses 12 to 15 live at physical 8 to 11, before the process's page 0 at 20: physical order does not matter.

Worked example 2, real sizes: Page size 4 KB = 4096 bytes. A process uses logical address 20000. Page number = 20000 divided by 4096 = 4, remainder 20000 minus 4 times 4096 = 20000 minus 16384 = 3616. So p = 4 and d = 3616. Suppose the page table says page 4 is in frame 7. Physical address = 7 times 4096 + 3616 = 28672 + 3616 = 32288. In hexadecimal it is even easier: address 0x3A7F with 4 KB pages has the last three hex digits as offset, A7F, and the rest as page number, 3. If page 3 is in frame 9, the physical address is simply 0x9A7F.

No external fragmentation, some internal: Any free frame can be used by any process that needs one, so paging has no external fragmentation. But the last page of a process is usually not completely full, so there is internal fragmentation. Example: with 2,048-byte pages, a process of 72,766 bytes needs 35 full pages, which is 71,680 bytes, plus 1,086 bytes. It gets 36 frames, and the last frame wastes 2,048 minus 1,086 = 962 bytes. On average, the waste is half a page per process. Smaller pages waste less, but need bigger page tables; that is the trade-off, and over the years page sizes have tended to grow.

The frame table: The OS also keeps a frame table, one entry per physical frame, saying whether it is free or which page of which process it holds. When a new process arrives needing n pages, the OS checks that at least n frames are free, takes them from the free-frame list, loads the pages and fills in the new process's page table.

Where page tables live: Each process has its own page table, kept in main memory. A register called the page-table base register, PTBR, points to the current process's page table. On a context switch, the OS just changes the PTBR, which is fast. But now there is a problem: every memory access by the program needs two memory accesses, one to read the page table entry and one for the actual data. That would make every program run about twice as slow.

The TLB: The fix is a small, very fast hardware cache called the translation look-aside buffer, or TLB. It holds a few recently used page-to-frame translations, typically between 32 and 1,024 entries, and it searches all entries in parallel. When the CPU generates a logical address, the MMU first looks for the page number in the TLB. If it is there, a TLB hit, the frame number is available almost at once. If not, a TLB miss, the page table in memory is read, and the translation is added to the TLB, replacing an old one if it is full. Because programs tend to reuse nearby addresses, which is called locality, hit ratios are usually very high.

Effective access time worked: Suppose one memory access takes 100 ns and we ignore the tiny TLB search time. With an 80 percent TLB hit ratio, a hit needs one memory access, 100 ns, and a miss needs two, 200 ns. Effective access time = 0.80 times 100 + 0.20 times 200 = 80 + 40 = 120 ns, a 20 percent slowdown compared with no paging. With a 99 percent hit ratio: 0.99 times 100 + 0.01 times 200 = 99 + 2 = 101 ns, only a 1 percent slowdown. That is why the TLB makes paging practical.

TLB and context switches: Different processes use the same page numbers for different frames, so the TLB must not mix them up. Either the TLB is flushed, emptied, on every context switch, which causes many misses afterwards, or each TLB entry carries an address-space identifier, ASID, that names the process it belongs to, so entries from several processes can live side by side. Some TLB entries, such as those for kernel code, can be wired down so they are never removed.

Protection: Each page table entry carries extra bits. A valid-invalid bit says whether the page is part of the process's logical address space; touching an invalid page traps to the OS. Protection bits say whether the page may be read, written or executed; writing to a read-only page, such as code, also traps. Some systems use a page-table length register, PTLR, to say how many entries the page table has, so addresses beyond the end are caught. Because a process can only reach frames listed in its own page table, it cannot touch another process's memory at all. Protection comes almost for free.

Shared pages: Paging also makes sharing easy. If code is reentrant, meaning it never modifies itself, several processes can map the same physical frames into their page tables. Example: 40 users run the same text editor, with 150 KB of code and 50 KB of private data each. Without sharing, that needs 40 times 200 = 8,000 KB. With shared code, it needs one copy of the 150 KB code plus 40 times 50 KB of data, which is 150 + 2,000 = 2,150 KB. Shared libraries like the C library, and the copy-on-write fork from the process lessons, both rely on shared pages.

Page table size: Page tables can be big. With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages, there are 2 to the power 20, about one million, pages. If each entry is 4 bytes, the page table alone takes 4 MB, for every process, and it must be contiguous in a simple design. With 64-bit addresses, a simple table would be astronomically large. The next lesson shows how hierarchical, hashed and inverted page tables solve this.

Real-life example 1, a big hostel's room list: A university hall has 500 identical rooms. When a new batch arrives, each student is given any free room, not necessarily next to friends. The office keeps a register: student roll 1 is in room 214, roll 2 in room 37, and so on. Students still talk about "roll 1, roll 2", their logical numbering, while the office translates to real rooms. No room is too small for a student, so no space is wasted between rooms. A student with a tiny amount of luggage still gets a whole room, which is internal fragmentation.

Real-life example 2, your laptop running Chrome and VS Code: When you open Chrome, the OS gives each of its processes pages scattered across RAM. Several Chrome processes, and other programs too, share pages for common libraries, so the code is in RAM only once. The TLB inside your CPU keeps recent translations, so even though each memory access is translated, programs run nearly at full speed. When you close a tab, its frames simply go back on the free-frame list.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often divide by the page size but forget to compute the offset as the remainder. Others multiply the page number, not the frame number, by the page size when finding the physical address. Many say paging has no fragmentation at all; it has no external fragmentation, but it does have internal fragmentation in the last page. In EAT problems, read whether the question includes TLB search time; if it does, add it to both the hit and miss cases. Typical questions: split an address into page and offset; translate logical to physical using a page table; compute the number of bits for page and offset; compute page table size; compute effective access time with a TLB; explain shared pages and protection bits.

Recap: Paging divides physical memory into frames and logical memory into pages of the same size, a power of 2. An address is split into page number and offset; the page table maps page to frame, and physical address = frame times page size plus offset. Paging removes external fragmentation but leaves internal fragmentation in the last page. Page tables live in memory, pointed to by the PTBR, and the TLB caches recent translations; with 100 ns memory, an 80 percent hit ratio gives 120 ns and 99 percent gives 101 ns. Valid-invalid and protection bits give protection, and shared frames let processes share code. Next lesson: smarter page table structures and segmentation.
key_points: Paging splits physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size, a power of 2 (commonly 4 KB).
A logical address = page number p (high bits) + offset d (low bits); with 4 KB pages the offset is 12 bits.
Physical address = frame number times page size + offset; the offset never changes.
Logical address 20000 with 4 KB pages is page 4, offset 3616; if page 4 is in frame 7, the physical address is 32288.
Paging has no external fragmentation, but has internal fragmentation in the last page of a process.
The TLB caches page-to-frame translations; with 100 ns memory, EAT is 120 ns at 80 percent hits and 101 ns at 99 percent hits.
Valid-invalid and protection bits in page table entries protect memory; reentrant code can be shared through shared pages.
lessons.tip: Before any paging calculation, write the page size as a power of 2 and note how many bits the offset uses. Then divide for the page number and take the remainder for the offset, and only then look in the page table.
lessons.task: Page size is 1 KB (1,024 bytes) and a page table says: page 0 to frame 3, page 1 to frame 7, page 2 to frame 0, page 3 to frame 5. Translate logical addresses 500, 1024, 2500 and 3100 to physical addresses. Then say what happens for logical address 4200 if the page table has only 4 entries.

quiz.q: With 4 KB (4096-byte) pages, what are the page number and offset of logical address 20000?
quiz.explain: 20000 / 4096 = 4 with remainder 20000 minus 16384 = 3616. So p = 4 and d = 3616.

quiz.q: Page 4 is in frame 7, and page size is 4096 bytes. What is the physical address for page 4, offset 3616?
Memory access takes 100 ns and the TLB hit ratio is 80 percent (ignore TLB search time). What is the effective access time?
quiz.explain: Hits need one access (100 ns), misses need two (200 ns): 0.8 times 100 + 0.2 times 200 = 80 + 40 = 120 ns.

quiz.q: Which kind of fragmentation does paging still have?
options: Internal fragmentation in the last page
quiz.explain: Any free frame can be used, so there is no external fragmentation. But the last page is usually only partly full, which is internal fragmentation.

quiz.q: A system has 32-bit logical addresses, 4 KB pages and 4-byte page table entries. How big is one process's simple page table?
quiz.explain: 32 minus 12 = 20 bits of page number, so 2^20 entries. 2^20 times 4 bytes = 4 MB.

lessons.title: Page Table Structures and Segmentation
lessons.content:
Imagine the phone directory of all of Bangladesh printed as one single list, one line for every possible phone number, even the numbers nobody uses. It would be thousands of pages long and mostly empty. A smarter directory would be split by district: first look up Dhaka, which tells you which booklet to open, then look up the number inside that small booklet. Districts with no phones need no booklet at all. Page tables face exactly this problem. The last lesson showed that a simple page table for a 32-bit address space takes 4 MB per process, and for 64-bit addresses a flat table would be impossibly huge. This lesson shows three smarter ways to organise page tables, and then a different way of dividing memory called segmentation.

The size problem: With 32-bit logical addresses and 4 KB pages, a process has 2 to the power 20, about one million, possible pages. A 4-byte entry for each gives a 4 MB page table. And in a simple design that table must be one contiguous block. But most processes use only a tiny part of their address space: some code and data at the bottom, a stack at the top and a huge empty gap in between. Storing a million entries, most of them marked invalid, is a waste.

Hierarchical paging: The first fix is to page the page table itself. In two-level paging, the 20-bit page number is split into two 10-bit parts, p1 and p2, followed by the 12-bit offset d. p1 indexes an outer page table, whose entry points to one of many inner page tables. p2 indexes that inner page table, whose entry gives the frame number. Each inner page table has 2 to the power 10 = 1,024 entries of 4 bytes, which is exactly 4 KB, one page. Because the translation goes from the outer table inward, this is also called a forward-mapped page table.

Two-level worked example: Take the 32-bit logical address 0x00403004. In binary, the top 10 bits are 0000000001, so p1 = 1. The next 10 bits are 0000000011, so p2 = 3. The last 12 bits are 0x004, so d = 4. The MMU reads entry 1 of the outer page table, which points to an inner page table; then reads entry 3 of that inner table, which gives a frame number, say 0x2A0; the physical address is then frame 0x2A0 joined with offset 0x004, which is 0x2A0004. Another example: 0x00C01ABC gives p1 = 3, p2 = 1 and d = 0xABC.

Why two levels save memory: Suppose a process uses 8 MB of code and data at the bottom of its address space and 8 MB of stack at the top. Each inner table covers 1,024 pages of 4 KB, which is 4 MB. So 8 MB at the bottom needs 2 inner tables, and 8 MB at the top needs 2 more. Add the outer table, and the total is 5 tables of 4 KB each, 20 KB. Compare that with 4 MB for a flat table: about 200 times smaller. The outer entries for the empty middle simply say "no inner table here".

More levels for 64 bits: For 64-bit systems, two levels are not enough, because the outer table itself would be enormous. Real 64-bit processors use more levels. x86-64 processors commonly use 48-bit virtual addresses with four levels of page tables: 9 bits for each of the four levels plus a 12-bit offset, which adds up to 48. Newer processors can use five levels to support 57-bit addresses. The price is speed: on a TLB miss with four levels, the hardware must read four page table entries before it can read the data, five memory accesses in total. This is why the TLB is so important; with high hit ratios, the extra levels rarely cost anything.

Hashed page tables: A second approach, useful for address spaces larger than 32 bits, is a hashed page table. The virtual page number is put through a hash function, giving an index into a hash table. Each slot holds a linked list of entries, each with three fields: the virtual page number, the frame number and a pointer to the next entry. To translate, the MMU hashes the page number, walks the list in that slot, and compares page numbers until it finds a match. If several pages hash to the same slot, they share the list. A variation called a clustered page table stores several consecutive pages in each entry, which suits programs whose addresses are scattered.

Inverted page tables: The third approach turns the idea upside down. Instead of one page table per process with one entry per virtual page, there is a single table for the whole system with one entry per physical frame. Each entry says which process, identified by a process ID, and which virtual page currently occupy that frame. A logical address is then the triple process ID, page number, offset. To translate, the system searches the table for the matching pair of process ID and page number; if found at entry i, the physical address is frame i joined with the offset. The big advantage: the table size depends only on physical memory, not on how many processes there are or how big their address spaces are. For 4 GB of RAM with 4 KB frames, the table has about one million entries in total, for all processes together.

Inverted table drawbacks: Searching the whole table on every lookup would be very slow, so a hash table is used to find entries quickly, and the TLB is consulted first anyway. Sharing memory is also awkward, because each frame entry can name only one process and one virtual page, while sharing means several processes map the same frame. Systems using inverted tables need extra tricks for that.

Segmentation: Now a different idea. Programmers do not think of memory as one long array of bytes. They think of a program as a collection of pieces: the main program, some functions, the stack, the global data, a symbol table, an array. Segmentation supports this view. A process's logical address space is a set of segments, each with a name, given as a number, and a length. A logical address is a pair: segment number s and offset d within that segment. Segments can have different sizes, and each can be placed anywhere in physical memory.

The segment table: Each process has a segment table. Each entry has a base, the starting physical address of the segment, and a limit, the length of the segment. To translate s and d: the hardware checks that d is less than the limit of segment s; if not, it traps to the OS with an addressing error. If it is, the physical address is base plus d. The segment-table base register, STBR, points to the table, and the segment-table length register, STLR, says how many segments the process has.

Segmentation worked example: A process has five segments. Segment 0: limit 1000, base 1400. Segment 1: limit 400, base 6300. Segment 2: limit 400, base 4300. Segment 3: limit 1100, base 3200. Segment 4: limit 1000, base 4700. A reference to byte 53 of segment 2: 53 is less than 400, so physical address = 4300 + 53 = 4353. Byte 852 of segment 3: 852 is less than 1100, so physical = 3200 + 852 = 4052. Byte 1222 of segment 0: 1222 is not less than the limit 1000, so the hardware traps; the process tried to go past the end of its segment.

Pros and cons of segmentation: Segmentation matches how programmers think, and it makes protection and sharing natural: you can mark the code segment read-only and execute-only, the data segment read-write, and share a whole library segment between processes by putting the same base and limit in their segment tables. But because segments have different sizes, segmentation brings back the problem of contiguous allocation: external fragmentation, with all the first-fit and best-fit headaches from two lessons ago.

Segmentation with paging: The two ideas can be combined to get the benefits of both. The logical address space is divided into segments, and each segment is itself divided into pages, with its own page table. Segments give the programmer's view and protection; paging removes external fragmentation. The classic example is the Intel 32-bit architecture, IA-32, which first translates a logical address through segmentation into a linear address, and then translates the linear address through two-level paging into a physical address. In 64-bit mode, x86-64 makes segmentation essentially flat, with bases of zero for normal code and data, and relies almost entirely on four-level paging. Most modern operating systems today, including Linux and Windows, use paging as their main mechanism.

Real-life example 1, a university's student records: A big public university with 40,000 students could keep one giant register with a line for every possible ID number from 000000 to 999999, mostly empty. Instead, it keeps a register of departments, which points to each department's own smaller register. Departments that do not exist have no register at all. To find a student, you first find the department, then the student within it. That is two-level paging: the outer table is the list of departments, and the inner tables are the department registers.

Real-life example 2, chapters of a textbook: A student thinks of her OS textbook as chapters of different lengths: chapter 1 is 30 pages, chapter 2 is 60 pages. To find "chapter 3, page 12", she looks up where chapter 3 starts and adds 12, checking that chapter 3 actually has at least 13 pages. That is segmentation: segment number, offset, base and limit. If the book were printed as loose sheets of equal size kept in different folders, with an index for each chapter, that would be segmentation with paging.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In two-level paging problems, students often split the bits wrongly; always count from the right: first the offset bits, then p2, then p1. In segmentation, many forget to check the offset against the limit before adding the base, or use less-than-or-equal instead of less-than. Another mistake is saying inverted page tables are per process; there is only one for the whole system. Typical questions: compute p1, p2 and d for a given address; explain why hierarchical paging saves memory; compare hashed and inverted page tables; translate segment-offset pairs using a segment table and identify illegal references; compare paging and segmentation.

Recap: Flat page tables are too big for large address spaces. Hierarchical paging pages the page table: a 32-bit address can be split into 10, 10 and 12 bits, and only the inner tables that are needed are kept, so a process using 16 MB needs about 20 KB of tables instead of 4 MB. x86-64 uses four levels with 9 bits each plus a 12-bit offset. Hashed page tables use a hash of the page number with chains. Inverted page tables keep one entry per physical frame for the whole system, saving memory but making search and sharing harder. Segmentation divides memory into variable-size logical units with base and limit checks, and can be combined with paging. Next lesson: virtual memory, where pages do not even need to be in RAM until they are used.
key_points: A flat page table for 32-bit addresses with 4 KB pages needs 2^20 entries, about 4 MB per process.
Two-level paging splits a 32-bit address into p1 (10 bits), p2 (10 bits) and offset (12 bits); only the needed inner tables exist.
Address 0x00403004 splits into p1 = 1, p2 = 3, d = 4.
x86-64 commonly uses four-level paging with 48-bit addresses (4 x 9 bits + 12-bit offset); a TLB miss may then need five memory accesses.
Hashed page tables hash the virtual page number into chains of (page, frame, next) entries.
An inverted page table has one entry per physical frame for the whole system, storing (process ID, page); it saves memory but makes search and sharing harder.
Segmentation uses (segment, offset) addresses checked against a limit and added to a base; it causes external fragmentation unless combined with paging.
lessons.tip: For multi-level paging, write the address in binary and draw vertical lines from the right: first the offset bits, then each level's bits. Converting each piece to decimal afterwards avoids most mistakes.
lessons.task: Using the five-segment table from this lesson (0: 1000/1400, 1: 400/6300, 2: 400/4300, 3: 1100/3200, 4: 1000/4700, written as limit/base), translate these references: (0, 430), (1, 10), (2, 500), (3, 400), (4, 112). Mark which are illegal and why.

quiz.q: In two-level paging with a 10-10-12 split, what are p1, p2 and d for address 0x00403004?
quiz.explain: The top 10 bits are 0000000001 (1), the next 10 bits are 0000000011 (3), and the low 12 bits are 0x004 (4).

quiz.q: Why does hierarchical paging usually save memory?
options: Inner page tables are only created for parts of the address space actually in use
It removes the need for a TLB
It stores only one page table for all processes
quiz.explain: Outer entries for unused regions point to nothing, so the large empty gap between code and stack needs no inner tables.

quiz.q: What is special about an inverted page table?
options: Each process has several of them
It has one entry per virtual page of each process
It removes all need for hashing
There is one table for the whole system with one entry per physical frame
quiz.explain: An inverted page table is indexed by frame, storing which process and page occupy it, so its size depends on physical memory only.

quiz.q: Segment 2 has limit 400 and base 4300. What is the physical address of byte 53 in segment 2?
quiz.explain: 53 is less than the limit 400, so the reference is legal. Physical = base + offset = 4300 + 53 = 4353.

quiz.q: Segment 0 has limit 1000 and base 1400. What happens on a reference to byte 1222 of segment 0?
options: The hardware traps with an addressing error
quiz.explain: The offset 1222 is not less than the limit 1000, so the reference is beyond the segment's end and the hardware traps to the OS.

lessons.title: Virtual Memory and Demand Paging
lessons.content:
When you install a 60 GB game on a laptop that has only 8 GB of RAM, the game still runs. How? The whole game can never fit in memory at once. The secret is that at any moment the game only needs a small part of itself: the current level, the characters on screen, the code for the actions happening now. The rest can wait on the SSD until it is needed. Think of a student going to school: she does not carry every book she owns, only the books for today's classes. If a surprise class needs another book, she runs home to fetch it. This idea, keeping only the needed parts of a program in memory and fetching the rest when they are used, is called virtual memory. It is one of the most important ideas in operating systems.

What virtual memory is: Virtual memory separates the logical memory a programmer sees from the physical memory that really exists. Each process gets a large, private virtual address space, for example 256 TB on a 64-bit x86 machine with 48-bit addresses, even if the computer has only 8 GB of RAM. Only the parts actually in use need to be in RAM; the rest lives on secondary storage, in a region called swap space or the paging file. The programmer simply writes code as if memory were huge and continuous.

Why it helps: Virtual memory has several big benefits. First, a program is no longer limited by the size of physical memory. Second, because each process uses less physical memory, more processes can run at the same time, raising CPU utilisation. Third, less I/O is needed to load or swap a program, because only the needed pages are loaded, so programs start faster. Fourth, it makes sharing easy: shared libraries and shared memory are just pages mapped into several address spaces. And it allows tricks like copy-on-write, which we will see soon.

Demand paging: The usual way to build virtual memory is demand paging: a page is loaded into memory only when it is first demanded, that is, accessed. A process starts with none or few of its pages in memory. The component that swaps individual pages is called a pager rather than a swapper, because it moves pages, not whole processes. If a program never uses its error-handling code, those pages are never loaded at all. Pure demand paging means never bringing in a page until it is needed, even the very first page.

The valid-invalid bit again: To know which pages are in memory, demand paging reuses the valid-invalid bit in each page table entry. Valid means the page is legal and is in memory. Invalid means either the page is not part of the process's address space at all, or it is legal but currently on disk. As long as the process only touches valid pages, it runs normally, at full speed.

Page fault: When a process tries to use a page marked invalid, the hardware traps to the OS. This trap is called a page fault. A page fault is not an error in itself; it simply means "this page is not in memory yet". The OS then handles it in steps.

Handling a page fault, step by step: Step one: the OS checks an internal table, usually kept with the process control block, to see whether the reference was valid or invalid. Step two: if the reference was truly invalid, for example a pointer to nowhere, the process is terminated; this is the famous segmentation fault. If it was valid but the page is not in memory, continue. Step three: find a free frame, taking one from the free-frame list. Step four: schedule a disk or SSD read to bring the page into that frame. While this slow I/O happens, the CPU is given to another process. Step five: when the read finishes, update the page table entry with the frame number and set the bit to valid. Step six: restart the instruction that caused the fault. The process now runs as if the page had always been there.

Restarting instructions: Restarting must work for any instruction. For a simple instruction, the CPU just fetches and runs it again. Harder cases appear when one instruction touches several memory locations, for example a block-copy instruction that moves 256 bytes and may cross a page boundary in the middle. If a fault happens halfway, part of the data may already have been changed. Hardware solves this either by checking both ends of the block before starting, or by keeping temporary registers that hold the old values so the instruction can be undone and restarted. This is why virtual memory needs careful cooperation between hardware and the OS.

Locality of reference: You might think a program would fault on every instruction. In practice it does not, thanks to locality of reference. Programs tend to use a small set of pages for a while, a loop's code, the current array, the stack, before moving on to another set. This set of pages being used together is called a locality. So after a few faults to load the current locality, the program runs for a long time without faulting. Locality is the reason both caches and virtual memory work.

Performance of demand paging: Page faults are very expensive, so we measure their effect with the effective access time, EAT. Let p be the page-fault rate, the probability that a memory access causes a fault, between 0 and 1. Then EAT = (1 minus p) times memory access time + p times page-fault service time. The service time includes the trap, the disk read, which dominates, and restarting the process, together typically about 8 milliseconds on a hard disk.

Worked example, the cost of faults: Memory access time is 200 ns and page-fault service time is 8 ms, which is 8,000,000 ns. EAT = (1 minus p) times 200 + p times 8,000,000 = 200 + 7,999,800 p nanoseconds. If one access out of 1,000 causes a fault, p = 0.001, then EAT = 200 + 7,999.8 = 8,199.8 ns, about 8.2 microseconds. The computer is slowed down by a factor of about 40, just because of one fault in a thousand. If we want the slowdown to be under 10 percent, EAT must be under 220 ns, so 7,999,800 p must be less than 20, which means p must be less than about 0.0000025, fewer than one fault per 399,990 accesses. Page-fault rates must be kept extremely low. With a fast SSD, the service time is much smaller, perhaps around 0.1 ms, but still hundreds of times slower than RAM.

Swap space: Disk I/O to swap space is generally faster than to the normal file system, because swap is allocated in large blocks and skips file lookups and indirect allocation. Some systems copy the whole program image to swap at start; others, like Linux and Windows, load code pages directly from the program file and only write to swap the pages that have been modified, called anonymous memory, such as the stack and heap. Code pages are never modified, so if they are thrown out of memory, they can simply be read again from the program file.

Copy-on-write: Recall that fork creates a child process as a copy of the parent. Copying every page would be slow and is often wasted, because the child usually calls exec right away and replaces its memory. Copy-on-write, COW, avoids this. After fork, parent and child share the same physical pages, all marked read-only and copy-on-write. Only when one of them tries to write to a shared page does the OS make a private copy of that one page for the writer. Pages never written are never copied. Example: a parent with 1,000 pages forks a child, and the child changes only 3 pages before calling exec. With COW, only 3 pages are copied, not 1,000. Free frames for these copies come from a pool, often zero-filled on demand, meaning cleared to zeros first so no old data leaks to the new owner.

vfork: Some UNIX systems also offer vfork, a variant where the child uses the parent's memory directly, with no copy-on-write at all, and the parent is suspended until the child calls exec or exits. It is very fast, but dangerous if the child modifies memory, because the parent will see those changes. It is meant only for a child that calls exec immediately.

Memory-mapped files: Virtual memory also lets a file be treated like memory. With memory mapping, the OS maps a file's disk blocks to pages in the process's virtual address space. Reading the file is then just reading memory: the first access to each page causes a page fault that loads that part of the file, and later accesses are ordinary memory reads and writes, with no read or write system calls. Changes are written back to the file later, for example when the file is unmapped or when the OS flushes dirty pages. Several processes can map the same file to share data. On Linux, the mmap system call does this, and Windows offers similar file-mapping functions.

Real-life example 1, the school bag: The student is the process, her bag is RAM and the bookshelf at home is the disk. She packs only today's books, the current locality. When a teacher suddenly asks for the atlas, which is not in the bag, she has a page fault: she must go home and fetch it, which takes much longer than taking a book out of the bag. If she packed well, such trips are rare. If the teacher keeps asking for books she did not bring, she spends all day running home and learns nothing, a preview of thrashing, which is next lesson's topic.

Real-life example 2, opening a big app: When you open Microsoft Word or a large game, it does not load all of its code at once. The OS maps the program file into memory and loads pages only as they are used. That is why the program appears quickly, and why the first time you open a rarely used menu there may be a tiny pause: a page fault loading that code. Phones do something similar, and Android uses copy-on-write when it starts new apps from a common prepared process called zygote, so the shared framework code is not copied for every app.

Common mistakes and exam questions: A frequent mistake is thinking a page fault is always an error; only an invalid reference is an error, while a fault on a valid page just loads the page. In EAT problems, students often mix up units; convert milliseconds to nanoseconds first, as 1 ms = 1,000,000 ns. Some forget that during the disk read the CPU runs other processes. Typical questions: define virtual memory and list its benefits; explain demand paging and the page-fault handling steps; compute EAT for a given fault rate; find the maximum fault rate for a given slowdown; explain copy-on-write with fork; explain memory-mapped files.

Recap: Virtual memory gives each process a large address space, keeping only the pages in use in RAM. Demand paging loads a page only on first access. Touching a page marked invalid causes a page fault; the OS checks the reference, finds a free frame, reads the page from disk, updates the page table and restarts the instruction. Locality of reference keeps faults rare. With 200 ns memory and 8 ms fault service, a fault rate of 1 in 1,000 gives an EAT of about 8.2 microseconds, so fault rates must be tiny. Copy-on-write makes fork cheap by copying only pages that are written, and memory-mapped files turn file I/O into memory access. Next lesson: what to do when there is no free frame, page replacement.
key_points: Virtual memory separates logical memory from physical memory, so programs can be larger than RAM and more processes fit at once.
Demand paging loads a page only when it is first accessed; pages not in memory are marked invalid.
A page fault is a trap on an invalid page: check the reference, find a free frame, read the page, update the table, restart the instruction.
Locality of reference means programs use a small set of pages at a time, so faults are rare.
EAT = (1 - p) x memory time + p x fault service time; with 200 ns and 8 ms, p = 1/1000 gives about 8.2 microseconds.
Copy-on-write lets parent and child share pages after fork and copies a page only when one of them writes to it.
Memory-mapped files map a file's blocks into virtual memory, so reading and writing the file becomes ordinary memory access.
lessons.tip: In EAT problems, convert everything to nanoseconds before you start (1 ms = 1,000,000 ns, 1 microsecond = 1,000 ns). Then write EAT = (1 - p) x m + p x s on one line and substitute; most wrong answers come from unit mix-ups.
lessons.task: Memory access time is 100 ns and the page-fault service time is 5 ms. Compute the EAT if p = 1/10,000. Then find the largest p that keeps the slowdown under 20 percent (EAT under 120 ns). Show each step.

quiz.q: What does demand paging do?
options: Loads all pages of a process before it starts
Loads a page into memory only when it is first accessed
Loads only the code pages, never the data pages
Keeps every page permanently on disk
quiz.explain: Demand paging brings a page in only when the process actually uses it; unused pages are never loaded.

quiz.q: A process accesses a page that is part of its address space but is currently on disk. What happens?
options: The process is terminated with a segmentation fault
The page is ignored and the instruction is skipped
A page fault occurs, the page is loaded, and the instruction is restarted
The whole process is swapped out
quiz.explain: A valid page on disk causes a page fault; the OS reads it into a free frame, marks it valid and restarts the instruction.

quiz.q: Memory access takes 200 ns, page-fault service takes 8 ms, and p = 0.001. What is the effective access time, approximately?
With copy-on-write, when is a shared page actually copied after fork?
options: When either process tries to write to that page
quiz.explain: Pages stay shared and read-only until a write happens; only then does the OS copy that single page for the writer.

quiz.q: Why does demand paging usually perform well despite the high cost of a page fault?
options: Because of locality of reference: programs use a small set of pages for a while
Because disks are faster than RAM
Because page faults never happen after the first second
Because the TLB stores whole pages
quiz.explain: Programs work within a locality of pages, so after loading it, they run for a long time without new faults.

lessons.title: Page Replacement and Thrashing
lessons.content:
Your study table has room for only three books. You are working on a project and keep needing different books: maths, then science, then the dictionary, then the atlas. When you need the atlas and the table is full, one book must go back to the shelf. Which one? If you put away the dictionary and need it again a minute later, you wasted a trip. If you put away the maths book you will not need until next week, you chose well. Operating systems face this exact choice millions of times a day. When a page fault happens and there is no free frame, the OS must pick a victim page to throw out. This lesson studies the rules for choosing, called page replacement algorithms, and what happens when memory is so short that the computer spends all its time swapping, which is called thrashing.

When replacement is needed: Demand paging lets the OS over-allocate memory: the total virtual memory of all processes is much bigger than RAM. Eventually a page fault happens and the free-frame list is empty. The OS then extends the page-fault steps: find the wanted page on disk; find a victim frame using a page replacement algorithm; if the victim page has been changed, write it to disk; read the wanted page into the freed frame; update the page tables; restart the process.

The dirty bit: Writing a victim to disk doubles the cost of a fault, two transfers instead of one. To avoid it when possible, each page has a modify bit, also called a dirty bit, which the hardware sets whenever the page is written. If the dirty bit is clear, the page has not changed since it was read in, so the copy on disk is still correct and the frame can simply be overwritten. Code pages are never dirty, so they are cheap victims.

How we compare algorithms: We run each algorithm on a reference string, a list of page numbers in the order a program uses them, and count page faults for a given number of frames. Fewer faults is better. Our main example: reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1 with 3 frames, all empty at the start. Every algorithm gets 3 faults just filling the frames with 7, 0 and 1.

FIFO: First-in, first-out replaces the page that has been in memory longest, like a queue. It is very easy to build. On the main string with 3 frames, FIFO gives 15 page faults. Its weakness: the oldest page might be one used all the time, like a page holding a frequently used variable. FIFO does not care; it throws it out anyway, and the next access faults it straight back in.

FIFO traced on a small string: Take the reference string 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 1, 2, 5 with 3 frames. 1, 2, 3 are faults, filling the frames. 1 is a hit. 4 is a fault: the oldest page is 1, so 1 is replaced, giving frames 4, 2, 3. 1 is a fault again, since we just threw it out: the oldest is now 2, giving 4, 1, 3. 2 is a fault: replace 3, giving 4, 1, 2. 5 is a fault: replace 4, giving 5, 1, 2. Total: 7 faults out of 8 references.

Belady's anomaly: You would expect more frames to always mean fewer faults. For FIFO, that is not always true. With the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, FIFO gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 faults with 4 frames. More memory made it worse. This surprising result is called Belady's anomaly. Algorithms that do not suffer from it are called stack algorithms; LRU and OPT are stack algorithms. For the same string, LRU gives 10 faults with 3 frames and 8 with 4 frames, improving as it should.

Optimal replacement: The optimal algorithm, OPT or MIN, replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future. It gives the lowest possible fault rate for any number of frames and never suffers Belady's anomaly. On the main string with 3 frames, OPT gives only 9 faults. On the small string: 1, 2, 3 fault; 1 hits; at 4, page 3 is never used again, so replace it, giving 1, 2, 4; 1 and 2 hit; 5 faults. Total 5. The catch: OPT needs to know the future, which a real OS cannot. So OPT is used as a yardstick, to measure how close real algorithms come to the best.

LRU: Least recently used replaces the page that has not been used for the longest time in the past. The idea is that the recent past is a good guess for the near future, thanks to locality. On the main string with 3 frames, LRU gives 12 faults: better than FIFO's 15, worse than OPT's 9. On the small string: 1, 2, 3 fault; 1 hits; at 4 the least recently used page is 2, so frames become 1, 4, 3; 1 hits; at 2 the least recent is 3, giving 1, 4, 2; at 5 the least recent is 4, giving 1, 5, 2. Total 6 faults, between FIFO's 7 and OPT's 5.

Implementing LRU: Exact LRU needs hardware help on every memory access. One way uses counters: each page table entry gets a time-of-use field, and the CPU copies a clock into it on every access; the victim is the page with the smallest time. Another way keeps a stack of page numbers: when a page is used, it moves to the top, so the bottom is always the LRU page. Both are too costly to do on every single memory access, so real systems use approximations.

The reference bit and the clock algorithm: Most hardware provides a reference bit for each page, set to 1 whenever the page is used. The OS can clear it and later see which pages were used since. The second-chance algorithm, usually built as the clock algorithm, uses this bit. Imagine the frames arranged in a circle with a clock hand pointing at one. When a victim is needed, look at the page under the hand. If its reference bit is 0, replace it. If it is 1, give it a second chance: clear the bit to 0 and move the hand to the next page. The hand keeps going until it finds a page with bit 0. A page used often keeps getting its bit set and is never chosen. If all bits are 1, the hand goes all the way round, clearing them, and it becomes FIFO.

Enhanced second chance: An improvement looks at both the reference bit and the dirty bit as a pair. (0, 0), not recently used and not modified, is the best victim. (0, 1), not recently used but modified, is next, but needs a write first. (1, 0) is recently used but clean. (1, 1), recently used and modified, is the worst victim. The algorithm replaces a page from the lowest non-empty class, saving disk writes. Other algorithms count how often pages are used, called LFU and MFU, but they are expensive and do not approximate OPT well, so they are rarely used.

Page buffering: Systems also keep a pool of free frames ready. When a fault happens, the wanted page is read into a free frame at once, before the victim is written out; the victim is written later and its frame returns to the pool. Some systems even remember which page was in each free frame, so if that old page is needed again soon, it can be reused without any disk read.

Allocating frames among processes: How many frames should each process get? Each needs some minimum, decided by the hardware: enough frames for every page a single instruction might touch. Beyond that, equal allocation gives everyone the same share, while proportional allocation gives each process frames in proportion to its size. Example: 62 free frames, process P1 with 10 pages and P2 with 127 pages, 137 pages in total. P1 gets 10 divided by 137 times 62, about 4.5, so 4 frames; P2 gets 127 divided by 137 times 62, about 57.5, so 57 frames. Replacement can also be global, where a process may take a frame from any process, or local, where it only replaces its own pages. Global replacement gives better throughput and is more common; local replacement makes a process's performance more predictable.

Thrashing: If a process does not have enough frames to hold the pages it is actively using, it faults, replaces a page it needs again soon, faults again, and so on. It spends more time paging than running. This is thrashing. It can spiral: as processes thrash, CPU utilisation drops because everyone waits for the disk; an old scheduler sees low CPU use and admits more processes to raise it; they steal frames from the others, causing even more faults, and CPU utilisation collapses. Graphed against the degree of multiprogramming, CPU utilisation rises at first, peaks, and then falls sharply when thrashing starts.

Working-set model: The cure is to give each process the frames its current locality needs. The working-set model defines a window of the last Delta page references; the set of distinct pages in that window is the working set. Example: with Delta = 10 and the most recent ten references 2, 6, 1, 5, 7, 7, 7, 7, 5, 1, the working set is {1, 2, 5, 6, 7}, size 5. If the sum of all processes' working-set sizes, D, exceeds the number of available frames, thrashing will happen, so the OS suspends a process, freeing its frames. Choosing Delta matters: too small misses the locality, too large covers several localities.

Page-fault frequency: A simpler, more direct approach watches each process's page-fault rate. Set an upper and a lower bound. If a process's fault rate goes above the upper bound, it needs more frames, so give it some. If it falls below the lower bound, it has more than it needs, so take some away. If no free frames are available for a process that needs them, suspend a process. This page-fault-frequency strategy directly controls the symptom of thrashing.

Real-life example 1, the study table: Your three-book table is a set of three frames, and the books you reach for are a reference string. FIFO is putting away whichever book has been on the table longest. LRU is putting away the one you have not touched for longest. OPT is magically knowing which book you will not need for the longest time. Thrashing is trying to write a project that needs ten books at once on a table that fits three: you spend all your time fetching and returning books, and the project never moves.

Real-life example 2, a slow computer with too many tabs: On a laptop with 4 GB of RAM, opening dozens of browser tabs together with a video editor can make everything freeze, the disk light flashes non-stop and the mouse barely moves. The OS is thrashing: every program needs pages that were just thrown out to make room for another. Closing a few programs reduces the total working set below the RAM size, and the computer suddenly becomes responsive again. Adding more RAM fixes it permanently.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In replacement problems, students often forget to count the first faults that fill empty frames. For LRU, look backwards from the current position, not forwards; for OPT, look forwards. Be careful that a hit in LRU updates the page's last-use time, while in FIFO a hit changes nothing. Belady's anomaly applies to FIFO, not to LRU or OPT. Typical questions: count faults for FIFO, OPT and LRU on a reference string with 3 or 4 frames; demonstrate Belady's anomaly; explain the clock algorithm; compute proportional allocation; define thrashing, its cause and cures; find a working set for a given window.

Recap: When no frame is free, a victim page is replaced, written back only if its dirty bit is set. On the string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, 1, 2, 0, 1, 7, 0, 1 with 3 frames, FIFO gives 15 faults, LRU 12 and OPT 9. FIFO can suffer Belady's anomaly; OPT is the unreachable best; LRU is good but costly, so real systems use the clock or second-chance algorithm with reference bits. Frames are allocated equally or proportionally, with global or local replacement. Thrashing happens when processes lack frames for their localities; the working-set model and page-fault-frequency control prevent it. Next lesson: the disks behind all this paging.
key_points: When no frame is free, the OS picks a victim page; it must be written to disk only if its dirty (modify) bit is set.
FIFO replaces the oldest page, OPT the page not needed for the longest future time, LRU the page unused for the longest past time.
Belady's anomaly: with FIFO, more frames can cause more faults (1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames, 10 with 4).
The clock (second-chance) algorithm approximates LRU using reference bits; a page with bit 1 gets its bit cleared and is skipped.
Proportional allocation gives frames by process size: 62 frames for 10- and 127-page processes gives about 4 and 57.
Thrashing is spending more time paging than running; the working-set model and page-fault-frequency control prevent it.
lessons.tip: For replacement problems, draw a table with one column per reference and one row per frame, and write F under each fault. For LRU look backwards to find the victim, for OPT look forwards; never mix the two directions.
lessons.task: Using the reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 1, 2, 3, 7, 6, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 6 with 4 frames, count the page faults for FIFO, LRU and OPT. Then explain in two sentences why OPT can never be beaten.

quiz.q: With 3 frames, how many page faults does FIFO give on 1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 1, 2, 5?
quiz.explain: 1, 2, 3 fault; 1 hits; 4 replaces 1; 1 replaces 2; 2 replaces 3; 5 replaces 4. That is 7 faults.

quiz.q: Which algorithm gives the fewest possible page faults but cannot be implemented exactly in a real OS?
options: OPT, because it needs to know future references
FIFO, because it needs a queue
Clock, because it needs a circular list
quiz.explain: OPT replaces the page used furthest in the future, which is the best possible choice, but the future is unknown, so it is only a yardstick.

quiz.q: What is Belady's anomaly?
options: LRU getting more faults than FIFO
The page-fault rate falling to zero
A dirty page being replaced without being written
More frames causing more page faults under FIFO
quiz.explain: With FIFO, the string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4 frames.

quiz.q: In the clock algorithm, the hand points at a page whose reference bit is 1. What happens?
options: The bit is cleared to 0 and the hand moves to the next page
The page is written to disk
quiz.explain: A set reference bit gives the page a second chance: the bit is cleared and the hand moves on to look for a page with bit 0.

quiz.q: What is thrashing?
options: When the CPU runs faster than memory
When processes spend more time paging than doing useful work
When the TLB hit ratio is 100 percent
quiz.explain: Without enough frames for their localities, processes keep faulting and replacing pages they soon need, so CPU utilisation collapses.

lessons.title: Mass Storage and Disk Scheduling
lessons.content:
Picture a lift in a tall building in Motijheel. People on many floors press the button: floor 9, floor 2, floor 15, floor 4. If the lift served them strictly in the order they pressed, it would race up to 9, down to 2, up to 15, down to 4, wasting time and electricity. A sensible lift goes up, stopping at every requested floor on the way, and then comes down, picking up the rest. A hard disk has the same problem. Its read-write head must move across the disk to reach the data each request needs, and moving is slow. The order in which the OS serves requests can make the total movement several times smaller. This lesson covers how disks and SSDs work, disk scheduling algorithms with worked numbers, and RAID, which combines many disks for speed and safety.

Hard disk drives: An HDD stores data on spinning platters coated with magnetic material. Each platter surface has a read-write head on an arm; all arms move together. A surface is divided into circular tracks, and each track into sectors, traditionally 512 bytes and now usually 4 KB. The set of tracks at the same arm position on all surfaces forms a cylinder. Platters spin fast, commonly 5,400 or 7,200 rotations per minute, RPM, in laptops and desktops, and up to 15,000 RPM in some servers.

Access time: Reading a sector takes three parts. Seek time is the time to move the arm to the right cylinder, typically a few milliseconds. Rotational latency is the time waiting for the right sector to spin under the head. Transfer time is the time to actually read the data. Example: a 7,200 RPM disk makes 120 rotations per second, so one rotation takes 1 divided by 120 seconds, about 8.33 ms, and the average rotational latency is half a rotation, about 4.17 ms. With an average seek of 5 ms, the average access time to reach a random sector is about 9 ms, before transfer. In 9 ms a modern CPU can run tens of millions of instructions.

Solid-state drives: An SSD has no moving parts; it stores data in NAND flash memory chips. There is no seek and no rotation, so random reads take tens of microseconds instead of milliseconds. Flash has its own rules. Data is read and written in pages, but can only be erased in much larger blocks, and a page cannot be overwritten without first erasing its block. So the SSD's controller writes new data to fresh pages and later cleans up old blocks, called garbage collection. Each block can be erased only a limited number of times, so the controller spreads writes evenly, called wear levelling. The OS helps with the TRIM command, which tells the SSD which blocks are no longer in use. NVMe SSDs connect directly to the PCIe bus and are faster still.

Why disk scheduling matters: Many processes send I/O requests at once, so a queue of requests forms. For an HDD, the main cost is seek time, which grows with the distance the head moves. We measure an algorithm by the total head movement in cylinders to serve the queue. Our example throughout: cylinders 0 to 199, the head starts at cylinder 53, and the queue in arrival order is 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67.

FCFS: First-come, first-served serves requests in arrival order. It is fair and simple, but the head swings wildly. The path is 53, 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. The moves are 45, 85, 146, 85, 108, 110, 59 and 2 cylinders, a total of 640 cylinders. Notice the big swing from 122 down to 14 and back up to 124.

SSTF: Shortest seek time first always serves the pending request closest to the current head position. From 53, the closest is 65, distance 12. Then 67, distance 2. Now the closest is 37, distance 30, nearer than 98 at 31. Then 14, distance 23. Then 98, distance 84. Then 122, 124 and 183. Total: 12 + 2 + 30 + 23 + 84 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 236 cylinders, far better than 640. But SSTF is like SJF scheduling: it can cause starvation. If new requests keep arriving near the head, a request far away might wait forever. And it is not always optimal.

SCAN, the elevator algorithm: The head moves in one direction to the end of the disk, serving every request it passes, then reverses and serves requests on the way back, just like a lift. If the head at 53 is moving toward 0: it serves 37 and 14, continues to cylinder 0, then reverses and serves 65, 67, 98, 122, 124 and 183. Total: 53 down to 0 is 53, plus 0 up to 183 is 183, giving 236 cylinders. If instead it were moving up toward 199: 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, on to 199, then back down to 37 and 14: 146 + 185 = 331 cylinders. The direction matters.

C-SCAN: SCAN has a fairness issue. Just after the head passes a region going one way, requests there must wait for the full trip out and back, while requests at the far end are served soon. Circular SCAN fixes this by treating the cylinders as a circle. The head serves requests in one direction only; when it reaches the end, it jumps straight back to the start without serving anything, and continues. Moving up from 53: 65, 67, 98, 122, 124, 183, on to 199, then jump to 0, then serve 14 and 37. Movement: 146 up, 199 for the return jump, and 37 more, a total of 382 if the jump is counted. Many textbooks count it, some do not, in which case the total is 183; always say which you are doing. C-SCAN gives a more uniform waiting time.

LOOK and C-LOOK: In practice, the head does not need to go all the way to the end of the disk. LOOK is SCAN that only goes as far as the last request in each direction, then reverses. Moving toward 0 from 53: 37, 14, then reverse, without going to 0, and serve 65 up to 183. Total: 39 + 169 = 208 cylinders, better than SCAN's 236. C-LOOK is C-SCAN that only goes as far as the last request, then jumps back to the lowest pending request. Moving up from 53: 65 to 183, which is 130, jump down to 14, which is 169, then 37, which is 23, total 322 cylinders with the jump counted.

Choosing an algorithm: SSTF is common and natural, giving good performance under light load. SCAN and C-SCAN, and their LOOK forms, perform better for systems with heavy load, because they avoid starvation. Linux has offered schedulers such as deadline, which sorts requests but also gives each a deadline so none waits too long, and others aimed at fairness between processes. For SSDs, seek distance does not exist, so the OS usually uses a simple FCFS-like scheduler, sometimes merging nearby requests, and the NVMe "none" scheduler skips sorting altogether.

RAID basics: Disks fail, and one disk can only be so fast. RAID, redundant arrays of independent disks, combines several disks to get reliability, speed or both. Two key ideas are used. Striping splits data across disks, so that block 0 is on disk 0, block 1 on disk 1, and so on, letting the disks work in parallel. Redundancy stores extra information, either full copies, called mirroring, or parity, so that data survives a disk failure.

RAID levels: RAID 0 is striping with no redundancy: fastest and uses all capacity, but if any disk fails, all data is lost. RAID 1 is mirroring: every block is written to two disks, so one can fail without losing data, but half the capacity is used for copies. RAID 5 stripes data and spreads parity blocks across all disks; it survives one disk failure, and with n disks it gives n minus 1 disks of usable space. RAID 6 stores two independent parity blocks per stripe and survives two simultaneous failures, giving n minus 2 disks of space. RAID 10, also written 1+0, mirrors pairs of disks and then stripes across the pairs, combining speed and safety at the cost of half the capacity. Example with four 1 TB disks: RAID 0 gives 4 TB, RAID 5 gives 3 TB, RAID 6 gives 2 TB and RAID 10 gives 2 TB.

How parity works: Parity uses XOR, exclusive or. The parity block is the XOR of the data blocks in its stripe. Example with 4-bit blocks: disk A holds 1011, disk B holds 0110, disk C holds 1100. Parity = 1011 XOR 0110 XOR 1100. First 1011 XOR 0110 = 1101, then 1101 XOR 1100 = 0001. If disk B dies, we can rebuild its block by XORing everything left: 1011 XOR 1100 XOR 0001. 1011 XOR 1100 = 0111, and 0111 XOR 0001 = 0110, exactly disk B's lost data. The cost: every small write must also update the parity, which makes writes on RAID 5 slower.

RAID is not backup: RAID protects against a disk failing. It does not protect against deleting a file by mistake, a virus encrypting your files, a fire, or a bug that writes garbage, because RAID faithfully copies the mistake to every disk at once. Real data safety still needs separate backups, ideally with one copy kept in another place.

Real-life example 1, the Motijheel lift: The lift is the disk head and floors are cylinders. Serving buttons in pressed order is FCFS. Always going to the nearest pressed floor is SSTF, but someone on the top floor might wait forever if people keep pressing floors near the bottom. Going up to the top and then down is SCAN. Only going as high as the highest pressed button before turning is LOOK. A lift that only carries people upward and then rushes empty back to the ground floor is C-SCAN.

Real-life example 2, a bank's servers: A bank in Dhaka keeps customer accounts on a storage server with many disks in RAID 6 or RAID 10. If one disk fails at night, the system keeps running and no account data is lost; a technician replaces the disk the next day, and the array rebuilds the missing data from the others. The bank still sends backups to a separate data centre, because RAID cannot undo a wrong transaction or survive a flood.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In disk scheduling, students often forget to include the move from the starting head position to the first request. In SCAN, check whether the head goes all the way to the end, 0 or 199; in LOOK it stops at the last request. For C-SCAN, state whether the return jump is counted. In SSTF, compare distances carefully when two requests are nearly equally close. Typical questions: compute total head movement for FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK; compute rotational latency for a given RPM; compare HDD and SSD; explain RAID levels and their capacity; recover a lost block using XOR parity.

Recap: HDDs use spinning platters and moving heads; access time is seek plus rotational latency plus transfer, about 9 ms for a random read on a 7,200 RPM disk. SSDs have no moving parts but need garbage collection and wear levelling. For the queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67 with the head at 53, FCFS moves 640 cylinders, SSTF 236, SCAN toward 0 also 236, LOOK toward 0 only 208, and C-LOOK upward 322. RAID 0 stripes, RAID 1 mirrors, RAID 5 uses one parity block per stripe, RAID 6 uses two, and RAID 10 mirrors then stripes. Parity is XOR and lets one lost block be rebuilt. RAID is not a backup. Next lesson: file systems, which organise data on these devices.
key_points: HDD access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time; a 7,200 RPM disk has an average rotational latency of about 4.17 ms.
SSDs have no seek or rotation; they need garbage collection, wear levelling and TRIM because flash is erased in blocks.
For queue 98,183,37,122,14,124,65,67 with head at 53: FCFS 640, SSTF 236, SCAN (toward 0) 236, LOOK (toward 0) 208.
SSTF picks the nearest request and can starve far requests; SCAN is the elevator algorithm; C-SCAN serves one direction and jumps back.
LOOK and C-LOOK only go as far as the last request instead of the end of the disk.
RAID 0 stripes, RAID 1 mirrors, RAID 5 has one parity block per stripe (n-1 disks usable), RAID 6 two (n-2), RAID 10 mirrors then stripes.
Parity is the XOR of the data blocks; XORing the surviving blocks rebuilds a lost one. RAID is not a backup.
lessons.tip: For disk scheduling, first sort the queue on a number line and mark the head position. Then draw the path as arrows and add the distances one by one; writing the path out first avoids most mistakes.
lessons.task: Cylinders are 0 to 199, the head is at 100 moving toward 199, and the queue is 23, 89, 132, 42, 187, 10, 160. Compute the total head movement for FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK. Which is best here?

quiz.q: With the head at 53 and queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67, what is the total head movement under SSTF?
Which disk scheduling algorithm can cause starvation of requests far from the head?
quiz.explain: SSTF always picks the closest request, so if new requests keep arriving near the head, distant ones may wait indefinitely.

quiz.q: What is the average rotational latency of a 7,200 RPM disk?
quiz.explain: 7,200 RPM is 120 rotations per second, so one rotation takes about 8.33 ms; on average we wait half a rotation, about 4.17 ms.

quiz.q: You have four 1 TB disks in RAID 5. How much usable space do you get?
quiz.explain: RAID 5 uses the equivalent of one disk for parity, so n minus 1 = 3 disks of space, 3 TB.

quiz.q: Data blocks are 1011 and 1100, and the parity block is 0001. A third data block was lost. What was it?
quiz.explain: The lost block is the XOR of everything left: 1011 XOR 1100 = 0111, then 0111 XOR 0001 = 0110.

lessons.title: File Systems
lessons.content:
Think of a big school library. Thousands of books sit on shelves, but nobody finds a book by walking along every shelf. There is a catalogue: each book has a card with its title, author and shelf number. Books are grouped into sections, science, history, stories, and a book that is too thick for one shelf may be split into volumes kept in different places, with a note saying where the next volume is. The librarian also keeps a list of empty shelf spaces for new books. A file system does the same job for a disk. The disk is just billions of numbered blocks; the file system turns them into named files and folders that you can open, save and organise. This lesson covers what a file is, how directories work, and how the OS decides which disk blocks belong to which file.

What a file is: A file is a named collection of related information stored on secondary storage. To the user, it is the smallest unit of storage: you cannot save data to disk except inside a file. A file can hold a program, a photo, a song, a spreadsheet or plain text. The OS does not usually care what is inside; it only manages the bytes.

File attributes: Besides its data, each file has attributes, also called metadata. Typical ones are: name, the human-readable label; identifier, a unique number used inside the file system; type, for systems that track it; location, a pointer to where its blocks are on the device; size; protection, who may read, write or execute it; and timestamps for creation, last modification and last access, plus the owner. On UNIX-like systems most of this is kept in a structure called an inode, while the name is kept in the directory.

File operations: The OS provides system calls to create, open, read, write, reposition within, which is called seek, delete and truncate files. Opening a file is important. Searching the directory for a file every time you read a few bytes would be slow, so open looks up the file once and adds an entry to an open-file table in memory. The call returns a small number, a file descriptor on UNIX or a handle on Windows, used in later calls. Each open file also has a current file-position pointer, so successive reads continue where the last one stopped. When a file is closed, its entry is removed.

Access methods: Sequential access reads or writes the file in order, one record after another, like playing a cassette tape. It is by far the most common, used by editors, compilers and media players. Direct access, also called random access, lets a program jump to any block by number, like jumping to any song on a phone; databases need this. Some systems build indexed access on top: a small index holds keys and pointers, so a program can find a record by searching the index and then jump straight to it.

Directory structures: A directory is a table that maps file names to file information. Different structures have been used.
