A single-level directory puts all files of all users in one list, so names must be unique, which becomes impossible with many users. A two-level directory gives each user their own directory. A tree-structured directory, used by every modern system, lets directories contain both files and subdirectories to any depth. Each file then has a path: an absolute path starts from the root, like /home/rina/notes.txt on Linux or C:\Users\Rina\notes.txt on Windows, and a relative path starts from the current directory, like notes.txt.

Acyclic graphs and links: Sometimes a file should appear in two directories, for example a shared project file used by two students. An acyclic-graph directory allows this using links. A hard link is a second directory entry pointing to the same inode; the file is only truly deleted when its last link is removed, which is tracked by a link count. A symbolic link, or shortcut, is a small special file that stores the path of another file; if the target is deleted, the symbolic link breaks. Cycles must be avoided, so most systems do not allow hard links to directories.

Mounting: A file system must be mounted before it can be used. Mounting attaches a device's file system at a point in the existing directory tree, called the mount point. On Linux, inserting a USB stick may mount it at /media/rina/USB, so its files appear inside that folder. Windows instead gives each volume a drive letter, like D:. Unmounting makes sure all pending writes are finished, which is why you should eject a USB drive before pulling it out.

File-system layout: On the disk, a file system keeps several structures. A boot control block can hold code to start the OS. A volume control block, called the superblock in UNIX, holds the number of blocks, block size, free-block count and pointers. A directory structure organises the files. And per-file control blocks, the inodes in UNIX, hold each file's details and block pointers. In memory, the OS keeps a mount table, a cache of recently used directories, a system-wide open-file table and per-process open-file tables.

Contiguous allocation: Now the core question: which disk blocks belong to which file? In contiguous allocation each file occupies a run of consecutive blocks. The directory just stores the start block and the length; a file starting at block 14 with length 3 uses blocks 14, 15 and 16. Both sequential and direct access are easy and fast, since block i of the file is simply start + i, and an HDD head barely moves. But it brings back the problems of contiguous memory allocation: external fragmentation as files come and go, and the difficulty of growing a file when the next block is already taken. Some systems use extents, contiguous chunks added as a file grows.

Linked allocation: In linked allocation each file is a linked list of blocks scattered anywhere on the disk. The directory stores pointers to the first and last blocks, and each block stores a pointer to the next one. There is no external fragmentation, and files can grow easily. But direct access is slow: to reach block 100 of a file, you must follow 99 pointers, each possibly a separate disk read. Pointers also use some space in each block, and if one pointer is damaged, the rest of the file is lost.

The FAT: A clever variation moves all the pointers into a single table at the start of the disk, the file allocation table, FAT, used by MS-DOS and still on many USB drives and memory cards today, often as FAT32 or exFAT. The table has one entry per disk block, holding the number of the next block in the file, or an end-of-file mark, or zero for free. Example: a file starts at block 217; FAT entry 217 says 618, entry 618 says 339 and entry 339 says end-of-file, so the file is blocks 217, 618, 339. Because the FAT can be cached in memory, following the chain is fast, which makes direct access practical.

Indexed allocation: Indexed allocation gathers all the pointers of a file into one index block. Entry i of the index block points to block i of the file. The directory stores the address of the index block. Direct access is fast, and there is no external fragmentation. The downside: even a tiny file needs a whole index block, and a large file may need more pointers than fit in one block. Solutions include linking several index blocks, or using a multilevel index, where the first index block points to second-level index blocks.

The UNIX inode, worked: UNIX file systems combine these ideas. Each inode holds, for example, 12 direct pointers, one single indirect pointer, one double indirect and one triple indirect. Suppose blocks are 4 KB and a pointer is 4 bytes, so one block holds 4,096 divided by 4 = 1,024 pointers. The 12 direct pointers cover 12 times 4 KB = 48 KB, so small files need no extra index blocks at all. The single indirect pointer points to a block of 1,024 pointers, covering 1,024 times 4 KB = 4 MB. The double indirect covers 1,024 times 1,024 times 4 KB = 4 GB. The triple indirect covers 1,024 cubed times 4 KB = 4 TB. Small files are quick, yet very large files are possible.

Free-space management: The file system must also track free blocks. A bit vector, or bitmap, uses one bit per block: 1 for free and 0 for allocated in the classic textbook convention, though some systems use the opposite. If blocks 2, 3, 4, 5, 8 and 9 are free in a small disk, the map begins 001111001100. It is simple and makes finding runs of free blocks easy, but it takes space: a 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks has 2 to the power 28 blocks, so the bitmap needs 2 to the power 28 bits, which is 32 MB. Other methods are a linked list of free blocks, grouping, which stores the addresses of n free blocks in the first free block, and counting, which stores a start block and the number of free blocks following it.

Journaling and consistency: If the power fails in the middle of an update, such as creating a file, which changes the directory, the inode and the free-space map, the file system may be left inconsistent. Old systems ran a slow consistency checker, like fsck on UNIX or chkdsk on Windows, scanning the whole disk after a crash. Modern journaling file systems, such as ext4 on Linux, NTFS on Windows and APFS on macOS, first write each set of changes as a transaction to a log, called the journal. Once the transaction is safely in the journal, the changes are applied. After a crash, the system only replays or discards the unfinished transactions in the journal, which takes seconds, not hours. Some file systems, like ZFS and Btrfs, use copy-on-write, never overwriting data in place.

Real-life example 1, the school library: Contiguous allocation is keeping each multi-volume encyclopaedia on one shelf in a row: easy to find any volume, but hard to add volume 13 if the next spot is taken. Linked allocation is each volume containing a note saying where the next volume is. The FAT is a single register at the front desk listing, for every shelf spot, where the following volume is. Indexed allocation is a card listing where every volume of the set is. The bitmap is the librarian's chart of empty shelf spaces.

Real-life example 2, your USB pen drive: A pen drive bought in a Dhaka computer shop usually comes formatted as FAT32 or exFAT, because Windows, macOS, Android and even smart TVs can all read it. FAT32 cannot hold a single file of 4 GB or more, which is why copying a big movie file sometimes fails with a "file too large" error even when there is plenty of free space; reformatting as exFAT or NTFS solves it. Your laptop's main drive, on the other hand, uses a journaling file system so a sudden power cut during load-shedding does not corrupt it.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often say deleting a hard link deletes the file; the data remains until the link count reaches zero. In inode problems, many forget that the number of pointers per block is block size divided by pointer size, or forget to add the direct blocks. Do not confuse the FAT with the bitmap: the FAT links blocks of files, while the bitmap tracks free blocks. Typical questions: list file attributes and operations; compare sequential and direct access; explain tree and acyclic-graph directories; compare contiguous, linked and indexed allocation; compute the maximum file size with an inode; compute bitmap size; explain journaling.

Recap: A file is a named collection of data with attributes such as name, size, location, protection and timestamps. Files are opened to get a descriptor, and accessed sequentially or directly. Directories are trees, with hard and symbolic links for sharing, and file systems are mounted into the tree. Contiguous allocation is fast but fragments; linked allocation avoids fragmentation but makes direct access slow, which the FAT fixes; indexed allocation uses index blocks. A UNIX inode with 12 direct pointers and 4 KB blocks covers 48 KB directly, 4 MB with single indirection and 4 GB with double. Free space is tracked by bitmaps or lists, and journaling keeps the file system consistent after crashes. Next lesson: I/O, protection, security and virtualisation, to wrap up the course.
key_points: A file is a named collection of data on storage, with attributes such as name, identifier, type, location, size, protection and timestamps.
Opening a file adds it to an open-file table and returns a descriptor; access can be sequential or direct.
Modern systems use tree-structured directories; hard links share an inode (deleted when the link count is zero), symbolic links store a path.
Contiguous allocation is fast but suffers external fragmentation; linked allocation avoids it but direct access is slow.
The FAT keeps all next-block pointers in one table; indexed allocation keeps a file's pointers in an index block.
A UNIX inode with 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers covers 48 KB directly, 4 MB single indirect, 4 GB double indirect, 4 TB triple indirect.
Free space is tracked with a bitmap (1 TB disk, 4 KB blocks: 32 MB bitmap) or free lists; journaling makes crash recovery fast.
lessons.tip: For maximum-file-size questions, first compute pointers per block = block size / pointer size. Then add direct blocks + p + p squared + p cubed, each multiplied by the block size, keeping units in powers of 2.
lessons.task: A file system uses 1 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers, and each inode has 10 direct pointers, one single indirect and one double indirect. Compute how much each part can address and the maximum file size. Then compute the bitmap size for a 64 GB disk with 1 KB blocks.

quiz.q: In a UNIX inode with 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers, how much data can the single indirect pointer address?
quiz.explain: One 4 KB block holds 4,096 / 4 = 1,024 pointers, each to a 4 KB block: 1,024 x 4 KB = 4 MB.

quiz.q: Which allocation method makes direct access slow because you must follow pointers block by block?
quiz.explain: In linked allocation each block points to the next, so reaching block i means reading the i blocks before it.

quiz.q: A file has two hard links. One link is deleted. What happens to the file's data?
options: It is moved to the root directory
It stays, because the link count is still 1
quiz.explain: The data is freed only when the link count drops to zero; the other hard link still points to the inode.

quiz.q: How big is the free-space bitmap for a 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks?
quiz.explain: 1 TB / 4 KB = 2^28 blocks, one bit each: 2^28 bits = 2^25 bytes = 32 MB.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a journaling file system?
options: After a crash, only unfinished transactions in the log need to be replayed or discarded
It removes the need for directories
It makes the disk spin faster
quiz.explain: Changes are first written to the journal as transactions, so recovery just checks the journal instead of scanning the whole disk.

lessons.title: I/O Systems, Protection, Security and Virtualisation
lessons.content:
A big hospital like Dhaka Medical College Hospital has many departments: the pharmacy, the lab, the X-ray room, the wards. The doctors cannot personally walk to the lab for every blood test; they send requests and get on with other patients, and the lab sends the result back when it is ready. Not everyone may enter every room: nurses can enter wards, only pharmacists can open the medicine store, and guards check who enters. And sometimes one building is divided so that several separate clinics run inside it, each believing it has its own space. An operating system does all three jobs: it manages slow I/O devices without wasting the CPU, it protects resources so each user and process can touch only what it is allowed to, and it can split one machine into several virtual machines. This final lesson covers I/O systems, protection, security and virtualisation, and then wraps up the course.

I/O hardware: Devices like keyboards, disks, network cards and printers connect to the computer through ports and buses, such as PCIe and USB. Each device has a device controller, a small piece of electronics with its own registers: a status register saying whether the device is busy or ready, a control register for commands, and data-in and data-out registers. The CPU talks to the controller by reading and writing these registers, either with special I/O instructions or through memory-mapped I/O, where the device registers appear at ordinary memory addresses.

Polling: The simplest way to wait for a device is polling, also called busy-waiting. The CPU repeatedly reads the status register until the device is ready, then transfers the data. If the device is fast and ready almost immediately, polling is efficient. But if the device is slow, like a keyboard waiting for a human, the CPU wastes millions of cycles asking "are you ready yet?" again and again.

Interrupts: The better way for slow devices is interrupts. The CPU starts the I/O and then goes on with other work. When the device finishes, its controller raises an interrupt signal. The CPU pauses, saves its state, and jumps to the interrupt handler for that device, using the interrupt vector to find it. The handler deals with the device, and then the CPU returns to what it was doing. Interrupts are what make multiprogramming practical: while one process waits for the disk, another uses the CPU.

DMA: Interrupts still have a problem for big transfers. If the CPU had to move every byte of a 4 KB disk block by itself, it would spend a lot of time copying. Direct memory access, DMA, solves this. The CPU gives a DMA controller the source, the destination in memory and the number of bytes, and the DMA controller moves the whole block directly between the device and memory. Only when the entire transfer is complete does it interrupt the CPU, once. The CPU is free for other work the whole time.

The kernel I/O subsystem: The OS provides several I/O services. Device drivers hide the details of each device behind a common interface, so the rest of the kernel can treat all disks alike. Buffering stores data in memory while it moves between devices, for example to smooth out speed differences between a fast network and a slow disk; double buffering lets one buffer fill while the other is being emptied. Caching keeps copies of frequently used disk data in memory. Spooling holds output for a device that can serve only one job at a time, like a printer: each print job is saved to a file, and the printer prints them one after another. I/O scheduling orders requests, as you saw with disk scheduling.

Blocking and non-blocking I/O: A blocking system call suspends the calling process until the I/O completes; it is simple to program. A non-blocking call returns at once with whatever data is available. An asynchronous call starts the I/O and returns immediately; the process is notified later when it finishes. Apps that must stay responsive, like a chat app that receives messages while you type, use non-blocking or asynchronous I/O, or multiple threads.

Protection versus security: Protection is about controlling access by processes and users to resources inside the system: which process may read which file, use which device, or call which kernel function. Security is about defending the system against attacks from outside and inside: thieves, viruses and intruders. Protection provides the mechanism; security uses it together with authentication, encryption and careful practice.

Principle of least privilege: A key guiding idea is the principle of least privilege: every program, user and system component should have only the privileges it needs to do its job, and no more. A music player does not need to read your banking app's files. A web server does not need to run as the administrator. If such a program is hacked, the damage is limited to what it was allowed to do. Modern phones follow this closely, asking your permission before an app can use the camera, microphone or location.

Domains and the access matrix: Protection can be described with an access matrix. Rows are domains, such as users or processes, columns are objects, such as files and printers, and each cell lists the access rights, such as read, write or execute. For example, domain D1 may have read on file F1, and D2 may have read and write on F2 and print on the printer. The matrix is mostly empty, so systems store it in parts. An access control list, ACL, stores each column with its object: file F2 keeps a list of who may do what to it. A capability list stores each row with its domain: like a set of keys a process carries, each one allowing certain access to certain objects.

UNIX permissions, worked: UNIX uses a compact form of ACL. Each file has an owner and a group, and three sets of rights, for the owner, the group and everyone else, each a combination of read r, write w and execute x. These are often written as three octal digits, with r = 4, w = 2 and x = 1. Example: rwxr-x--- means the owner has rwx = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, the group has r-x = 4 + 0 + 1 = 5, and others have nothing, 0, so the mode is 750. The command chmod 644 notes.txt gives rw- = 6 to the owner and r-- = 4 to the group and others: the owner can read and write, everyone else can only read. Linux and Windows also support full ACLs for finer control.

Security threats: Programs can be attacked in many ways. A buffer overflow happens when a program writes more data into a buffer than it can hold, overwriting nearby memory, such as the return address on the stack, which can let an attacker run their own code. Modern defences include non-executable stacks, address space layout randomisation, ASLR, which places memory regions at unpredictable addresses, and stack canaries. Malware includes viruses, which attach to programs; worms, which spread over networks by themselves; Trojan horses, which pretend to be useful programs; and ransomware, which encrypts your files and demands payment. Denial-of-service attacks overload a system so real users cannot use it.

Authentication and encryption: Before granting access, the system must know who you are, which is authentication. Passwords are the most common method; systems must never store them in plain text, but as salted hashes, so a stolen password file does not directly reveal passwords. Stronger methods add a second factor, like a one-time code sent to your phone, or biometrics, like a fingerprint. Encryption protects data in storage and on networks: symmetric encryption, like AES, uses the same key to lock and unlock, while public-key encryption, like RSA, uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock. Full-disk encryption, like BitLocker on Windows and FileVault on macOS, protects a stolen laptop's data.

Virtualisation: Virtualisation lets one physical computer run several operating systems at once, each in its own virtual machine, VM, believing it has its own hardware. A layer called the hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, manages the VMs. A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, like VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V and KVM in Linux; data centres and cloud providers use these. A type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a normal OS, like VirtualBox or VMware Workstation; students use these to try Linux inside Windows. Modern CPUs have hardware support, Intel VT-x and AMD-V, that makes VMs nearly as fast as real machines.

Containers: Containers are a lighter alternative. Instead of each VM having its own full OS kernel, all containers share the host's kernel, but each gets its own isolated view of files, processes and network, using kernel features like namespaces and control groups on Linux. Docker is the best known tool. Containers start in about a second and use little memory, so a server can run many of them. The trade-off is weaker isolation than full VMs, and all containers must use the same kind of kernel.

Real-life example 1, the hospital: The doctors are the CPU; sending a blood sample and attending to other patients until the lab calls is interrupt-driven I/O, while standing at the lab door asking "is it ready?" every minute is polling. The porter who carries a whole box of samples to the lab and back without bothering the doctor is DMA. The rules about who may enter which room are the access matrix, the guard checking ID cards is authentication, and splitting one building into several independent clinics is virtualisation.

Real-life example 2, your phone and the cloud: When a Bangladeshi startup runs its app on a cloud server, it does not get a whole physical machine; it gets a VM, or several containers, on a server shared with other customers, isolated by a hypervisor. On your phone, each app runs in its own sandbox with its own user ID, the principle of least privilege in action, and asks permission before reading your contacts. Your phone's storage is encrypted, so if it is stolen, the thief cannot simply read your photos.

Course wrap-up: Over this course you have seen the whole job of an operating system. It provides services and system calls, guarded by dual mode and interrupts. It runs programs as processes and threads, and shares the CPU using scheduling algorithms like FCFS, SJF, priority and round robin. It keeps cooperating processes safe with locks, semaphores and monitors, and handles deadlocks with prevention, avoidance through the banker's algorithm, or detection. It manages memory with paging, multi-level page tables, virtual memory and page replacement. It organises storage with disk scheduling, RAID and file systems, drives devices with interrupts and DMA, protects resources, defends against attacks and can even virtualise the whole machine. Every app you use relies on all of this every second.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up protection and security; protection is the internal mechanism, security is defence against threats. Remember that DMA interrupts the CPU once per block, not once per byte. In octal permissions, r is 4, w is 2 and x is 1, and the digits are in the order owner, group, others. Do not confuse type 1 hypervisors, on bare hardware, with type 2, on a host OS. Typical questions: compare polling, interrupts and DMA; explain buffering, caching and spooling; draw an access matrix and convert it to ACLs or capability lists; decode UNIX permissions; explain buffer overflow and its defences; compare VMs and containers.

Recap: Devices are controlled through controller registers; polling wastes CPU on slow devices, interrupts let the CPU work meanwhile, and DMA moves whole blocks with one interrupt at the end. The kernel I/O subsystem provides drivers, buffering, caching, spooling and scheduling. Protection follows the principle of least privilege and is described by the access matrix, stored as ACLs or capabilities; UNIX mode 750 means rwxr-x---. Security deals with threats like buffer overflows and malware, using authentication with salted password hashes and encryption. Virtualisation runs many VMs on one machine using type 1 or type 2 hypervisors, and containers share one kernel for lighter isolation. That completes the operating systems course.
key_points: Polling makes the CPU repeatedly check a device's status; interrupts let the CPU do other work until the device signals it is done.
DMA moves a whole block between a device and memory without the CPU, interrupting only once when the transfer finishes.
The kernel I/O subsystem provides device drivers, buffering, caching, spooling and I/O scheduling.
Protection controls access inside the system; security defends against threats. Follow the principle of least privilege.
The access matrix (domains x objects) is stored as access control lists per object or capability lists per domain.
UNIX permissions use r = 4, w = 2, x = 1 for owner, group and others: rwxr-x--- is 750, and 644 is rw-r--r--.
A type 1 hypervisor runs on bare hardware, a type 2 runs on a host OS; containers share the host kernel and are lighter than VMs.
lessons.tip: For UNIX permission questions, split the nine characters into three groups of three and convert each with r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. Writing the groups under the words owner, group, others prevents most mix-ups.
lessons.task: Write the octal mode for these permissions: rw-------, rwxr-xr-x and rw-rw-r--. Then draw an access matrix with two users and three files of your choice, and convert it into access control lists for each file.

quiz.q: Which technique lets a device move a whole block of data to memory and interrupt the CPU only once at the end?
quiz.explain: With direct memory access, the DMA controller transfers the block itself and raises a single interrupt when it is complete.

quiz.q: What does the UNIX permission mode 750 mean?
options: Owner rwx, group r-x, others none
Owner rw-, group r--, others r--
Owner r-x, group rwx, others none
quiz.explain: 7 = 4 + 2 + 1 = rwx for the owner, 5 = 4 + 1 = r-x for the group, and 0 = --- for others.

quiz.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
options: Every user should be an administrator
Programs should run with as many privileges as possible
Only the kernel may access files
Each program and user should get only the privileges needed for its job
quiz.explain: Giving only the needed rights limits the damage if a program or account is compromised.

quiz.q: A printer can only print one job at a time, so the OS saves each job to a file and prints them in order. What is this called?
quiz.explain: Spooling holds output for a device that can serve only one job at a time, queuing the jobs until the device is free.

quiz.q: How are containers different from virtual machines?
options: Containers each run their own full OS kernel
Containers share the host OS kernel, so they are lighter but less isolated
quiz.explain: Containers isolate processes, files and network using kernel features but share one kernel, so they start fast and use little memory.
